articles.title: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
articles.summary: There were violent clashes between demonstrators and riot police throughout Saturday in the capital Tirana.

blocks.text: Watch: The BBC reports from Tirana, where violent protests grew on Saturday
ByNick Thorpe
CorrespondentReporting fromTirana, Albania
Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row.
Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests.
The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time.
Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration.
Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street.
The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday.
During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard.
Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days.
Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic.
Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Demonstrators come equipped to clean tear gas from people's eyes

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Demonstrators come equipped to clean tear gas from people's eyes
Black smoke from a burning vehicle and the sirens of police cars and ambulances split the afternoon.
As dusk fell, police special forces arrived to reinforce the riot police.
Many people have been injured on both sides, 80 people have been charged with disorder so far, and hundreds more have been arrested, or are under investigation.
The centre of the Tirana looks increasingly like a war zone, scattered with broken glass and burnt debris.

George, a 19-year-old medical student who works as an electrician to fund his studies, stood near the burnt-out education ministry building, a scarf wrapped round his face and goggles covering his eyes.
He is one of the thousands who have taken part in the increasingly intense protests which began in early June.
In his gloved hands he clutched two rocks intended for the police.
Asked if he was concerned about injuring them, he said: "We have mothers too. We have family too.
"We were peaceful for 135 days. Now we are trying to do like in France… we are trying to make a revolution.
"Our government doesn't want peace, so we are using violence."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Klodi, 21 and Klea, 17, were among the young student protesters in Tirana on Saturday

blocks.text: Klodi, 21 and Klea, 17, were among the young student protesters in Tirana on Saturday
Many of the protesters were even younger. Klea, 17, is in her first year of university in Tirana.
She said: "All the students are boycotting their university classes and left school to fight for our rights."
She alleged there were provocateurs among the protesters, smashing up stores and banks, to discredit the demonstrations.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protesters and riot police fought running battles throughout the day in the centre of the capital

blocks.text: Protesters and riot police fought running battles throughout the day in the centre of the capital
Socialist Party Prime Minister Edi Rama has been in power for 13 years and has dominated Albanian politics, much like his main rival Sali Berisha, of the opposition Democratic Party, did for decades.
The students say they are against "the whole corrupt political class". So what is the alternative?
Osman Stafa, a prominent journalist for the News24 channel, who also describes himself as an activist for change, called for a "neutral, caretaker government for one year, to organise new elections".
The irony for the wider European community during this latest wave of unrest is that Rama has long been viewed favourably by the EU, which Albania aspires to join.
In a social media post on Saturday morning, he urged Albanian to "not forget that we have achieved extraordinary things".

He blamed the protests on the opposition Democratic Party, and on what he called "the sinister agenda of foreign actors, intent on halting our progress" towards EU membership, which he has promised by 2030.
He did not name which "foreign actors" he had in mind.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protesters threw bricks at police on the city's main boulevard

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Protesters threw bricks at police on the city's main boulevard
The latest protests have seriously tarnished Rama's carefully cultivated image as a charming leader, steering his country towards prosperity.
Parallel to the protests, a series of investigations by the special prosecution service also threaten his rule.
Set up under EU and US pressure in 2019, the prosecutors recently arrested the powerful secret service chief Vlora Hyseni.
She stands accused of helping a prominent businessman, former government official, and personal friend of Rama, Ergys Agasi, evade justice. The 39-year-old is under arrest.

Agasi, speaking through his lawyer, denied the allegations against him and said he had nothing to do with corruption. Hyseni told prosecutors that she contacted Agasi to try to recruit him to the intelligence services.
Several Albanian media outlets claim he acted as an intermediary between the prime minister and organised criminal groups.
Rama has admitted that he knows Agasi but denies any knowledge of illegal transactions.
"Edi Rama is caught between a rock and a hard place," Lutfi Dervishi, a political analyst and university lecturer, told the BBC.
"He's the victim of his own success. By concentrating so much power in his own hands, he has made himself the only person the people blame for their grievances."
Rama's Socialist Party has a comfortable majority, with 83 out of 140 seats in the Albanian Parliament. The next parliamentary elections are not due till 2029.

articles.title: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze as hundreds arrested after France protests
articles.summary: Disorder broke out in cities across the country on a day in which more than half a million joined cost of living protests.

blocks.text: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze as hundreds arrested after France protests
Image source, Getty Images
Demonstrators set fire to Lyon's local tourism office, according to the AFP news agency and local media
Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against education standards and the cost of living.
At least 400 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets.
In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds.
Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse.
Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeted against city halls and businesses also reported.

blocks.caption: Image caption, La Barrique bar in Paris was set on fire

blocks.text: La Barrique bar in Paris was set on fire
Sixty law enforcement officers were injured, including two who were taken to hospital unconscious, France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said.

In Paris, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC they were "pacifists" who are "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving".
However, as the day wore on some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles, including in iconic locations in the city centre like the Place de la République.
Shops were ransacked, at least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups.
Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A car was set alight at the Place de la République in Paris

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
A car was set alight at the Place de la République in Paris

In Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy" for the city, telling BFMTV "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building".
Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze.
Fire crews also battled the fire at Limoges town hall, which the local prefecture said caused part of the building to collapse.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Limoges town hall was "largely lost" in a blaze, the prefecture said

blocks.text: Limoges town hall was "largely lost" in a blaze, the prefecture said
A young man "had his hand blown off by a grenade" in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media, adding: "Such a tragedy should never have happened."
The interior ministry said the protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers.
Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence.
Clothes and food shops were raided in Paris, while an Apple store in Lille was broken into and emptied.
Footage authenticated by BBC Verify showed a tourist train in Grenoble being driven by masked men along a narrow street in the city centre towards at least three riot police officers.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Rapid-response riot police were deployed in Paris

blocks.text: Rapid-response riot police were deployed in Paris
Hundreds of thousands of students have protested in recent weeks over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées - secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.
On Saturday, their numbers were bolstered by trade union members and other protest groups.

These groups include the so-called gilets jaunes 'yellow vest' movement, who demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.
While France is no stranger to outbreaks of protest and disorder, this round comes as the country heads into a period of deep political uncertainty.

French President Emmanuel Macron will leave office next year and polls suggest April's presidential election could come down to a fight between the leader of the National Rally, Marine Le Pen, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the hard-left La France Insoumise party.
The latter took part in demonstrations in France and later accused police officers of "unleashing" on protesters, while condemning looting and arson.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Shops were looted in Paris, and other cities, during demonstrations on Saturday

blocks.text: Shops were looted in Paris, and other cities, during demonstrations on Saturday
Watch: 'The mood has really shifted' at the Paris student protests
France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said his comments were "dangerous and cynical".

He earlier said police had faced "violence of extreme intensity" and some groups were using the protests as a "warm-up" for the presidential elections, adding: "No-one will impose their political agenda through violence."
Le Pen said "legitimate demands" voiced by protesters had been "held hostage by the far left", accusing Mélenchon of fuelling the violence.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Police fired water cannon at protesters in the Place de la République, Paris

blocks.text: Police fired water cannon at protesters in the Place de la République, Paris
French President Emmanuel Macron said: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished."
The government has made apparent attempts at concessions, with Education Minister Édouard Geffray promising 3,000 extra supply teachers, during a television interview on 8 October.
However, the protests have continued and intensified.

articles.title: No action to be taken against wife of PM’s aide over Palestine Action post
articles.summary:
Tweet by Sarah Helm, wife of national security adviser Jonathan Powell, ‘does not meet criminal threshold’

No further action will be taken against Sarah Helm, the wife of the prime…

blocks.text: No further action will be taken against Sarah Helm, the wife of the prime minister’s national security adviser, after she was accused of supporting the banned protest group Palestine Action.
Helm, a journalist and author who is married to Jonathan Powell, posted on X on Thursday: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.”
The Metropolitan police said on Friday the post was “in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required”.
In an update on Saturday, a force spokesperson said: “On Thursday 15 October, we were made aware of a post on X relating to Palestine Action.
“The post was assessed by specialist officers and it was determined that it did not meet the criminal threshold. No further police action will be taken.”
Helm was responding on X to a discussion about the Irish author Sally Rooney, who has said she can no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for Palestine Action.
It is understood there was insufficient evidence that the post was capable of encouraging support for a proscribed organisation.
The ban, which began in July 2025, made membership or support of the direct action group a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
Downing Street has distanced itself from Helm’s remarks.
The Campaign Against Antisemitism (CAA) had called on the police to investigate.
after newsletter promotion
The group acknowledged that “spouses are entitled to independent views”, but said Helm’s post “raises extremely serious questions for Jonathan Powell and the government.
“Clearly, the police need to investigate and Sarah Helm must face the full force of the law, just like others who appear to express support for any proscribed terrorist organisation.”
Earlier, a government spokesperson said: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”

articles.title: At least 17 dead in crush at Hindu festival event in India
articles.summary: Many more have been injured at an event in the Indian city of Kolkata to mark a Hindu festival.

blocks.text: At least 17 people have been killed and many more injured in a crush at an event in the Indian city of Kolkata to mark the Hindu festival of Durga Puja, officials say.
The incident occurred during sudden rainfall, which witnesses say prompted a surge of people to try to seek shelter.
West Bengal's Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari said a seven-year-old girl was among the dead, and that 25 people were being treated for injuries.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi described it as a "tragic" incident and said the regional government was providing help to affected families.
Six of the dead have been identified, Adhikari said.

A senior police official told the AFP news agency that an announcement caused "commotion" after it started raining and the crowd started "pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede.".
Deadly crowd incidents, including during religious festivals, are not uncommon in India due to poor management and lack of adequate safety precautions.
Two years ago, 121 people were killed in Uttar Pradesh during a Hindu religious gathering.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar: The US Democrat targeted by Donald Trump
articles.summary: Donald Trump has described her as "garbage" and a "criminal" who does nothing but "bitch." Congress member Ilhan Omar has long been the target of angry verbal attacks from the US president. But why…

image.caption: Ilhan Omar has been the subject of repeated attacks by Donald TrumpImage: Richard Tsong-Taatarii/Star Tribune/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Ilhan Omar, whatever the hell her name is, with the little – with the little turban, I love her. She comes in, does nothing but bitch."

"Ilhan Omar is garbage. She's garbage. Her friends are garbage. […] These aren't people that work. These aren't people that say, let's go. Come on, let's make this place great. These are people that do nothing but complain."

"She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other. And she comes into our country, and she says, 'I have a constitutional right.' She's telling us about the constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet."

These are just three of Donald Trump's many attacks on US Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar. Few people have been targeted as ferociously by the US president. But why has Trump singled her out for such hostility?
Who is Ilhan Omar?

Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, 44, was born in Mogadishu, the capital of Somalia. She fled the civil war in the country while still a child, and spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She finally came with her family to the US in 1995, at the age of 12, and became a US citizen in 2000. She joined the Democratic Party, and made a career as a politician on the party's left wing. Since January 2019, she has served as representative for the state of Minnesota and one of the first two Muslim women to enter the US Congress.

Ilhan Omar is a practising Muslim who wears a hijab, and Congress altered a 180-year-old rule for her that prohibited head coverings in the chamber of the House of Representatives. Politically and socially, Omar champions progressive values, and often makes a connection between her faith and her commitment to social justice, human rights, and the protection of minorities.

Omar campaigns on issues such as universal health insurance, increasing the minimum wage, climate protection, and the cancellation of student debt. She is also one of Donald Trump's most prominent and outspoken critics, repeatedly accusing him of racism and systematically fomenting hatred against minorities, immigrants, and Muslims. She has frequently condemned raids by the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE), which she describes as a "militarized campaign of fear." She has also accused the president of corruption in office.

blocks.caption: Minneapolis, the capital of Minnesota, is home to the largest Somali community in the United StatesImage: Jessie Wardarski/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Criticism of Israel and accusations of antisemitism

Young, outspoken, female, Muslim, and a left-wing Democrat – politically, Ilhan Omar is almost the polar opposite of the 80-year-old Republican Trump. But she is also a controversial figure within her own party.

Omar is one of the fiercest critics of Israel in US politics, and has repeatedly called Washington's support for the country into question. She has been accused of antisemitism, and of supporting the movement BDS (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions), which encourages people to boycott Israeli businesses. Omar has defended BDS as a legitimate form of non-violent protest and freedom of expression. In 2019, she even introduced a resolution in the US Congress that aimed to strengthen the right of Americans to boycott, with a view to countering laws that restrict what the BDS movement can do.

In early 2023, Republicans removed her from the House Foreign Affairs Committee over a number of controversial tweets, including a comment she made in 2021 that seemed to equate the actions of the US and Israel with those of the Taliban in Afghanistan, and the Palestinian group Hamas. The latter is classified as a terrorist organization by the US and many other countries around the world.
Accusations of embezzlement and immigration fraud

Her critics also tried to link Omar to a corruption scandal in her home state of Minnesota. During the COVID-19 pandemic, around $250 million (€220 million) were misappropriated from a government-funded food program for children. Omar had previously called for the rules of the program to be eased.

Many of those convicted were from the state's Somali community, something that political opponents, including Trump, seized on to claim Omar was involved. No law enforcement authorities have ever accused her of any wrongdoing.

The most recent accusation against Omar concerns her immigration to the US. For years, her opponents have claimed that she made false statements during the procedure, even alleging that she entered into a fraudulent marriage with her biological brother to help him secure a US visa. On October 12, federal officials ordered a search of Omar's home, investigating allegations that Omar's father lied about her age on her immigration application.

blocks.caption: Officers from the Department of Homeland Security raided the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar on October 12, 2026Image: J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Controversial house search

Omar has repeatedly denied the accusations, describing them as part of a "campaign of political intimidation" and "an attempt to target political enemies." Several leading Democratic politicians have come to her defense, accusing the Trump administration of weaponizing the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security against its political opponents.

Former immigration officials told the Reuters news agency that it is extremely unusual for a house search to be conducted as part of such an investigation, as the government should already have all the relevant immigration documents.

Many see a raid on the home of a sitting member of Congress over a formality from 26 years ago as excessive, and have been especially critical of the timing of the raid, just three weeks before the Congressional elections in which Omar is standing for re-election.

The long-standing, unwritten "60-Day Rule" holds that authorities do not take any public action against political candidates in the two months before an election, so as not to influence the outcome. Critics see the fact that this practice has been ignored in Omar's case as amounting to election interference.
'Timing wildly suspicious' — Unpacking the search of Ilhan Omar's home
Other Muslim politicians also targeted

With the midterm electionslooming, Trump is battling with plummeting approval ratings, and Omar is not the only Muslim politician the president has been attacking. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate in the Senate election in Michigan, is another.

At a rally last Saturday in Tennessee, Trump said of El-Sayed: "I call him Mohammed. Somebody said, 'His name isn't Mohammed, it's Abdul.' I said, 'To me, it's Mohammed.' I'm the president. I can call him whatever the hell I want. To me, he's Mohammed, and he's a radical jihadist."

blocks.caption: Abdul El-Sayed is the Democratic Party's candidate to represent the state of Michigan in the US SenateImage: Emily Elconin/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: There is no intelligence whatsoever to suggest that El-Sayed has any extremist connections. The 41-year-old epidemiologist was born and brought up in Michigan. He went to university there, then won a Rhodes scholarship to Oxford, where he gained a doctorate in public health. For many years, he was the health director of the city of Detroit. Like Omar, he too belongs to the progressive left wing of the US Democratic Party.

During the election campaign, El-Sayed has repeatedly emphasized that he is not the one responsible for the rise in food prices, the expensive rents, and other political grievances. He has placed the blame squarely on what he describes as the failed policies of the administration in Washington.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: ICE agent who crashed into man in Texas was targeting suspect who died years ago, family says
articles.summary:
Federal officer slammed vehicle into a construction worker while pursuing a man who died in similar circumstances

A federal officer slammed a vehicle into a Houston…

blocks.text: A federal officer slammed a vehicle into a Houston construction worker and broke his leg, believing him to be a man who apparently died years ago, the dead man’s family said on Friday, further calling into question the account given by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The worker, 48-year-old Miguel Parra Hernandez of Mexico, remains hospitalized with multiple leg fractures and needs reconstructive ankle surgery, according to FIEL, a Houston-based immigration advocacy group. At a news conference on Friday, the group said the alleged suspect’s family had shared documentation proving his death.
After the episode on 10 October, ICE said in a statement that officers had observed a suspect they were targeting, identified as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, enter a vehicle with Parra Hernandez.
But on Friday, Rafael Lemaitre, spokesperson with the Harris county district attorney’s office, told the Associated Press that Mendoza-Cervantes was not in that vehicle.
ICE did not respond to requests for comment on Friday.

“ICE is lying,” said Cesar Espinosa, FIEL’s executive director. “Either somebody is not telling the truth or all of a sudden these two ICE agents have developed a sixth sense and are able to see dead people.”

ICE released a photo of a man it identified as Mendoza-Cervantes. But the man in the photo is actually Jose Hector Jimenez, who died years ago while being pursued by federal immigration authorities as he was trying to re-enter the US, according to FIEL.

The man’s daughter provided his death certificate from the Mexican government, which has been turned over to the district attorney, Espinosa told the AP. US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) did not respond to a request for comment.
Jimenez’s daughter, Jamie Jimenez, did not respond to requests for comment from the AP. Her husband, Andres Rendon, confirmed to the AP that Jimenez was his wife’s deceased father.

Criminal charges against the ICE officer who drove the vehicle are being considered by Harris county district attorney Sean Teare, who has said surveillance footage contradicts ICE’s claim that Parra Hernandez stepped in front of the vehicle.

The video shows a black SUV speeding over a median and driving toward a man who is running away. The video does not show the car hitting him – that view is blocked by another vehicle – but it shows the SUV inches from the fleeing man. The video then shows him on the ground.
US House member Sylvia Garcia, a Democrat who represents Houston, said that ICE appears to be lying about what happened.

“If ICE was pursuing a man who died years ago, it raises serious questions about how these operations are being carried out and whether agents are even verifying who they’re looking for before putting people’s lives at risk,” Garcia said in a statement to the AP. “It’s outrageous – but frankly, not surprising.”
ICE has been met with nationwide criticism throughout Donald Trump’s second presidency for its aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics.
Just in 2026, the second year since Trump returned to the White House, more than 30 people have died during interactions with immigration officials, the Guardian reported in late September.
Parra Hernandez’s attorney, Kim Bruno, told reporters that her client was suffering from depression in federal custody, especially after learning that he was not the target of the operation.
“This never should have happened in the first place,” Bruno said.

Miguel’s brother, Roberto Parra, said the two would work construction all day together and he just wants his brother treated with humanity. He said Parra Hernandez has a family to support, and his only crime was coming to a country out of necessity.
FIEL is seeking Parra Hernandez’s release before he is moved from a hospital to a federal detention center.
Nidia Delfín, the sister of Luis Enrique Delfín, who was detained in the ICE vehicle that hit Parra Hernandez, called for her brother’s release from federal custody so he could serve as a witness.
“He’s still very concerned, still very afraid,” she said. “He’s not the same guy that was out” before Parra Hernandez was struck on 10 October.
Guardian staff contributed

articles.title: Reform candidate filmed saying asylum seekers should be put in ‘concentration camps’
articles.summary:
Would-be MP recorded telling undercover reporter in ITV investigation that Muslims could not be British


A would-be Reform UK MP told an undercover reporter that Muslims could not be…

blocks.text: A would-be Reform UK MP told an undercover reporter that Muslims could not be British and asylum seekers should be put in “concentration camps”.
The comments were recorded as part of the undercover investigation by ITV that has already seen Reform accused of “appalling behaviour” and “extreme racism”.
Reform has said it had opened investigations where activists or members had “clearly behaved inappropriately”, adding there was “no room for racism” in the party.
In footage due to be broadcast on Sunday, a Reform activist and aspiring MP, who has yet to be publicly identified, described himself as “pretty hardline about Islam”.
He said: “If a Muslim’s prepared to de-convert, I’m happy.

blocks.caption: Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson has described himself as a ‘British Muslim patriot’. Photograph: Guy Corbishley/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

blocks.text: “But if they want to remain faithful to Islam, then this would be, I would have disagreements, especially with, um, I mean, as far as I understand, [Reform home affairs spokesperson] Zia Yusuf is a Muslim … to me … you cannot be a Muslim and British … it’s like oil and water.”

Discussing people crossing the Channel in small boats, the same activist said: “In the first week of election, build concentration camps, and everyone who comes across on the Channel, you’re in there.”
Excerpts from the investigation released earlier in the week included councillors and candidates within Reform using racist language.
In one excerpt, black children were referred to as “animals”, while in another a Reform member said his area had become “infested” with Asian families.
Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said Nigel Farage’s response to the revelations showed he was “completely unfit to lead”.
She said: “Bad apples don’t fall far from the tree. The sleaze, scandals and appalling revelations of racism and rank misogyny piling up by the day go right to the top of Reform UK.
“Nigel Farage is incapable of taking responsibility and getting his house in order because he himself shares culpability.”
Speaking earlier in the week, Farage said that while Reform carries out vetting “you can’t vet people for what they say in the future”.

In a statement to ITV, Reform said: “Reform UK has improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting.
“This is the same for all organisations. However good the vetting, one cannot vet a future comment.
“There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases.”
On Friday, Alan Feeney resigned as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after racist comments he had made were uncovered in the investigation.

blocks.caption: Alan Feeney resigned as Reform councillor after racist comments he made were uncovered. Photograph: ITV

blocks.text: ITV revealed secretly recorded footage of Feeney making racist comments about Asian homeowners, calling them “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”, during a local election campaign.

In a subsequent Facebook post, Feeney wrote: “There is no excuse for my comments. With responsibility comes accountability, and it is for that reason that I have resigned every post I hold on both Solihull borough council and Birmingham city council.”

He added: “My remarks were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable. They do not reflect the standards that the public rightly expects from an elected representative, and I take full responsibility for what I said.”

articles.title: Plover, not a fighter: masked lapwing nesting on Tasmanian cricket ground indifferent as play continues
articles.summary:
While masked lapwings have a reputation for swooping during nesting season, Windsor Park oval’s resident plover just wants a good innings

At Windsor Park in Riverside, just outside…

blocks.text: At Windsor Park in Riverside, just outside Launceston in northern Tasmania, a masked lapwing has claimed prime real estate in the middle of a community sports ground, showing complete indifference to the weekend cricket matches taking place around it.
Warming a nest of eggs, the bird has been affectionately dubbed “Faf Swoop Plessis” by locals – a play on former South African cricket captain Faf du Plessis.
Because the species is protected under state law, carrying fines of up to $21,300 for disturbing nests, ground staff have had to mow around the site, while players steer clear.
During a match early in the season, Great Northern Raiders player Caleb Brewer drew the short straw and was stationed directly beside the nest.
“At the start it was pretty weird, but towards the middle we kind of got used to it and the plover wasn’t too bad at the end,” Brewer told local paper The Examiner.
The following weekend, Riverside first-grade opener Josh Partridge was tasked with fielding near the plover, but reached a peaceful “mutual understanding”, according to The Examiner.

“It was like the plover knew there was a game of cricket going on,” he said. “We weren’t interfering with what was going on in its life, so it didn’t want to interfere with what was going on in ours.”
That kind of sporting truce is common, according to Mark Holdsworth OAM from BirdLife Tasmania.

“Lapwings will often become accustomed to the local patterns of people using a site and in many situations people modify their behaviour to avoid the core nesting area,” Holdsworth said. Everyone has learned to live with each other.”

While masked lapwings – widely known across Australia as plovers – have an intimidating call and reputation for swooping during spring nesting season, choosing a wide-open lawn is actually a calculated survival tactic.
Sports ovals are a “fantastic place” for them to nest, Holdsworth said, because unobstructed views mean parent birds can spot threats early.
Sean Dooley from BirdLife Australia also said that what looks like eccentric behaviour to humans makes sense for plovers.

“The places they choose to nest can seem crazy from our perspective, but there is logic to it,” Dooley said. “They like to nest out in the open so they can see danger coming and they rely on camouflage to hide their eggs and their chicks. So by nesting on an oval, they have a clear view in all directions.”
He said that when people give the bird a wide berth, lapwings generally realise they are not under threat.
“They definitely aren’t out to get us by nature, they really only care about making sure their chicks aren’t being threatened …

“Swooping isn’t their only tactic; they also put on a display that mimics having a broken wing to lure potential threats away. They’re just being good parents and doing all they can to protect their young.”

Lapwing eggs hatch after 28 to 30 days of shared incubation by both parents. If a clutch is infertile, incubation can continue for several weeks, while birds will often nest again at the same site if their eggs are destroyed.
after newsletter promotion
Once hatched, the chicks quickly leave the nest. Dooley said parent birds carry stray egg fragments away to avoid attracting predators, before guiding their offspring across the turf.
“If we can just give them their space, they can move away from the nest area once they are walking,” he said.
The West Tamar mayor, Christina Holmdahl, said council maintenance teams look after dozens of parks and sporting grounds across the municipality, encountering at least 10 nesting sites every year.

“Given the protected listing of the masked lapwings in Tasmania, our staff take their responsibility of looking after these birds very seriously and take extra precautions to protect the birds and any nests they find,” Holmdahl said.
Council workers maintain strict buffer zones around the birds and their nests when conducting maintenance.
“The plovers never act aggressively towards our staff on the ground,” she said.
The standoff coincides with the annual Aussie Bird Count which runs from Monday 19 October.

Now in its 13th year, the national citizen science project invites the public to record bird sightings to help researchers track how native species are coping with urban development and a changing climate. Last year, the Australian magpie was the most commonly spotted species, while the rainbow lorikeet recorded the highest overall tally.

“The count is a great opportunity to discover the birds that share your neighbourhood and understand more about them,” BirdLife Australia’s James Johnson said.” For many of us, that’s likely to include the amazing masked lapwing.”
Register for the 2026 count here.

articles.title: Almost all NSW homes destroyed in black summer bushfires were within 100 metres of flammable vegetation
articles.summary: Exclusive: Research confirms official advice about high-risk properties and warns worsening conditions will make more homes unsafe
articles.byline: Graham Readfearn Climate and environment correspondent

blocks.text: Almost every home destroyed in New South Wales during the black summer bushfires of 2019 and 2020 was inside the 100 metre buffer zone used to identify properties most at risk, new research has found.

The findings are an endorsement of the risk maps used by authorities, but the research warns that as global heating generates ever-worsening fire conditions firefighters may have to extend the recommended distances between homes and vegetation to keep homes safe.
The NSW rural fire service said the findings reinforced how homes in high risk areas should be built to higher fire standards as it prepared for a potentially “challenging” fire season.
More than 3,000 homes were lost across the country during the unprecedented fires six years ago that took 33 lives and killed or displaced almost 3 billion native animals.
Of the 2,475 homes lost in NSW, the research, published in the International Journal of Wildland Fire, found 94% were less than 100 metres away from flammable vegetation such as trees.

The 100 metre buffer is a key part of the widely used maps of bushfire prone land that firefighters use to plan local outreach activities, and planning authorities use to assess how bushfire-resistant new homes and renovations should be.

Associate professor Owen Price, an expert in bushfire risk at the University of Wollongong who led the research, said the findings showed a key aspect of the method to identify buildings at risk from bushfires was “more or less spot on”.
“That’s reassuring. Distance to vegetation is really important and that 100 metre rule that they apply is pretty good,” he said.
But the research also examined fire danger ratings – an index that combines temperature, wind, humidity and the dryness of fuel – on the days when each home was lost.
When the fire danger ratings – known technically as the Forest Fire Danger Index – reached extreme or catastrophic conditions, “houses further away [than 100 metres] were burning,” said Price.
“That’s a warning sign, because we know that index is going to get worse [from global heating]. We know the direction of travel.”

He said wildfire researchers were alarmed by the increasing number of fires around the world hitting and moving through urban areas, including the 2025 Los Angeles Eaton fire that killed 19 people and destroyed or damaged thousands of homes and businesses.
Part of his own research was aimed at understanding if similar events could be replicated in Australia.
“Being very close to another house [that is on fire] is another risk factor, which is why it’s important we stop houses from burning,” he said.
The research warned that the “current regulation may become less useful over time” as the climate crisis increased the risk of homes being lost.
after newsletter promotion

Melissa O’Halloran, responsible for work on bushfire planning at the NSW rural fire service, said the research showed that “houses in that [bushfire prone] area should be built to a higher construction standard”.
“The conditions in 2019 were extreme and outside what we would usually prepare for and, even under those conditions, our policy has stood up pretty well.
“This reinforces why we want people to have bushfire protection measures in place.”
O’Halloran said investigations carried out after previous fires had shown that not all residents knew they were actually living in a bushfire prone area.
Homes within bushfire prone land in the state are allowed to remove trees within 10 metres of a house and clear understory within 50 metres.
She said the service was reviewing its main bushfire protection policy that would consider the increasing climate risk.
“We’re seeing the impacts of climate change already. It isn’t just temperatures, it’s also about how quickly the landscape dries out, as well as extreme pyroconvective fires,” she said.
Inspector James Morris, of the NSW rural fire service, said there was already heightened risk this year for fires in northern parts of the state, in the central west and the far south coast.
“They’ve had high rainfall, and it does not take long for those fuels to dry out. It is important residents do their bit and prepare,” he said.
“We could be in for a challenging fire season.”

articles.title: Ontario to import U.S. electricity this winter, months after Ford threatened to cut power exports
articles.summary: Ontario will import power from the United States this winter, the province's independent electricity operator has announced, just a few months after Premier Doug Ford threatened to cut exports to the…

blocks.text: Toronto

Ontario will import power from the United States this winter, the province's independent electricity operator has announced, just a few months after Premier Doug Ford threatened to cut exports to the U.S. amid the ongoing trade war.
Province's electricity operator signs 6-month contract with U.S.-based Alpha Generation
Ontario set to import New York electricity this winter after Ford threatened to cut the U.S. off

The contract will help secure additional short-term capacity for the winter, while "facility maintenance" takes place, the Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO) said in an Oct. 1 news release about the deal.
The six month contract with U.S. based Alpha Generation for 600 megawatts will start on Nov. 1, IESO said.
While IESO did not detail the maintenance work taking place, the province began a multi-year refurbishment project at the Pickering Nuclear Generating Station in September.
The contract undercuts recent statements by the Ford government, according to Lewis Krashinsky, a postdoctoral fellow at Harvard University who studies U.S.-Canada politics.

IESO is an independent body that monitors the province's electric grid and is not associated with the provincial government. Despite that, Krashinsky said the contract will "undercut" Ford's position on using electricity as a bargaining chip with the U.S.
Ontario is exporting seven time more electricity to neighbouring jurisdictions than it did in 2025, said the IESO in an emailed statement. (Colin Butler/CBC)
"For all the tough talk, I think it doesn't look at all that good for Doug Ford," he said.

In August, Ford said he was willing to cut off electricity and critical minerals to the U.S. as the trade war drags on. Ontario sends power to about 1.5 million people in Michigan, New York and Minnesota.
"The best [Ford] can hope for is that this story doesn't hit too many American outlets," Krashinsky said.
"[If it reaches] the ears of senior American leaders, they're going to just say, 'Great, we're cancelling this contract or we're not taking you seriously, because you still need our energy too.'"
Contract part of 'normal' planning: IESO

Despite the new contract, Ontario is a "net-exporter of power," IESO said in an emailed statement Friday. IESO's mandate is to ensure a reliable and affordable supply of electricity for Ontarians, it said.
Ontario is exporting seven times more electricity to neighbouring jurisdictions, such as Quebec and New York, than it imported in 2025, IESO said.

The Alpha Generation contract is a part of "normal system planning" to secure additional short-term capacity as a way to manage "system-wide maintenance needs" and to cover peak demand over the winter months, IESO said.
CBC News asked Alpha Generation for more information on the deal.
The province did not respond Friday to questions on the contract, referring CBC News to IESO.
This Pickering, Ont., nuclear plant is getting a revamp
Province needs to invest in clean energy: expert

Keith Brooks, programs director for advocacy group Environmental Defence Canada, argues the province could have avoided importing electricity from the U.S. entirely by shifting to more clean energy sources in the past few years.
The Ford government cancelled several clean energy projects and removed the requirement to create a long-term energy plan when they first came into power, Brooks said.

"The government has mismanaged this file," he said, adding the province has become overly reliant on nuclear and gas systems that are expensive to maintain and have remained active "much longer than originally intended."
"The reality is we've been burning more and more gas in Ontario because we haven't been building clean energy," he added.

In the summer of 2025, the Ford government announced the province's first-ever integrated energy plan, which seeks to secure energy for "generations to come," according to a news release from June 12, 2025. The plan includes a commitment to nuclear energy, with the goal of reaching 99 per cent zero-emissions electricity by 2050.

items: Ford doubles down on 'kiss my ass' comment to Trump amid Canada-U.S. trade war
Ford doubles down on threat to cut off energy to U.S. amid spectre of trade war

blocks.text: Ford's threats on withholding energy are "idle," Brooks said, given the U.S. provides most of the gas Ontario uses for power.
"[The U.S.] could have shut off the gas, which meant we couldn't even turn our own lights on, let alone sell electricity to them," he said.
The solution is to invest more in clean energy, including wind and solar, Brooks said. Homegrown clean energy wins "hands down" for Brooks.
"We don't need to rely upon the U.S. to give us the gas nor the electricity. We can generate it here ourselves," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Arrthy Thayaparan is a writer at CBC Toronto with interests in health, climate, education and community stories. You can contact her at arrthy.thayaparan@cbc.ca.
With files from Gabriela Silva Ponte and Lorenda Reddekopp

articles.title: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
articles.summary: The Israeli military condemns the violence but the prime minister's office says it is part of a "smear" campaign.

blocks.text: A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys and called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating.
But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened and suggested it was part of a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel".
The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank.
The diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah.
They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest.
Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown.
The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle.
Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice.

"Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said.
"As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice.
"Impunity for violent settlers must end. Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them."

Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved.

But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security."
The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters."
"According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added.
But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack.
It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility".

A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible."

It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge".

Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence.
The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground.
"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."
"The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said.

articles.title: Israeli settlers attack European diplomats in West Bank
articles.summary:
French mayor and archbishop also attacked during violent attempt to stop Palestinians harvesting olives

Israeli settler militants have attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and the…

blocks.text: Israeli settler militants have attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of Cambrai in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank, injuring three people and damaging a car, in the latest violent attempt to prevent Palestinians from harvesting olives on their own land.

Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground on Saturday.

The masked militant shouted “Vive la France” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife, and Vincent Dollmann, archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.

The group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.

Settlers first attacked a group working on the lower slopes of hills near Taybeh. As well as stealing olives, they kicked, abused and assaulted a Palestinian woman in her seventies and beat a man so badly he needed six stitches for a head injury.

Then they approached the diplomats and Badoux, who was in Taybeh for the launch of a twinning agreement with his town in northern France. During the attack, the militants smashed the window of an armoured car belonging to the Belgian mission.

blocks.caption: The smashed window of mayor Badoux's car.  Photograph: Emma Graham-Harrison/The Guardian

blocks.text: Maxime Prévot, Belgium’s deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs, condemned the violence against Palestinians, foreign diplomats and journalists, and said his country would continue to push for European Union sanctions on settlers.

“Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack,” he said. “This violence cannot be separated from Israel’s illegal settlement policy … The occupation of the Palestinian territory must end.”

Palestinian residents of Taybeh have lived with years of escalating attacks from Israeli militants, but settlers had never targeted foreign diplomats there, said Father Bashar Fawadleh, the town’s parish priest.

“What happened today is not an isolated incident. It represents a deeply disturbing escalation in settler violence,” Fawadleh said. Since the start of the annual olive harvest in late September, Israeli militants have used violence to stop Palestinians bringing in a crop that is economically and financially vital to their communities.

Since 27 September, settlers have launched more than 170 attacks, Israeli rights group Yesh Din said. They killed at least four people, injured more than 100 and damaged thousands of trees, according to Palestinian authorities.
Even the presence of Israeli activists, diplomats, senior clergy and journalists no longer serves as a deterrence to extreme violence.

“If such violence can take place before international witnesses, one must ask what protection remains for local families and farmers when those witnesses are no longer present,” Fawadleh said. “No individual should have to risk physical assault simply to harvest olives from their own land.”

On Friday, Israeli militants attacked and severely injured Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine as she reported on the harvest in the town of Abu Falah. She required surgery on Saturday morning and is now in “moderate” condition, according to a spokesperson for Israel’s Beilinson hospital where she is being treated.

Israel had already severely restricted the harvest this year by imposing new rules barring Palestinians from trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.

Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, condemned the attacks and said police had opened an investigation. He said foreign diplomats risked attacks from Israeli civilians if they travelled in the occupied West Bank without military coordination.

Demanding diplomats give advance notification of travel violates both diplomatic conventions international law, said one western diplomatic source who asked not to be named. “Israel is in charge of security in Area B and C (the majority of the West Bank), so is obliged to assure safety there for all,” the source said.

A culture of near total impunity for Israeli violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has prompted former prime minister Ehud Barak to call for the international criminal court to intervene.

Gadi Eisenkot, an opposition politician and former general hoping to unseat prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu in elections held later this month described the attack as “Jewish terror under the auspices of the Israeli government”.

Eisenkot backs Jewish Israeli expansion in occupied Palestine but wants militant violence brought under control because the attackers are “harming the settlement enterprise in [the West Bank] and national security”.

articles.title: Do Alberta’s temporary residents pay little tax, reap lots of benefits? We asked economists
articles.summary: The province has been sharing a lot of big dollar figures in the lead-up to the Oct. 19 referendum — many of them supporting the claim that temporary residents pay little in taxes compared to what…

image.caption: The provincial government says it estimates the total provincial taxes paid annually by temporary residents to be $150 million. It estimates the same group costs the province over $1 billion annually in health, education and other social services. (Graeme Roy/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: The province has been sharing a lot of big dollar figures in the lead-up to the Oct. 19 referendum — many of them supporting the claim that temporary residents pay little in taxes compared to what they get out of provincially funded public and social services.
“For every $1 of taxes a guest worker generates, taxpayers are covering $10 in services. This is not sustainable,” one social media post from Alberta Premier Danielle Smith reads.

The provincial government says it estimates the total provincial taxes paid annually by temporary residents to be $150 million. It estimates the same group costs the province over $1 billion annually in health, education and other social services.
The province clarified to CBC News via an emailed statement that the $150 million figure only reflects the income taxes paid to the province by non-permanent residents in Alberta.

But since that figure does not include federal income taxes paid by non-permanent residents, economists specializing in tax policy and public finance say that calculation doesn’t capture the full picture.

items: What you need to know about Alberta referendum questions 2, 3 and 4 on immigration
Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: Gillian Petit, an economist at the University of Calgary, studies tax and transfer policies in Canada and Alberta, focusing on groups that are overlooked in tax discussions. She says it’s critical to consider federal income tax contributions in these comparisons because Ottawa gives a portion of federal income tax to the province through federal transfers, which then help fund public services.
Crunching the numbers herself, Petit estimates that in 2025, non-permanent residents in Alberta paid at least $835 million in provincial and federal taxes.

And Petit says $835 million is likely a conservative estimate, because it only accounts for working age, non-permanent residents and relies on 2020 incomes and 2020 dollars (so it does not include wage growth or inflation since then).

Gillian Petit, an economist at the University of Calgary, studies tax and transfer policies in Canada and Alberta, focusing on groups that are overlooked in tax discussions. (Submitted by Gillian Petit)

Her calculation also leaves out payroll taxes such as the Canada Pension Plan and Employment Insurance contributions, and sales taxes such as the GST, fuel and other commodity taxes, and property taxes, which non-permanent residents also pay.

“I think people need these numbers … to be able to make a good decision on the referendum,” Petit said. “Social media posts are only so long and you can [only] stick so much in them. It's really important to qualify a lot of those numbers.”

items: Everything you need to know about the 10 questions in Alberta's Oct. 19 referendum

blocks.text: Ron Kneebone, a professor emeritus in economics at the University of Calgary, says it’s also important to remember that temporary residents are subject to the same tax rules as Canadian citizens and permanent residents, under Canada’s progressive income tax system.
“The tax system is blind to your religion, your skin colour, your date of arrival in Alberta,” Kneebone says.
That means tax rates are split up into income brackets. The higher a bracket someone is in, the more in taxes they pay — and that’s true regardless of immigration status.
Ron Kneebone, a professor emeritus in economics at the University of Calgary, pictured here in 2018. (Robson Fletcher/CBC)

“When the government tells you that newly arrived immigrants are paying much less in taxes than they are receiving in terms of government services, I just want to emphasize to you that that's true for every single adult Albertan,” Kneebone said.
He said the government’s messaging is “a little bit disingenuous.”
The premier’s office did not respond to CBC’s question on why temporary residents' federal tax contributions are not included in the province's estimates.
How much do temporary residents cost in public, social services?
Then, there’s the $1-billion figure: the provincial government’s stated cost of providing health, education and social services to temporary residents.

Using Statistics Canada data, the province based its calculations on having an estimated 281,857 non-permanent residents in Alberta as of the fourth quarter of last year. This number has since been updated by the federal agency to around 292,000.
Alberta Education estimated “the operational cost of providing education to the approximately 45,544 children of temporary residents to be $600 million.”
The remaining $400 million is attributed to health care, but the government’s referendum website notes “health costs are less precise to track.”

The province arrived at that number by reviewing “direct costs they track and found that 1.27 per cent of costs was for temporary workers and international students,” who make up the bulk of non-permanent residents.
Non-permanent residents made up about 5.8 per cent of Alberta’s total population at the end of 2025.

The “non-permanent resident” category includes those on work, study and other temporary permits, plus asylum seekers — the latter group receives limited access to health care through a federal program, not a provincial one.
Are ‘guest workers’ getting $10 in services for every $1 they pay in taxes?

On the province’s claim that taxpayers cover $10 for every $1 a “guest worker” pays, a government spokesperson said it included “increased capital costs such as [school] spaces for approximately 45,544 children of temporary residents” in its calculation.
“For example, the province is spending $8.6 billion to build and renovate more than 100 schools across the province,” the spokesperson said.
“Given 45,000 additional students of temporary residents have [come] to our province, this requires larger spending on school capital needs.”

For every $1 of taxes a guest worker generates, taxpayers are covering $10 in services. This is not sustainable. Albertans have paid into their schools, hospitals and services their whole lives. It should be there for them when they need it. That is why Albertans are backing our referendum questions on changes to immigration. This poll shows a supermajority now want Alberta setting its own immigration levels and ensuring that guest workers contribute to the costs they incur in our health care and education systems. Just as any Albertan would expect if they were a guest in another country. Read the fully story: https://t.co/VjYEpLKn2J—ABDanielleSmith

Petit says the challenge in quantifying how much non-permanent residents reap in services is that the exact data on costs is not publicly available — if it is collected at all. But, she says, the numbers can be put into context.

For example, temporary residents typically skew younger than the rest of Canada’s population, so “it's also likely that their use of health care is lower than Canadian citizens, again, on a per person basis,” Petit said.
Statistics Canada reported about 60 per cent of non-permanent residents were between 20 and 34 years old, based on the 2021 census.

Petit points out that non-permanent residents are not eligible for all the same provincially-funded social support programs that citizens and permanent residents are, and are therefore paying into a system that does not allow them to access certain supports. Take Assured Income for the Severely Handicapped and Family Support for Children with Disabilities as two examples.

And while work and study permit holders and asylum claimants may be eligible for the Alberta Child and Family Benefit, they must first qualify for the federal Canada Child Benefit, which requires that someone has lived in Canada for 18 consecutive months, according to Petit’s report with the Muttart Foundation.

“Roughly speaking, our income taxes that we pay in Alberta cover about half the cost of health care. So again, am I [a Canadian citizen or permanent resident] somehow a slacker because my taxes don't cover the cost of health care, never mind education, social assistance?” Kneebone said.
“No, that's just the way the system is set up. And we are fortunate in Alberta and able to access a lot of oil and gas royalties that can pay the difference.”

articles.title: Romanian fighter jets shoot down 2 drones over Black Sea
articles.summary: Romanian Air Force F-16s shot down drones over Romanian territorial waters. Earlier this week, two chemical tankers were hit by drones near Romania's Black Sea coast.

image.caption: F-16 fighter jets of the Romanian Air Force engaded drones over the country's territorial watersImage: Vadim Ghirda/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Romanian F-16 fighter jets have shot down two drones over the country's territorial waters, according to the Romanian Defense Ministry.

"Two drones were engaged and shot down a few minutes ago by Romanian military pilots over the Black Sea, moments after they had illegally entered our country," Defense Minister Radu Miruta wrote on Facebook.
So far, no information has been released regarding the country of origin of the drones.
What do we know about the incident?
F-16 fighter jets shot down the drones some 20 kilometers (13 miles) southeast of Sulina.
"The first drone entered national airspace at 17:59 (14:59 GMT) and was shot down within two minutes," Miruta said.
He added that the second one was shot down at 6:05 p.m., five minutes after entering Romanian airspace.
"The Black Sea will be safe again," Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu wrote on X. She added that NATO will discuss the issue at a North Atlantic Council meeting on Tuesday.
Drone attacks endanger navigation in the Black Sea
This drone incursion is the latest in a series of incidents believed to be a result of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In October, several drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea were reported off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria.
The most recent attack occurred on Thursday, when two chemical tankers were attacked off Romania's coast, leaving seven crew members missing.
Both vessels were anchored near the Sulina Canal, which connects the Danube River to the Black Sea. The canal serves as an export route for Ukraine.
Romania, an EU and NATO member, shares a 614-kilometer (381-mile) border with Ukraine, part of which is along the Danube.
The country has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions into its airspace since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Romania began shooting down these drones earlier this year.

articles.title: Egypt's Ssisi says he'll defend Saudi Arabia, if asked
articles.summary: The Egyptian president said his country was ready to defend Saudi Arabia "if requested." The comments come amid escalating Houthi attacks.

image.caption: Egypt's parliament will hold an emergency session on Sunday to consider whether to authorise potentially assisting in Saudi Arabia's defence.Image: Fatih Mubarok/AFP

blocks.text: Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sissi on Saturday said that his country stood ready to defend Saudi Arabia, if asked to so.
Sissi said that while Egypt was "not looking for a role to play" in regional conflicts, it was "inconceivable that we would allow Saudi Arabia, ⁠its security ⁠or stability to be harmed."
The comments came as Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi targets, including strikes on energy facilities and Riyadh's main airport.
'We are speaking only about defense,' says Sisi

"Egypt, of course, with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, will carry out any measure to protect you or defend you," Sissi said at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian military academy.
"I'm not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone," Sissi said. "We are speaking only about defense."
"I know this ​requires the approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I ask that an emergency session be held so that it can give us that ⁠authorization ​if we are asked," the Egyptian leader said.
An emergency session in Egypt's parliament is expected to be held on Sunday to consider whether to authorise potentially assisting in Saudi Arabia's defence.
Saudi Arabia on the backfoot in the war against the Houthis
Houthi-Saudi conflict
The Houthis have clashed with Saudi Arabia since the kingdom stepped into Yemen's civil war to lead a military coalition against the Iran-backed fighters in 2015.
The Houthis have launched repeated attacks against Saudi Arabia, also attacking the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
A week ago, one of those attacks killed 13 people in what was the deadliest in the country in over a decade.
Egypt and Saudi Arabia share strong strategic and economic ties. Egypt was part of the Saudi-led coalition that stepped in 2015 to support the Yemeni government against the Houthis.
Disruption in the Red Sea as a result of Houthi attacks has impacted the revenue coming from shipping traffic in the Suez Canal.
