articles.title: West Bank: Israeli settlers attack EU diplomats, French mayor
articles.summary: A group of Israeli settlers attacked vehicles carrying European diplomats in the West Bank. Belgium has condemned the attack.

image.caption: The olive harvest this year has been marked by a high level of violence in the occupied West Bank [FILE: October 16, 2026] Image: Ammar Awad/REUTERS

blocks.text: Belgium's Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said on Saturday that masked settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank had attacked Palestinians, Catholic representatives, and Western diplomats and officials.
Prevot said that the Belgian consul general and French and Polish diplomats, as well as a French mayor, were among those attacked.
In a post on X, he condemned "in the strongest terms" the attack in which a Belgian vehicle was also damaged.
Israeli police said they have opened an investigation into the alleged assault of diplomats in the occupied West Bank.
In a separate statement, the Israeli military said the visit was not coordinated with them and there were no soldiers present.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office reacted to the incident by criticizing an alleged a "smear" campaign against settlers.

"These reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge," his office said in a statement, using the biblical name for the West Bank.
What do we know about the incident
According to witnesses, cars from the French, Belgian, and Polish embassies had brought diplomats to visit Taybeh, a predominantly Christian village in the occupied West Bank.
Settlers then descended upon the area to prevent Palestinians from gathering olives.
Masked men reportedly surrounded a diplomatic vehicle with their off-road vehicles, then demanded identification and smashed a window.
A witness and two diplomats also told the AFP new agency that the settlers beat up Bernard Baudoux, the 78-year-old leftist mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, a town in northern France.
West Bank olive harvest under attack
French mayor says attackers were 'completely enraged'
Badoux told AFP that he was fine, having suffered minor injuries, but he expressed concern about the residents in the area.
"The whole world needs to know what's happening there," Badoux said.

Badoux said he was visiting Taybeh with the French consul general in Jerusalem, along with a priest from his home parish, to sign a goodwill cooperation agreement with his city, which has an olive emblem.
The mayor, who was wearing a sash in the French tricolour, said that the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground.
"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."
"It's absolutely incredible that settlers can behave like this," he said. "I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government," he added.
Israel FM condemns 'rioters'

In a rare statement critical of settlers, which was released before Netanyahu's statement, Israel's foreign minister condemned the attack by Israeli "rioters" on the European diplomatic delegation in the West Bank.

"I strongly condemn the severe acts of violence by Israeli rioters in the area of Taybeh," said Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, who also faulted the diplomats for not coordinating with the Israeli military.
The West Bank has experienced an especially violent olive harvest season this year. Israeli settlers have tried to stop Palestinians from harvesting their crops by using physical force.
Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine was injured on Friday when she was attacked by a group of Israeli settlers while reporting in the occupied West Bank.

This violence is occurring during the final days of the election campaign. In hopes of gaining their support in the upcoming election, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has championed the cause of the settlers.
Netanyahu's final campaign? — Israel heads to the polls

articles.title: Revealed: French police used UK-funded 4x4 vehicles to charge student protesters
articles.summary:
French government launches investigation into why cars funded by UK to prevent asylum seekers crossing Channel were used in school protests

French police have used 4x4 vehicles paid for by…

blocks.text: French police have used 4x4 vehicles paid for by British taxpayers to charge at student protesters during the school protests that have swept the country.

The French government has confirmed that an investigation has been launched into why the cars, funded by the UK government specifically to prevent asylum seekers crossing the Channel, were used during a protest involving school students in Dunkirk.

School protests have been taking place across France for a third week with an estimated 160,000 people involved, with protesters raising concerns about crumbling schools and teacher shortages. Demonstrators have criticised policing tactics after teargas was fired at protesters in two areas.

The incident involving the UK-funded 4x4, a land cruiser known as Masstech VEZI (Vehicule d’Eclairage de Zone d’Intervention), was reported by French media outlet BFM TV on 10 October. The report included footage of the VEZI driving at speed, reversing backwards then driving forwards again with a bin caught under the vehicle’s front wheel and dragged along. Students can be heard screaming and scattering from the path of the vehicle.

blocks.caption: French police use UK funded 4x4 vehicle during student protest in Dunkirk

blocks.text: According to reports, a 14-year-old girl was injured by the vehicle and was taken to hospital, sustaining a haematoma. She was later discharged from hospital. She is now recovering, but she told reporters that what happened to her was “unacceptable”.

The VEZI was earmarked for UK-funded operations on French beaches to stop asylum seekers boarding dinghies, part of an Anglo-French border agreement signed in January 2018 and known as the Sandhurst treaty.

This treaty specifies cooperation between France and the UK in combating irregular immigration and secures UK financial support for French efforts through the “Sandhurst funds”. These funds enable France’s National Gendarmerie (police service) to acquire additional resources such as all-terrain vehicles suited to dunes and beaches, including the VEZIs, which are reinforced with grilles.

According to a recent French parliamentary cross-party inquiry into Anglo-French border agreements known as Le Touquet, nine of these specialised VEZI vehicles have been bought under the terms of the Sandhurst treaty. The inquiry report states that to be eligible for Sandhurst funding the equipment must contribute directly to combatting illegal migration in the UK.

A spokesperson from the office of Laurent Nuñez, France’s minister of the interior, when asked why a vehicle funded by the UK and specifically earmarked for border control was used to counter a schools protest, said: “We can confirm the opening of an investigation into this.”
Sources close to the investigation said: “I don’t think the British are aware that their money is being used to beat French kids.”
Another expressed concern about the expanding militarisation of French policing to support authoritarian policies.

A spokesperson for Utopia 56, a French association that provides support to asylum seekers in northern France, said: “In Dunkirk, the 4x4 that ploughed into high school students during the protests is a vehicle funded by the British Sandhurst fund – money earmarked for combating Channel crossings. The practice of using 4x4s to chase people in the student protest is the same one used on the beaches.

“Disproportionate force is employed to silence, intimidate, and deter. The repressive tactics being tested at the border to prevent crossings should serve as a warning to everyone. These are surveillance, control and repression methods that will be replicated in other contexts. The incident involving the vehicle in the student protest is proof of this.”
The UK Home Office declined to comment.

articles.title: DOH readies hospitals for El Niño patient surge
articles.summary: In anticipation of an influx of patients due to an intensified El Niño, the Department of Health is preparing to temporarily assign hospital personnel from other departments to provide medical…

blocks.text: October 18, 2026 | 12:00am
DOH Assistant Secretary Tagumpay Maniquis said the agency has a surge plan that allows hospitals to deploy additional staff when needed.
THE STAR / Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — In anticipation of an influx of patients due to an intensified El Niño, the Department of Health is preparing to temporarily assign hospital personnel from other departments to provide medical attention to patients suffering from heat-related illnesses.
“We have a surge plan for this. There are hospital personnel we can assign for this kind of situation,” Maniquis said. “If early on, we can see the trend, we can activate the surge plan.”
Maniquis said the DOH is also monitoring other illnesses that may be triggered by heat aside from heat exhaustion and heat stroke, including asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
The DOH earlier announced plans to establish dedicated fast lanes in hospital emergency rooms for patients with heat-related illnesses as El Niño intensifies.
Hospitals have also been instructed to prepare for an increase in emergency room consultations and activate the special lanes when necessary.
Meanwhile, the Department of Labor and Employment said workers who sustain heat-related injuries while on duty may claim compensation through the Employees’ Compensation Commission.

articles.title: Lacson hits minority senators for unfair vote in Tulfo case
articles.summary: Sen. Panfilo Lacson described as unfair the move of three minority senators who opposed the Senate Electoral Tribunal’s ruling that dismissed the quo warranto petition against Lacson’s…

blocks.text: October 18, 2026 | 12:00am
Members of the Senate Electoral Tribunal pose for a photo on Friday during a meeting to discuss the quo warranto petition against Sen. Erwin Tulfo.
Sen. Robinhood Padilla Facebook page

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Panfilo Lacson described as unfair the move of three minority senators who opposed the Senate Electoral Tribunal’s ruling that dismissed the quo warranto petition against Lacson’s fellow majority member Sen. Erwin Tulfo.

Lacson was reacting to news that the SET on Friday met and dismissed the quo warranto petition seeking the removal of Tulfo as senator over citizenship issues, with six members voting in favor and three against.
Sens. Robin Padilla, Camille Villar and Pia Cayetano reportedly voted against the majority decision.

“Senate Electoral Tribunal: Justice and fairness went out of the window when three minority senator-members voted in favor of an out-of-time motion for reconsideration filed by a petitioner without legal standing,” Lacson posted on X.
“Their motive may be deeper than personal issues against Sen. Tulfo,” he added.

Members of the SET composed of senators and Supreme Court justices met at the Senate on Friday to deny the motion for reconsideration filed by the petitioner Berteni Causing for being filed beyond the prescribed period and for failing to comply with filing and service requirements of the SET rules.

Causing’s appeal had sought to reverse the SET resolution dated March 2 summarily dismissing his quo warranto petition for being insufficient in form in his allegations that Tulfo was ineligible to be senator for not being a Filipino citizen and belonging to a political dynasty.
According to a press release signed by SET secretary Luis Jose Geronimo, six members of the SET voted in favor of denying the appeal while three voted against.
Lacson lauded the three Supreme Court justices and three other senators who based their decision on the procedural flaws of the petition.

“More on the Senate Electoral Tribunal: Let’s give credit to the three SC justice-members and the other three senator-members who undoubtedly knew the obvious procedural flaw which resulted in a 6-3 vote, thus dismissing the motion for reconsideration,” Lacson said.
Supreme Court Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen chairs the SET, with fellow SC Justices Henri Jean Paul Inting and Ramon Paul Hernando as members.
Cayetano, Padilla and Villar sit in the SET for the minority bloc, while Sens. Kiko Pangilinan, Bam Aquino and Lito Lapid sit for the majority.
Reporters sought the minority senators’ side for their reaction yesterday but they have yet to issue a statement.

articles.title: ‘VP could still be convicted outside impeachment’
articles.summary: The evidence uncovered on Vice President Sara Duterte’s alleged misuse of confidential funds could still lead to her criminal conviction, according to House prosecution panel spokesman Rep. Zia…

blocks.text: October 18, 2026 | 12:00am
In this photo uploaded on Facebook on March 19, 2026 shows Vice President Sara Duterte at the 54th Datu Bago Awards Conferment 2026 in Davao City.
Vice President Sara Duterte via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — The evidence uncovered on Vice President Sara Duterte’s alleged misuse of confidential funds could still lead to her criminal conviction, according to House prosecution panel spokesman Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong.
He cited as basis the Commission on Audit’s notice of disallowance of P73.287 million in confidential expenses incurred by the Office of the Vice President in December 2022.

Adiong said the COA findings could be used as basis for the filing of criminal cases against the Vice President, adding that the audit development strengthened rather than weakened the prosecution’s assessment of the confidential funds evidence.
“That will only prove that there was really prima facie evidence of misuse of public funds to benefit one’s interest or oneself,” he said.

During the impeachment trial, the prosecution presented witnesses and documents involving acknowledgment receipts, the transfer of confidential funds to security officers and compliance with government rules governing confidential expenditures.

However, the prosecution ultimately decided to drop Article I, along with two other Articles of Impeachment, which Adiong said removed a possible additional route to conviction before the Senate impeachment court.

The prosecution said it only needs one conviction to carry the constitutional consequences it seeks against Duterte and decided to concentrate on Article II, which accused the Vice President of amassing unexplained wealth.

articles.title: Infrastructure funds eyed for additional education budget
articles.summary: The Senate is looking to strip funding from controversial infrastructure projects to finance the Department of Education request for an additional P149.67 billion, including P15.6 billion for a…

blocks.text: October 18, 2026 | 12:00am
Education Secretary Sonny Angara answers questions from senators during the agency’s budget hearing for fiscal year 2027 before the Senate committee on finance subcommittee B.
Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate is looking to strip funding from controversial infrastructure projects to finance the Department of Education (DepEd)’s request for an additional P149.67 billion, including P15.6 billion for a remedial learning program that remains without a dedicated budget.
During a Senate finance subcommittee briefing on Friday, DepEd requested an additional P147.93 billion, while six attached agencies sought P1.74 billion.
The House of Representatives previously approved a P969.79-billion budget for the education sector, P6.17 billion lower than the proposed National Expenditure Program (NEP).
Senate finance subcommittee chairman Sen. Bam Aquino proposed redirecting funds from controversial infrastructure projects to education, including feeding programs and classrooms.

“In 2025, we gave zero budget to flood control. At that time, it was mired in controversy and still mired in controversy until now,” Aquino said. “Let’s strip those projects of their funding and put it into feeding programs and classrooms. Let’s make the welfare of our youth a priority in our budget.”
The proposal comes amid renewed efforts to address the country’s learning crisis and strengthen school security following recent incidents of violence on campuses that led to the deaths of students.

If approved, the additional funding sought by DepEd would cover personnel improvements, school security upgrades such as perimeter fences and metal detectors and the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) program.
P15.6 billion for ARAL
DepEd Secretary Sonny Angara specifically requested P15.6 billion for ARAL, which seeks to help students struggling with key competencies catch up with their peers.
“We know from international assessments and from national assessments that we have been doing very poorly over the years,” DepEd Undersecretary Carmela Oracion told the panel.
“So now we have a clear basis for a program that will provide remediation for reading, for mathematics and for science. Unfortunately, the law is unfunded,” he added.
Department of Budget and Management director Vivien Labastilla explained that ARAL received no dedicated funding because it lacks a specific line item in the budget.
The program is instead funded through an allocation attributed to the textbook budget, with teachers conducting tutorials compensated through overtime pay.
Sen. Erwin Tulfo criticized the arrangement, stressing the need for remedial classes, particularly in remote and rural communities.

“Your NEP has zero funding for this. Yet, you can see that in the past few years, our students have been performing poorly. They need this, especially those in remote areas and rural communities,” Tulfo said.
Buddy system
Meanwhile, DepEd is pursuing additional measures to address school safety and student well-being, including a peer support initiative and the involvement of barangay security personnel.
The department launched its “My Buddy” system to build safer and more supportive school environments as part of its mental health and psychosocial support framework.
The initiative encourages students to seek help early through structured buddy pairings or small peer groups modeled after a “big brother/big sister” arrangement.
Training tanods

In a related move, the Philippine National Police (PNP) will train barangay tanods to help secure schools and surrounding areas following an agreement between the Department of the Interior and Local Government and DepEd.

PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. directed police chiefs to conduct training programs to strengthen barangay tanods’ patrol skills and prepare them for other security-related duties. — Bella Cariaso, Emmanuel Tupas

articles.title: Survey: Dissatisfaction with government deepens
articles.summary: Filipinos dissatisfied with the way the government handles different issues have increased over the past year, a survey conducted by Pulse Asia showed.

blocks.text: October 18, 2026 | 12:00am
Porters at Divisoria Market in Manila are seen working on July 2, 2025.
STAR / Ryan Baldemor
MANILA, Philippines — Filipinos dissatisfied with the way the government handles different issues have increased over the past year, a survey conducted by Pulse Asia showed.
Results of the Sept. 17 to 24 survey showed that the government received highest dissatisfaction rating on controlling inflation at 81 percent.
It increased by 17 points from 64 percent in a similar survey in September 2025.

The survey also found double-digit increases in dissatisfaction over the past year on issues such as fighting criminality (57 percent, from 44 percent), promoting peace (47 percent, from 35 percent), addressing the widespread sale and use of illegal drugs (71 percent, from 61 percent), reducing poverty (67 percent, from 57 percent) and defending Philippine territory (34 percent, from 24 percent).

The government also obtained majority disapproval ratings in three other issues: fighting graft and corruption (70 percent), lowering the price of gasoline (65 percent) and reducing the amount of taxes paid (30 percent).

Meanwhile the administration obtained higher approval than disapproval ratings in three issues: protecting overseas Filipinos (52 percent approve, 21 percent disapprove), responding to the needs of areas affected by calamities (40 percent approve, 35 percent disapprove) and providing assistance to farmers (35 percent approve, 34 percent disapprove).

Like in previous polls, it obtained lowest approval in terms of controlling inflation (10 percent), reducing poverty (11 percent), fighting illegal drugs (13 percent), lowering the price of gasoline (14 percent) and fighting graft and corruption (15 percent).
Most survey respondents identified inflation as their most urgent concern.
The survey had 2,400 respondents and a margin of error of plus/minus two percent.

articles.title: 2nd-hand aircon demand heats up ahead of El Niño
articles.summary: As the country braces for a super El Niño, more than 115,000 people belong to a Facebook group where users buy second-hand air conditioners at significantly lower prices than new units,…

blocks.text: October 18, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — As the country braces for a super El Niño, more than 115,000 people belong to a Facebook group where users buy second-hand air conditioners at significantly lower prices than new units, despite concerns over higher electricity costs, maintenance expenses and potential safety risks.
Businessman Peejay Lim sold his two-year-old, 1.5-horsepower non-inverter window-type air conditioner for P4,500 on Sept. 29, far below its original price of more than P20,000.
In his post, Lim said the unit had no issues, cooled the room quickly and had been used “fairly” at about 70 percent of its capacity.
“Someone bought it immediately after I posted,” he said.

The transaction reflects a thriving second-hand aircon market in the Philippines, where up to 300,000 used units are sold annually, equivalent to about one-third of new-unit sales, according to studies cited in the ninth ASEAN Energy Outlook report released earlier this month.
The report noted that price remains the primary consideration for consumers buying appliances, often outweighing energy efficiency.

“The lower upfront price of second-hand aircons outweighs energy efficiency considerations in purchasing decisions, potentially leaving lower-income consumers exposed to higher electricity costs over the remaining life of the appliance,” the report stated.
Lim said he sold his window-type unit because his home in Marikina is undergoing renovation.
“We want everything new,” he said. “We also want to refresh good energy inside our home.”

According to a 2022 journal article by Babette Never of the IDOS German Institute of Development and Sustainability, sales of second-hand air conditioners among micro and small enterprises typically peak from February to May, coinciding with the summer season. During off-peak periods, these businesses turn to repair and reassembly services.
Second-hand units are commonly sourced from condominium buildings, hotels, offices and large restaurants undergoing renovation or demolition, the study said.
Most units sold are window-type models with capacities ranging from one to 1.5 horsepower.

Never’s study, titled “Green and Social Regulation of Second-Hand Appliance Markets: The Case of Air Conditioners in the Philippines,” found that the industry is thriving among middle-class consumers seeking affordable appliances.
“There was high agreement among interviewees that the competition in the second-hand aircon market is strong, as profit margins are high,” the article said.
“As the very poor cannot afford aircons, individual customers are mostly middle-income enterprises or middle-class people looking for a bargain,” it added.
Costs and risks
While buying second-hand air conditioners is not inherently problematic, poorly maintained or defective units can prove more expensive and riskier in the long run.
Meralco Power Lab manager John Pocholo Pabilona warned that even failing to clean an air conditioner’s indoor air filter can increase electricity costs.

“It can already incur around P95 monthly for a one-horsepower unit,” Pabilona told The STAR. “There are other cases where aircons not maintained for a year can incur an additional P500 to P600 per month.”
Meralco Power Lab tested a 2.5-horsepower floor-mounted air conditioner with a baseline electricity cost of P3.36 per hour.
After three years without maintenance, the cost rose by 17 percent to P3.93 per hour. Cleaning the unit brought the figure down to P3.39 per hour, nearly returning it to baseline.
Air conditioners typically last five to 10 years, Pabilona said, during which newer and more energy-efficient models become available.
Inverter-type air conditioners are now 30 to 70 percent cheaper than conventional models, he said.

Unlike traditional units, which operate their compressors at full capacity during cooling cycles, inverter models slow down their compressors once the room reaches the desired temperature, reducing electricity consumption.
Wear and tear also raises concerns about the structural integrity of second-hand units.
“Given the wear and tear of our products, the fan and the compressor are definitely more prone to breakage over time,” Pabilona said.

Refrigerant leaks pose another concern. The compound absorbs heat from inside a room and releases it outdoors. Leaks, combined with electrical sparks or an overheated compressor, can create fire risks.

To address these concerns, the ASEAN report urged the government to strengthen minimum energy performance standards to ensure that appliances passed on to subsequent households meet higher efficiency requirements.
It also called for stricter product registration, testing and enforcement to limit the entry of inefficient appliances, alongside targeted financing and replacement programs.

articles.title: ICC prosecutor wants 5 more testimonies admitted
articles.summary: An International Criminal Court deputy prosecutor has requested five more prior recorded testimonies of witnesses to be admitted in the crimes against humanity case against former president Rodrigo…

blocks.text: October 18, 2026 | 12:00am
Photos courtesy of the International Criminal Court show former president Rodrigo Duterte during his first in-person appearance before the tribunal since his arrest in March 2025.
Photos / ICC | via Janvic Mateo

MANILA, Philippines — An International Criminal Court (ICC) deputy prosecutor has requested five more prior recorded testimonies of witnesses to be admitted in the crimes against humanity case against former president Rodrigo Duterte.
The request filed on Friday brings the total number to nine. The ICC Trial Chamber III has so far accepted the prior recorded testimony of one witness.
In its latest filing, deputy prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang requested the admission of the testimonies of witnesses identified as P-1087, P-1151, P-1158, P-1161 and P-1204.
The prior testimonies were described as “relevant, reliable and probative.”

Witness P-1087 testified “how killings were normalized (redacted) during Mr. Duterte’s presidency. Specifically, he notes that the president Rodrigo Roa Duterte list (PRRD list) provided officers with a feeling of impunity and that Mr. Duterte’s speeches contributed to a culture in which killing was normalized.”

P-1151 described “the killings perpetrated by the PNP,” the Operation Double Barrel and the PRRD list. The witness also discussed the rewards system for police officers involved in killings; P-1158 gave proof of the policy to “neutralize” alleged criminals in the Philippines and Duterte’s individual criminal responsibility; P-1161 discussed Duterte’s involvement in the PRRD list and P-1204 described the changes within the PNP after Duterte became president.
“Their evidence is particularly relevant to the policy to ‘neutralize’ through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines,” the filing read.
Even if their prior recorded testimonies are accepted by the judges, all five witnesses will still be presented in person for supplementary examination.

“The introduction of the five witnesses’ prior recorded testimonies into evidence would not be prejudicial to or inconsistent with the rights of the accused, as the defense will have ample opportunity to cross-examine them,” the prosecution said.
“The defense has been notified of the prosecution’s intention to call these witnesses… and have adequate time to prepare for their cross-examination,” it added.
Niang said granting the request “will enhance the expeditiousness of the proceedings.”

During the case’s fourth status conference on Oct. 13, ICC presiding judge Joanna Korner urged the prosecution to re-examine its list of witnesses to further trim down the expected length of the trial.
Trial lawyer Edward Jeremy said the prosecution has reclassified some of its intended witnesses, including filing a request for admission of prior recorded testimony to streamline their presentation.
Duterte’s defense lawyer Peter Haynes has repeatedly called out what it described as “sheer volume of material” disclosed by the prosecution.
The trial will commence on Nov. 30, with the final status conference set on Nov. 2.

Duterte is charged with alleged extrajudicial killings in his war on drugs as Philippine president and mayor of Davao City. He was arrested in Manila in November 2025 and has been detained in The Hague, The Netherlands.

articles.title: First female PMA Commandant of Cadets named
articles.summary: The Philippine Military Academy named Col. Leah Lorenzo Santiago its first woman Commandant of Cadets, breaking another barrier for women in the military.

blocks.text: October 18, 2026 | 12:00am
Col. Leah Lorenzo Santiago
STAR / File
BAGUIO CITY, Philippines — The Philippine Military Academy (PMA) named Col. Leah Lorenzo Santiago its first woman Commandant of Cadets, breaking another barrier for women in the military.
A trailblazer from PMA KalasagLahi Class of 1997, Santiago ranked third overall and first academically in the academy’s first class to include women graduates.
She became PMA’s first female summa cum laude graduate, setting a milestone in the institution’s history.

Commissioned as a second lieutenant in the Philippine Army, Santiago rose through operational and leadership posts, serving as platoon leader, executive officer and company commander of the 30th Infantry Battalion under the 4th Infantry Division.
She returned to PMA as senior tactical officer from 2016 to 2019, later commanded the 9th Field Artillery Battery in Sulu and held key personnel posts at Army headquarters.
Santiago served as director of the Personnel Management Center before becoming the Army’s assistant chief of staff for personnel, G1.

She completed military courses in the Philippines and Australia, and earned three master’s degrees in public management, strategic studies and business administration from the Development Academy of the Philippines, Australian National University and Ateneo Graduate School of Business.
Santiago is married to Col. Jerome Erwin Santiago of the Philippine Air Force, with whom she has two children.

In her assumption speech, Santiago expressed her gratitude to Almighty God, President Marcos, the national defense and military leadership and everyone who contributed to her appointment and professional development.

She emphasized that leadership is never achieved alone, recognizing the sacrifices of her family, the support of friends and colleagues and the guidance of mentors and superiors throughout her military career.

Reflecting on her journey – from overcoming a life-threatening accident to serving in combat operations, staff positions and command assignments – Santiago highlighted the importance of resilience, humility, discipline, integrity and commitment to service.

articles.title: DILG wants tighter airport cargo checks
articles.summary: Security measures in the country’s airports have been tightened, and intelligence-driven operations against drug syndicates have intensified in the wake of a foiled shipment of 521 kilos of…

blocks.text: October 18, 2026 | 12:00am
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said they are investigating potential lapses in security that could allow large quantities of illegal drugs to enter the country through airports.
STAR / Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — Security measures in the country’s airports have been tightened, and intelligence-driven operations against drug syndicates have intensified in the wake of a foiled shipment of 521 kilos of suspected shabu, valued at P3.5 billion, from Laos into the country.
“We have loose ends to tie up. We have to make more stringent inspections of all cargo arriving through private aircraft,” Remulla said in a statement.
He is pushing for tighter airport cargo checks after Laotian authorities intercepted the drug shipment.
Remulla identified former Bangsamoro Parliament member Edrieza Hadji Nasser Rimbang as the one who financed the operation to smuggle the drugs into the country.
Rimbang is among the 11 persons of interest (POI) named by Remulla in connection with the drug shipment.

The other POIs whom Remulla identified are Fahad Mulok Dibarosan, Rioklyn Pizarras Toledo, Police Master Sergeant Aileen Jayne Manalo Mendoza, Abdullah Rimbang Macarimbang, Aldren Nadal Samante, Rudy Isidro, Abdulkarim Macalatas, Christian Fabrigas, Rohaniah Rimbang and Hilario de Vera.

Remulla said the aircraft, intercepted at Luang Prabang International Airport in Northern Laos, was allegedly scheduled to land at a hangar in Pasay on the last week of September. It was allegedly arranged by Mendoza, a member of the police Aviation Security Group.
After she was implicated in drug smuggling, Philippine National Police chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. sacked Mendoza from her post and placed her under restrictive custody.

Stressing that police officers are bound to uphold the law and protect the public, Nartatez said they will never tolerate any personnel who are involved in illegal drugs and other nefarious activities.

“Should evidence establish the officer’s involvement in illegal drug activities, appropriate criminal and administrative proceedings will be pursued in accordance with the law,” he said in a statement.
Police units in Metro Manila, meanwhile, have intensified intelligence-driven operations against members of drug syndicates, including suppliers, distributors and networks.

articles.title: Sara denies owning fastfood franchise
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte denied owning a popular fastfood restaurant following the testimony of a prosecution witness that a company listed in her statement of assets, liabilities and net worth…

blocks.text: October 18, 2026 | 12:00am
Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Senate in Pasay City on July 7, 2026 to meet with members of her defense team ahead of the continuation of her impeachment trial.
The Philippine STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte denied owning a popular fastfood restaurant following the testimony of a prosecution witness that a company listed in her statement of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN) owns at least five franchises in Davao City.

“I do not own a Jollibee franchise or any other franchise. I previously invested in a company that is part of a legitimate business organization owned and operated by individuals with an established reputation for integrity and good standing,” Duterte said in a statement.

Accountant-lawyer Alexander Cabrera claimed that Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio had unexplained wealth amounting to at least P1.5 billion based on voluminous bank, tax and other government records.
Cabrera bared the computation upon impeachment court presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero’s query as the prosecution presented its case on Article II or unexplained wealth against Duterte.
The witness explained that his original findings were based on a conservative examination of financial records involving Duterte and her husband.

Cabrera cited P475 million in confidential funds that he had excluded, around P100 million in additional financial discrepancies and potentially higher amounts involving GenCorp Industries Inc., a company linked to the couple.
Duterte maintained that investing in a company does not automatically equate to owning the company itself, much less owning, managing or operating its individual businesses or franchises.

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 11:49pm
Various government agencies, transportation hubs and cemeteries are preparing for the influx of visitors during the commemoration of All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day, collectively known as Undas.
In Bernadette Reyes' "24 Oras" Weekend report on Saturday, cleaners at the Manila North Cemetery began tidying the grounds, while others repainted tombs ahead of the annual observance.

The Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange is expecting two million passengers from Oct. 25 to Nov. 4, with about 20,000 passengers expected on Oct. 30 alone.
The Department of the Interior and Local Government and the Philippine National Police said they will double the number of police officers deployed for Undas compared with last year’s 50,000.

articles.title: SNP says campaign for next referendum on independence ‘has already begun’
articles.summary:
John Swinney tells party conference SNP will use ‘six-figure war chest’ to renew argument for leaving UK

John Swinney has said that the second referendum campaign for Scottish independence…

blocks.text: John Swinney has said that the second referendum campaign for Scottish independence “has already begun”, revealing a nationwide effort to renew the argument for leaving the UK in his keynote address to the SNP party conference.

On Saturday, the Scottish first minister said that the SNP would launch its “most sophisticated campaign in history” to convince Scottish of the benefits of independence, backed by “a six-figure war chest”. Called Choose Scotland, the campaign aims to build the consensus for leaving the union.

John Swinney told the SNP party conference in Aberdeen that the “stars were aligning” for the pro-independence cause, arguing that nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland had panicked pro-union parties.

“For centuries, people in the Celtic nations have been told that we are not good enough. Our languages were derided, our cultures suppressed, our histories rewritten,” he said. “When I stood on a stage recently with pro-independence leaders from Wales and Ireland, it certainly upset some of our opponents.

“From their point of view, they are right to be worried. Watching us pledge to work together and seeing the love and respect we feel for each other’s nations. Never again can they portray us as separatists.”

During the event in Aberdeen, leading SNP figures said that a hung Westminster parliament is the most realistic path to securing a second independence referendum in Scotland as the nationalists would probably “hold the balance of power” in forming a future progressive government.

The party currently holds just eight MPs in parliament, but recent polling indicates that if a vote was held today, that number would surge at the Labour party’s expense in Scotland, although there is uncertainty surrounding how many seats they would gain.

Deputy first minister Jenny Gilruth said that her party would welcome an early general election to reenergise the push for independence. “The polling, of course, suggests that the SNP would hold the balance of power in a hung parliament and really strong support for the SNP across the country allowing us to regain a number of seats,” she said.

The sentiment was echoed by Lara Bird, the MP for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry, who told a podcast by the pro-independence newspaper The National that they could negotiate another poll if the overall results were tight.

“We have a really great opportunity at the next general election to be in a position where that negotiation can seriously start with the next iteration of the Westminster government, whether we have a hung parliament, which is looking very likely, or different coalitions. Perhaps now we are talking about a Lib Dem-Labour coalition. The SNP are polled at getting somewhere between 40 and 50 MPs at the general election. That’s huge. Let’s put it to Westminster and put the onus on them to meet us at the table and set that plan out for us,” she said.
The latest MRP polling by Electoral Calculus this week predicted a narrow Labour victory, with the SNP winning 28 seats, although previous polls have indicated they could win even more.

In a visit to Lanarkshire on Friday, UK prime minister Andy Burnham said the Scottish government needed to “move beyond” the question of independence while offering to work more closely on devolving power from Holyrood with Swinney’s administration. The Westminster government would have to grant a second vote on Scottish independence.

“I just feel we all have to move beyond the constitutional questions. In my view, people in Scotland are suffering the cost of living crisis, like they are in England and everywhere else. And I think our job is to focus on the practicalities, to focus on solutions for people. Right now, too much time is wasted on those dramas. It consumes too much energy,” he said, when asked about the issue.
Although it is not in Swinney’s power to call a second independence referendum, he told the conference in Aberdeen that another vote could happen sooner than expected.

“Our independence is very close,” he said. “Our nearest neighbours will always be our closest friends and our strongest allies. I will always want the very best for the people living in England, Wales and across Ireland. But friends, in the long arc of history, nothing is static. And those that try to hold on to the past fail to grasp the opportunities of the future. In this period of history, the nations of the United Kingdom are evolving into a new relationship. That is something to welcome,” he said.

articles.title: How big is Russia's threat against Germany?
articles.summary: Experts believe that, so far, Germany has been ill-prepared — both militarily and mentally — for Russian provocations. They also warn against the idea that ending support for Ukraine would make…

image.caption: Germans have been protesting both for and against supporting Ukraine in its war with RussiaImage: DW

blocks.text: Warnings keep mounting about Russia's threat to Germany. On October 12, Sinan Selen, president of Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, said that Russia's covert attacks and destabilization efforts against Germany and other European countries are "not a temporary development but a long-term hybrid attack."

Even if the war in Ukraine were to end, said Selen, the Russian threat would not disappear. "For Russia, this is about completely redrawing the map of Europe and redefining its own role within Europe and in global politics."
He added that Russia's aggression would continue to be felt not only in Ukraine, but also in the Baltic states, in Poland and in Germany.
Russia is tied down in Ukraine — for now

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has described the threat situation as one in which "our country is not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare." Russia's goal, he said, is not to defeat Germany militarily "but to subdue us politically and socially."

Security experts, however, are not so sure that Russia is only interested in exercising political and social influence. Last year, political scientist Carlo Masala told the political talk show Maischberger that "Russia is preparing for a major war." And he didn't mean just a cyberwar. Inspector General Carsten Breuer, the Bundeswehr's highest-ranking officer, agreed.

For now, though, Russia remains tied up in its war against Ukraine. According to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, there is no immediate military threat to NATO territory. But according to military experts, European intelligence agencies, and the German Defense Ministry, Russia will have the personnel and equipment to wage a conventional war against NATO by 2029. The Russian defense industry is running at full speed, and Moscow plans to expand its armed forces to 1.5 million soldiers.

At the moment, Russia has other objectives, believes Stefan Meister, an expert on Eastern Europe at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP): "I don't think Russia has any interest in a direct military conflict with NATO right now. It wants to test NATO and also display its capabilities," he tells DW.
If Russia attacked NATO, would Germany be prepared?
An accidental military confrontation?

An example of Russia's hybrid war might be the failed attack with an explosive-laden drone against a Ukrainian transport aircraft at Leipzig-Halle Airport in August. Soon after, the German government stated that it was certain Russia was behind the attack.
Security expert Nico Lange told DW at the time that Germany was very lucky the explosives did not detonate: "Honestly, it was pure coincidence and not the result of German defensive measures."

As for why Germany was targeted specifically, Lange said: "I believe that Germany has always been a primary target of Russian influence and hybrid warfare. Russia believes that Germany is the key to European decision-making. Germany is now leading the way in supporting Ukraine."

Moscow swiftly responded to the German government's accusation with an angry denial. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said it was "the beginning of a real war," though there was no immediate further escalation.

Nevertheless, there is always the risk that things could spiral out of control following a Russian provocation and subsequent response, according to Stefan Meister: "Accidentally shooting down an aircraft that they were trying to intimidate would trigger a counter-reaction. But I don't believe that Russia is currently aiming for a direct war but rather for provocations, polarization, and sowing uncertainty among the population."
AfD says less money for Ukraine means more for Germany
Not everyone shares the assessment that Russia poses a threat to Germany — some believe that the threat can be averted.

Despite the war in Ukraine, politicians from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the populist left-wing Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) want to improve relations with Russia, resume Russian energy supplies and end support for Ukraine.

AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said in early September, "People are fed up with this escalation against Russia, with the billions being squandered there on a system that is actually funded by German taxpayers' money."

The message appears to have resonated among the population, especially in eastern Germany. The AfD saw strong gains in all three state elections in September. In Saxony-Anhalt, it became the strongest party by far and may even run the government there soon, which would be the first time that a far-right party has held power in Germany since the end of WWII.

The CDU's security policy expert Roderich Kiesewetter disputed the claim made by the AfD and BSW that ending aid to Ukraine would mean greater security and more money for German schools and infrastructure: "Spending on education, social policy, and infrastructure is only possible if we live in freedom and democracy — and, above all, in peace and security. Anyone who believes that we'll have more money for social programs if we stop supporting Ukraine and let Russia have its way is either gravely mistaken or is making themselves a tool of Russian propaganda."

blocks.caption: German high school students have gone on strike to protest plans to reintroduce military conscriptionImage: Snowfield Photography/picture alliance

blocks.text: A decades-long pacifist mindset

The perceived security threat has led the German military, the Bundeswehr, to fast-track significant modernization through substantial investment. But it is struggling to find enough recruits for its planned expansion. Many young Germans have taken to the streets to protest against plans to reintroduce conscription. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius faced criticism from inside his own party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), for saying that Germany must become "capable of waging war." Many found the statement to be too militaristic.

Is Germany prepared for a military threat? "Not at all. Germany is not well prepared militarily or in the civilian sector, and the population isn't mentally prepared for it either," said Meister. "Just look at the demonstrations against conscription and the military that continue to take place, even though Germany needs a draft. For decades, we've grown up in this culture of pacifism, in a comfort zone. I believe there is very limited societal resilience, but above all, we are not at all mentally prepared for war."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) are under increasing political pressure — especially from the far right — to scale back support for Ukraine. But Merz never tires of emphasizing that Ukraine will continue to receive support under his chancellorship, calling it a matter of Germany's security. He recently visited Kyiv once again and, together with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, surveyed the destruction caused by Russia.

But this also means that the threat from Russia will continue and even intensify, says Stefan Meister: "I believe we will see a massive increase in attacks such as the one in Leipzig, of provocations involving drones. We will see attacks on infrastructures and possibly also on specific individuals within the military-industrial complex. I believe this is the real, concrete danger facing Germany in the coming months."
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Chinese envoy's remarks seen as 'wolf warrior diplomacy'
articles.summary: Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan"s controversial remarks are an example of “wolf warrior diplomacy,” according to defense analyst Renato Castro.

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 10:58pm
Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan’s controversial remarks are an example of “wolf warrior diplomacy,” according to defense analyst Renato Castro.

In a report by JP Soriano on "24 Oras" Weekend on Saturday, Jing claimed that China would "easily win" if it resorted to force in the West Philippine Sea. Several Filipino officials and government agencies have described the remarks as a threat.

“Dito sa wolf warrior diplomacy, talagang ginagamit mo ang lahat para takutin and, to a certain degree, bastusin mo yung host government, na nakikita natin ngayon, ‘no? So, in a way, talagang ginagawa niya yung trabaho niya,” Castro said.
(In wolf warrior diplomacy, you use everything to intimidate and, to a certain degree, disrespect the host government, as we are seeing now. So, in a way, he is doing his job.)
Sen. Risa Hontiveros called on Jing to apologize, warning that he should be declared persona non grata if he refused.
Jing’s remarks prompted President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to summon the Chinese envoy.

“Hindi naman sasabihin niya na isang diplomat, kung wala po talagang ibig sabihin po ‘yan. Kung baga, talagang veiled threat na ho sa atin ‘yan. Let's expect the worst. Kasi talagang gigil na gigil na sa atin ang mga Tsino ho, dahil ho talaga, hindi tayo nagpapatinag sa kanila,” Castro said.

(A diplomat would not say something like that if it did not mean anything. In other words, it is really a veiled threat against us. Let’s expect the worst because the Chinese are extremely frustrated with us for refusing to back down.)
Tensions between the Philippines and China have continued to rise amid their territorial dispute in the West Philippine Sea.

China continues to claim most of the disputed waters despite a 2016 arbitral ruling that invalidated the legal basis of its expansive maritime claims under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.
The ruling, issued under the arbitration proceedings at the Permanent Court of Arbitration, was in favor of the Philippines.—Jean Mangaluz/MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: Police clash with protesters as tens of thousands take to streets across France
articles.summary:
Police fire teargas in Paris and protesters storm town hall in Marseille – with officials blaming violence on ‘ultra-left’

Police have fired teargas and clashed with protesters supporting…
articles.byline: Kim Willsherin Paris and William Christou

blocks.text: Police have fired teargas and clashed with protesters supporting high school student grievances, as demonstrations across France were boosted by other groups angry over high prices and the fraying of a social welfare system.

Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across the country, and tensions erupted on the fringes of the nationwide demonstrations over absent teachers, decrepit school buildings and police violence.

blocks.caption: A masked protester holds the French flag as he stands on the statue of the Place de la Réepublique Photograph: Jack Taylor/Reuters

blocks.text: In Marseille, protesters stormed the town hall, ramming the door with security barriers they removed from the street. They briefly managed to enter the municipal building, where a protester spray-painted an “A” for anarchy on a wall before the police removed them.

Around Place de la République in central Paris, a peaceful march turned violent, with police firing teargas at black-clad and masked rioters who threw fireworks and paving stones, attacked a bank and looted a sports shop.
“We’re taking the Bastille!” one demonstrator yelled.

Others set wheelie bins on fire and threw firecrackers inside or pushed over glass recycling bins and picked up the bottles inside to use as missiles. A lorry was set on fire and flames spread to a nearby building.
Residents in surrounding streets were forced to close windows and doors as huge clouds of teargas rose to roof level.
French authorities detained dozens of protesters across the country, with more arrests expected.
Saturday’s mobilisation follows calls on social media to revive the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) movement, which emerged in 2018 against social injustice.

The protests began last month at schools ⁠in the poor northern suburbs of Paris, where ⁠anger over teacher ​absences and shabby facilities quickly morphed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.
Saturday’s protests called for teachers and students, labourers, pensioners and farmers to join the protests and widen the movement.
French authorities said 140 protests involving 32,800 people had been recorded outside Paris by midday, blaming the unrest and violence on what they said was the “ultra-left”.

blocks.caption: French riot police detain a protester in Marseille.  Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The CGT, one of France’s biggest labour unions, has also backed the protests, calling for “higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people’s needs”.
About 45% of French people are worried about the rising cost of living and inflation, according to a 2,000-person survey conducted in October.
Protesters ⁠in hi-vis vests blocked streets, an echo of the unrest that dogged President Emmanuel Macron’s previous term, and in Marseille rubbish bins were set ​alight.
Both the far left and far right in France sought to capitalise on the protest movement, with the left positioning itself on the side of the protesters and the right backing the police.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, marched in a demonstration on Tuesday and has expressed support for student protesters.

blocks.caption: Protesters block a road in Nancy in north-eastern Frace in preparation for an afternoon rally.  Photograph: Muhammed Said Tako/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: A large police presence was visible in central Paris, especially near landmarks such as ⁠the Avenue des Champs-Élysées and the Arc de Triomphe, which were excluded from the routes of the two official demonstrations.
About 100 people walked towards the police at the beginning protest yelling, “all cops are bastards!”.

“We are fighting because the cost of living is ‌too harsh, because the price of ‌fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to ‌protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions,” said a 19-year-old protester in Paris who gave her name as Lola.
after newsletter promotion
Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, leaving behind a polarised electorate and a badly fragmented political landscape.

blocks.caption: Police officers clash with protesters in Paris. Photograph: Kiran Ridley/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: On Friday, the president appealed for calm and respect for people and property as officials warned of possible violence.

“There is a constitutional right to protest and to express oneself, and I have always been vigilant and attentive that that right is fully respected,” he said. “But this right comes with the need to respect. Respect for people, respect for property, and therefore a commitment not to insult or destroy.”
Macron denounced as “unacceptable” the potential presence of people “solely to cause damage and create unrest”.

blocks.caption: A protester waves a French national flag during clashes before a demonstration in Marseille.  Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said hundreds of protest actions and more than 80 marches were expected nationwide, including spontaneous gatherings, street demonstrations and blockades.

Police banned some other proposed gatherings in central Paris. Many Métro stations were closed on Saturday at the police’s request, including those around the Champs-Élysées and near the presidential palace, parliament and government offices.

blocks.caption: Protesters vandalise a municipal police station in Marseille.  Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: In recent weeks, there have been thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries, and schools set on fire as the new school year descended into nationwide student protests that are influencing the country’s presidential election campaign and drawing international attention.
The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence, while the French prime minister said that more than 900 police officers had been injured.

Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons. Nuñez suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against the young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand, but said that they could be used on Saturday.
On Tuesday, the climate and social justice activist Greta Thunberg joined students at a school in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.
Agencies contributed reporting

articles.title: China's influence in the gaming industry is growing
articles.summary: Home to more than 700 million gamers, China is the world's largest gaming market — but it's also one of the most tightly regulated. The effects reach far beyond China, impacting players around the…

image.caption: The Chinese game 'The Defiant' is set during the Second Sino-Japanese WarImage: 4Divinity

blocks.text: In a dark underground hideout, dim light spills from a handful of oil lamps. A comrade fiddles with a rifle. A red flag hangs on one of the roughly hewn stone walls, bearing a hammer and sickle on a white star — the symbol of the ChineseWorkers' and Peasants' Red Army. Weapons are scattered on the ground. One is picked up, and soon the action moves into the snowy forest, where gunfire erupts among the trees.

Such a scene could fit in a new installment of "Call of Duty," the popular first-person shooter game that transports players to battlefields past, present, and future. But it is actually from "The Defiant." The game is currently being developed by the Chinese studio Hoothanes Technology in Hangzhou. It tells the story of Chinese forces fending off the Japanese army in the 1930s and 1940s.

Developer Connor Xu tells DW the weapons featured in the game are unique. They were used only in Asia and are therefore unfamiliar to many Western players, he says. The same goes for the story, which Xu says has never before been told in a video game.

blocks.caption: Game developer Connor Xu wants to tell stories from Chinese historyImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: "The Defiant" is also designed to appeal to an international audience. In just a few years, China has emerged as a major player in the global gaming industry despite strict regulations, censorship and a former ban on video game consoles.
Gaming is part of everyday life in China

More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games. According to market research company Newzoo, most consider gaming an important part of their lives. Many use games to stay in touch with friends.

"Games make life more interesting," developer Xu says. "I can try different roles, different stories, different characters, because we only have one life to live, but we can play a role in another story. That's really attractive, I think, to Chinese users."

blocks.caption: 'Honor of Kings' is largely unknown outside China, but it's one of the country's most popular gamesImage: Tencent/Level Infinite/TiMi Studio Group

blocks.text: People in China primarily play games on PCs and smartphones, while consoles are much less common. There are historical reasons for that: While gamers in Europe and North America debated whether PlayStation or Xbox was the better console in the early 2000s, the devices were not officially sold in China between 2000 and 2014. Chinese authorities said the restrictions were intended to protect children and teenagers from becoming addicted to gaming.
Limits on gaming time and extensive controls

Minors in China are currently allowed to play online games for no more than three hours a week. There are no such limits for adults, but gaming is subject to strict controls. Anyone who wants to play must register using their real name and a personal identification number. That effectively allows the state to track who plays what and when, as well as whom they communicate with.

There is also a gray area that the Chinese government appears to tolerate. Some players log in using VPNs, giving them access to games that are not officially available in China. Some younger players use their parents' accounts to get around the limits on gaming time.

blocks.caption: The Chinese role-playing game "Genshin Impact" bears visual and gameplay similarities to "The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild"Image: Cognosphere/miHoYo/HoYoverse

blocks.text: Despite its strict controls on underage gamers, China has become increasingly receptive to video games in general, having recognized the industry's enormous economic potential. Early on, games released for Chinese players often appeared to be copies of Western titles. At the same time, Chinese tech companies such as Tencent and NetEase invested in numerous Western gaming companies.
No license? No sales in China

One distinctive feature of the Chinese market is its licensing system. "Unlike a lot of the other big video games markets in the world, China has a tightly regulated and licensed official video games market," George E. Osborn tells DW. The journalist advises NGOs and governments on video games and spoke at the Gamescom congress. In his book "Power Play," he describes how authoritarian states use video games to pursue political objectives.

blocks.caption: The strategy game 'Heroes of Might and Magic III Remake' is currently being developed by Ubisoft's studios in Chengdu and ShanghaiImage: Ubisoft

blocks.text: The rule for all games in China is simple: No license, no sales. "That system essentially forces developers who want to release their video games to go through multiple layers of approval from China's Ministry of Propaganda, Ministry of Culture," Osborn says.
Strict criteria for video games

Games are prohibited from containing material that threatens China's unity, sovereignty or territorial integrity, among other restrictions. Pornographic content and gambling are also banned. Games may not incite crimes that threaten national security or spread information authorities believe could disrupt public order.

"The whole point around this criteria is that it's deliberately designed to be pretty vague," Osborn says. Whether a game violates the rules is a matter of interpretation. Sometimes games are altered even after release. In the 2025 action role-playing game "Wuchang: Fallen Feathers," for example, enemies based on famous Chinese figures from the Ming Dynasty suddenly could no longer be killed. Instead, they would collapse from exhaustion.
Chinese culture is an international hit

The Chinese action role-playing game "Black Myth: Wukong" became an unexpected international hit in 2024. By then, it was clear Chinese developers could do more than cater to the domestic market — they could create successful games for a global audience as well. The game was inspired by the 16th-century Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."

blocks.caption: The video game 'Black Myth: Wukong' became an international hitImage: Game Science Interactive Technology Co

blocks.text: Osborn sees nothing wrong with bringing Chinese culture to audiences around the world. The question, he says, is how much the state actually intervenes in the games themselves. "I think in general, video game players are actually quite deeply skeptical of these kinds of things. They are generally very good at spotting when someone might be selling to them or someone might be propagandizing. And so I think if it's too obvious, it won't work," he says.
The problem of self-censorship

Because of the licensing system, Western developers also have to comply with government requirements if they want to sell their games in China. And they do want to, Osborn says, because the market is too big to ignore. "But I think when you start thinking about the potential impact this has on creative standards around the world, I think it's really important that developers ask themselves the question of what will we or won't we compromise on here?"

He fears the real danger lies in self-censorship. That could lead developers, for example, to leave queer characters out of their games. That would represent a major step backward, he says, because games help many people explore their identities.

China is not the only country where games are modified to comply with national regulations. In Germany, for example, symbols that violate the country's constitution, such as the swastika, may not be shown in games unless the game in question explicitly contributes to the country's culture of remembrance. Depictions of extreme violence also have to be removed from German versions.
History from a Chinese perspective

Glorifying violence is prohibited in China, too, yet Xu's team is still allowed to develop a war game. How does this add up? Xu explains it this way: "I think in this game, the most important thing is not violence. The most important thing is to tell history."
Xu says the team is committed to delivering a historically accurate product. Whether it succeeds will be for historians to judge.
This article was translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal.

articles.title: France shaken by fiery street protests uniting students, workers and 'yellow vests'

blocks.text: France is about to wake up to an uneasy morning after.

On Saturday, the country saw massive — and unusually violent — cross-generational protests that brought together high schoolers, trade unions and "yellow vest" demonstrators, all choking the streets of Paris, Lille and other French cities.
While many aspects of this day of protests were peaceful, there were also fierce confrontations between brick-throwing protesters dressed in black and police armed with water cannons and tear gas.
The confrontations left parts of Paris looking like a war zone.

One minister estimated 400 people had been arrested, with 110,000 demonstrators in Paris alone. French TV aired video of businesses and retail stores that had been looted and the city's mayor said entire streets had been vandalized.
While the tear gas and smoke from burning vehicles cleared relatively quickly, the violence will no doubt leave a deep scar on the city.
Tear gas, arrests and chaos as protests grip France

Saturday's events also speak to a deeper, more ideological cleavage over values, spending priorities and crucially, whether the French state should protect its economic standing, or its most vulnerable first.
'Turning point'
What began weeks ago as high schoolers demanding repaired classroom boilers has transformed into an existential battle over the very definition of the French Republic.
"France is coming to a major turning point," Bally Bagayoko, the left-wing mayor of the working-class Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, told CBC News.

"Today, unfortunately, this France is in sadness. It is unable to provide concrete answers to the legitimate demands of high schoolers ... and the only concrete answer it can provide is a heavy handed police response.”

Over the last three weeks of the teenagers' protest, supporters have harshly criticized police tactics. One young person lost part of an arm during an especially violent confrontation and there were reports Saturday in Paris of other people enduring similar injuries.
A view of the momument in La Place de la République after police fired tear gas at protesters to try to disperse the crowd. (Chris Brown/CBC News)

The involvement of the yellow vest movement amplifies the stakes for France's government. Initially formed by disillusionsed working class voters a decade ago to battle high fuel prices, the movement petered out during COVID lockdown. Its reconstitution now could help potentially transform the student's school-focussed protests into a cause with much longer staying power.

In the aftermath of Saturday's violence, France's key political leaders were unanimous in their condemnation of the violence on the streets, and attempted to separate the instigators from those who were there peacefully.

"We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who seek only to bring down our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so," posted French President Emmanuel Macron.
The country's centrist Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu took a similar approach.
"Today, ultra-left groups have orchestrated violence in several French cities; delinquents have joined in to pillage and destroy," he wrote.
France's far-right party, the Rassemblement National (RN), rejected the protesters and their message, and instead praised the conduct of the security forces.
Mayor Bally Bagayoko represents the Paris subburb of Saint-Denis. He put himself between protesters and police at a student demonstration earlier this month. (Adrian Di Virgilio/CBC News)
Toxic convergence
On the surface, the current crisis looks like a familiar French budget dispute.
But on the ground, the view from inside the student movement reveals a toxic convergence of fiscal collapse, class warfare, systemic racism and a worrying escalation of state force.
In the days leading up to this weekend's mass protests, CBC News went inside the student movement in the northern city of Lille to better understand the issues driving it.
Many of the organizers are very young — some just 14 years old. CBC News required their parents' permission to speak to them.
At the fences of Lycée Faidherbe, amidst the thick black smoke of smouldering plastic bins that some students had set ablaze, the teenagers' demands sounded immediate and concrete.
"We hope the school will be closed," Lille organizer Soan Rauch, 16, told CBC News, standing near the barricades.
Soan Rauch, 16, has taken a lead role organizing high schoolers in the city of Lille, France. (Jason Ho/CBC News)
When asked why shutting down their own education is a victory, his fellow classmate, 15-year-old James Caron, didn't hesitate.
"It helps put pressure on the government," Caron said. "Because if everything is burning, the government can't ignore us."

While conservative critics have attempted to dismiss the movement as the political manipulation of minors by populist left-wing politicians, independent analysts say the teenagers' grievances are grounded in real, physical decline.
"Actually, they do understand what they're doing, and they're not manipulated," Blanche Leridon, a political analyst with the Paris-based think-tank Institut Montaigne, told CBC News.
"There is a huge topic about the deterioration of the condition of education, and deterioration of their buildings. [Teachers] are missing and it's really hard for them to learn in good conditions."
Rauch took CBC News to Lycée Fénelon, his shuttered school, pointing out student-painted banners demanding "respect" written in multiple languages.
Beyond the political slogans, he said that the daily reality inside French public classrooms has become untenable.

"We ask for classrooms that are much less crowded — we are 35 students per class," said Rauch. "More particularly, we have problems with hallways and thermal boilers. It means that it's very hot in summer and very, very cold in winter."
French riot police stand in position amid clashes with protesters during a demonstration at La Place de la République in Paris. (Abdul Saboor/Reuters)

As the student disruptions have rippled across the nation, the Macron government attempted to quell the anger by offering a temporary package consisting of thousands of new substitute teachers. The student unions swiftly dismissed the proposal, calling it an empty gesture.
The race factor

Mayor Bagayoko argues that this structural neglect is concentrated heavily in diverse, working-class communities plagued by high unemployment, like Saint-Denis, which sits at a staggering 35 per cent jobless rate.
"When you grow up in the working-class neighbourhoods, you are treated less well than in the beautiful Parisian neighbourhoods," said Bagayoko.
"All the children of France must be treated equally."
The Macron administration continues to claim its hands are tied, pointing to a crushing sovereign debt crisis and severe warnings from global credit rating agencies.
But inside the student strategy meetings that CBC News sat in on, that economic narrative is rejected as a corporate myth.

"I don't think the government should reduce its social spending, but they should rather try to increase [it]," argued 14-year-old Lille student Bastien Duprez. "And probably decrease budgets to, for example, budgets to the army and, for instance, subsidies to big corporations.”
"We know that a lot of money from the government goes to rich people," added Alice Note, 17. "So we also think that the money that the rich people have will go to us, to education."
Leridon, the French political analyst, sees France as a country stuck in an economic vice.

"We are really aware of the specific difficulties we have regarding our debt or deficits ... but [people] are not prepared to make any sacrifices. They don't want higher taxes, they don't want to work longer," she said.
Masked protesters walk past burning barricades amid clashes in Paris. (Jack Taylor/Reuters)
Clashing priorities
This clash of priorities has translated into an exceptionally aggressive law-and-order response.

Prior to the weekend, more than 8,000 high school students had been arrested nationwide, the vast majority of them minors. Mayor Bagayoko claims hospital rooms continue to fill up with teenagers suffering from broken jaws, fractured limbs, and severe chemical gas inhalation.
The protest line violence became so intense that on Oct. 6 in Paris, he physically placed his own body between charging riot police and fleeing high schoolers during a protest at Place de la Nation.
"I made the choice to intervene by trying as much as possible to protect the high schoolers first, because I remember that they were minors," Bagayoko said.
The video of his intervention flashed around the country, transforming him into a central figure in the ongoing crisis.
France is less than six months away from a pivotal presidential election.
With the centrist government entirely paralyzed and unable to pass a budget through a deeply fractured Parliament, the political void is rapidly being filled by the far right.

Marine Le Pen, who will be the Rassemblement National's candidate in the upcoming presidential election this spring, appears to be in a commanding position. She has called for strengthened anti-riot legislation and largely ignored the issues at the centre of the student's complaints, instead focusing on the need to restore order on the streets.
For the teenagers holding the barricades, a right-wing takeover isn't just a political shift, it's a direct threat to their safety.
"We're afraid. We have a lot of fear," Rauch admitted. "We don't know what's going to happen tomorrow.
