articles.title: Independence supporters rally outside Alberta's legislature Saturday
articles.summary: Pro-independence supporters gathered at the Alberta legislature in Edmonton Saturday afternoon, less than 48 hours before referendum day.

image.caption: Separation supporters gathered at the Alberta legislature building for the pro-independence rally organized by Let Alberta Decide on the afternoon of Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Tristan Mottershead/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton
Pro-independence supporters gathered at the Alberta legislature in Edmonton Saturday afternoon, less than 48 hours before referendum day.
Event comes less than 48 hours before referendum day

Crowds of Alberta independence supporters filled the plaza at the legislature in Edmonton on Saturday afternoon, chanting and waving flags in a last push to rally support for the separatist cause ahead of Monday's referendum.
Let Alberta Decide initially scheduled the event for 3 p.m. MT, but strong winds in the region led organizers to push the start time to 4 p.m.

Ten speakers are lined up for the event, including Keith Wilson, a lawyer who co-chairs the organization and heads the Alberta Transition Council, which has formed a plan should the province ultimately secede from Canada.

People from across the province were expected to attend, with the pro-separatist group arranging buses to take people from various cities to the Alberta legislature. According to the group’s website, 10 buses were rented to transport people living outside the capital city for a round-trip fee. Two buses each from Calgary and Leduc have sold out.

The Edmonton Police Service issued a traffic advisory Saturday morning, saying the demonstration could affect traffic in the city's core and around the legislative grounds. It advises motorists about potential delays in that area and to consider taking alternate routes.

According to the Let Alberta Decide website, 10 buses were rented to bring separation supporters living outside Edmonton to the pro-independence rally the group organized at the Alberta legislature on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Tristan Mottershead/CBC)
The scheduled rally is just one of several that have happened, or are planned, over the final days before Monday’s provincewide referendum, which will feature 10 questions.

The most notable question asks Albertans whether they want the province to remain in Confederation, or if they want the provincial government to start the legal process to hold a binding secession referendum.
According to Elections Alberta, hundreds of thousands of Albertans have already cast their ballots via mail or advance polls, which close at 8 p.m. Saturday.

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: On Monday, voting locations are open from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. If there are any lineups, stations will stay open longer to allow people to finish voting.

Polling has consistently suggested that most Albertans want to stay in Canada. But according to Elections Alberta, a significant number of Albertans back the independence movement: it verified almost 222,600 signatures for the Stay Free Alberta citizen initiative petition, headed by Mitch Sylvestre, leader of the Alberta Prosperity Project.
In late August, hundreds of people gathered at the legislature for another pro-separation rally.
With files from Nicholas Frew

articles.title: Pope Leo discharged from hospital after cancer operation
articles.summary: Doctors say pontiff is ‘fit for discharge’ after operation to remove cancerous tumour from his lung

blocks.text: Pope Leo has been discharged from hospital in Rome after undergoing an operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung.
Leo, 71, was deemed “fit for discharge”, his doctors, Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritoria, said in a statement published by the Vatican.
He walked unaided from the hospital on Saturday afternoon, to cheers from well-wishers.

Leo, who in May last year became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church, has been in the Gemelli hospital since Tuesday, when doctors removed part of his right lung in order to extract the tumour.
“Considering the blood tests, the chest X-ray done this morning, and evaluating the clinical picture, the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge,” the statement said.

Doctors said on Wednesday that Leo’s recovery from the operation was progressing normally. They are waiting for the results of tests to determine whether the cancer has spread and if more treatment will be needed.
Leo was diagnosed with the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma.
The pontiff celebrated mass in his room on the 10th-floor of the Gemelli hospital in the north-west of the Italian capital before being discharged.

blocks.caption: Leo celebrating Mass at the Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic in Rome. Photograph: Vatican Media/AP

blocks.text: The Vatican said he would recite the Angelus prayer on Sunday “from the window of the papal apartment”. It was during his angelus last week, in a rare moment of Vatican transparency, that Leo made the shock announcement to the crowd gathered in St Peter’s Square that a small nodule on his lung had been detected during a check-up.

The pope has worked from hospital, including making a phone call on Friday to Vladimir Putin, during which he urged the Russian president to call a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
The Vatican had originally estimated a week-long stay in hospital. The pope’s appointments had been cancelled until 20 October.
It is uncertain if he’ll make an intense 12-day trip to South America planned in November.
Cardinal ​Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s secretary of state, told reporters on Friday that Leo may need to readjust his trip schedule, at least with regard to South America, depending on his health.
Before the cancer diagnosis, Leo, who enjoys sports, especially playing tennis, was generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.

blocks.caption: The Gemelli hospital in Rome. Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/AP

blocks.text: The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish a high-security papal suite.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Trump’s lifting of sanctions on Russia will intensify war in Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukrainian president calls the move a ‘reward’ for Vladimir Putin as Russia strikes country’s power plants

blocks.text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Donald Trump’s decision to roll back sanctions on Russia will intensify the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine, as Moscow launched one of its worst strikes yet on Ukraine’s power plants in an attempt to black out the country’s cities before winter.

The Ukrainian president also said he expected the Trump administration to lift more sanctions against Russia in the future and called for Europe to establish its own negotiations with Moscow as the US has sought better ties and business deals with the Kremlin.

“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the ‘diesel deal’ is the first step,” said Zelenskyy on Saturday. “Unfortunately, it seems to me that this cannot stop Putin; on the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that he has such support.”
In a social media message earlier, Zelenskyy described Trump’s latest actions as a “reward” that would embolden the Russian president.

“A US ⁠sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground,” said Zelenskyy. “We must keep trying to end the ‌war. To end it, not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely.”

In its latest effort to reduce tensions with Russia, Trump announced on Friday that he would put a hold on a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.

The act, named for the late senator Lindsey Graham, who championed the legislation, would have introduced tough new sanctions on Russia including a 100% tariff on major importers of Russian oil such as China and India, as well as sanctions on Russia’s energy sector, financial institutions and shadow fleet of oil tankers.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said the decision to waive the sanctions would encourage Vladimir Putin to intensify the war in Ukraine and called for support in the US to resurrect the bill.

“At the time when the Russians launched such a massive strike against our energy sector, in America, regrettably, a decision was made to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war,” he wrote in a statement. “This law could have – and still can! – help a great deal. But the law needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters.”

The move was greeted by the Russian presidential envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, who wrote on social media: “The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment.”
The legislation, which sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps the country’s energy supplies moving, was due to be implemented in two days.

It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

Friday’s announcement comes a week after Trump said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.

Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1m tonnes “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional 3m tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
after newsletter promotion

The Trump administration’s decision to waive the sanctions is the latest consequence of a brutal quarrel between Trump and Zelenskyy. Several times this week, the US did not provide intelligence of impending ballistic missile attacks to Ukraine, and the White House reportedly ordered the Pentagon to throttle the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet network used by Ukraine’s armed forces to run its drone operations on the frontline.

“We very much hope – and I personally hope – that the president of the United States of America will do everything so that Putin stops the killings, stops the strikes on our energy infrastructure, and stops this war,” Zelenskyy said on Saturday. “But once again, you cannot achieve this by restricting Ukraine’s responses to Russia for killing our people. And even less so by lifting sanctions.”

Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries, as he has blamed the war in Ukraine, rather than the closure of the strait of Hormuz, for the worldwide spike in diesel prices. Ukraine unilaterally halted the strikes after Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, but resumed them when it became clear that Russia was stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian power plants and substations.

Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia had launched one of its worst strikes yet against the country’s energy infrastructure, hitting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities and causing “severe consequences”.

He also indicated that Ukraine’s dwindling stock of anti-air weapons made it difficult to shoot down many of the loitering munitions, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles being launched each night at Ukraine.

“Although our warriors are shooting down a significant number of them,” he said, the “sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia’s strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences.”

articles.title: Isabel Allende wins €1m Spanish literary prize under pseudonym
articles.summary:
Chilean-American author awarded Premio Planeta for sequel to her 1982 debut novel, The House of the Spirits

The Chilean-American author Isabel Allende has won Spain’s €1m (£843,000) Premio…

blocks.text: The Chilean-American author Isabel Allende has won Spain’s €1m (£843,000) Premio Planeta, one of the world’s most lucrative literary prizes, under a pseudonym, with a sequel to her celebrated debut novel, The House of the Spirits.

Allende, 84, won the 75th edition of the award on Thursday with La hora antes del alba, which returns to the characters of her 1982 novel, a multigenerational family saga set against political upheaval in a country inspired by Chile.

The new story follows Alba, the granddaughter of Esteban Trueba and Clara del Valle, as she tries to recover from imprisonment and torture during Pinochet’s dictatorship, according to Reuters. Allende said the book would bring the universe of The House of the Spirits to a close. The 1982 novel is often read alongside Daughter of Fortune and Portrait in Sepia as part of a loose trilogy of interconnected family sagas.
Speaking at the award ceremony in Barcelona, attended by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, Allende said it was “like winning the Nobel”.
“I had never entered a competition because I wanted to avoid the embarrassment of coming last,” she said. “At my age, there is very little to lose.”

She said she had been prompted to write the sequel by decades of readers asking what happened to Alba. She also drew parallels between the political circumstances surrounding the novel and the contemporary rise of extremism. Allende was forced into exile after the 1973 military coup led by Augusto Pinochet that overthrew the Chilean president Salvador Allende, a cousin of her father. Allende had been Latin America’s first democratically elected Marxist leader. Under Pinochet’s regime, an estimated 40,000 people were tortured and more than 3,000 killed.
“Now that I see so many democracies threatened by authoritarianism, extreme nationalism and even fascism, I feel again the fear that led me to leave my country,” she said.

Allende is one of the best-known writers in the Spanish-speaking world, whose books have sold more than 80m copies worldwide and been translated into more than 40 languages. The prize is open to unpublished manuscripts, with the option of submitting under a pseudonym, and Allende entered under the name Luz Ventura, with the fictional title Los que faltan.

However, the judges may have been able to pick up on Allende’s style. “I’d be very surprised if the judges did not know that it was Isabel Allende,” said Prof Duncan Wheeler, the chair of Spanish studies at Leeds University and president-elect of the Association of Hispanists of Great Britain and Ireland. “You have to bear in mind that the Planeta prize is one of the most generously remunerated in the Spanish-speaking world, but definitely not the most prestigious.”

The prize has at times faced criticism over the choice of winner. In 2021, the prize was awarded to La bestia, a thriller published under the pseudonym Carmen Mola, which had been marketed as the identity of a female author. At the awards ceremony, it was revealed that Mola was in fact three male writers – Jorge Díaz, Agustín Martínez and Antonio Mercero.

The prize is run by Planeta, one of the largest publishing groups in the Spanish-speaking world, and includes the condition that the winning book be published by them. Allende has been published by Plaza & Janés, an imprint of Penguin Random House, since The House of the Spirits, so this marks a significant coup for Planeta.

Despite the option to submit pseudonymously, the prize has a history of favouring established writers and TV figures: past winners of the prize have included prominent Spanish-language authors such as Juan Marsé and Manuel Vázquez Montalbán, and the controversial TV personality Juan de Val.

Asked about the perceived trend of awarding the prize to figures known for appearing on TV shows, José Creuheras, the president of the Planeta Group, said, according to the Spanish newspaper El País: “I’m not in a position to say whether the Planeta Prize has more or less prestige than it did in the past. We have some of contemporary literature’s biggest names among our winners and finalists. The prize’s reach, as measured by the figures, speaks for itself, and the number of people taking an interest in the Planeta is growing.”
The runner-up was the Spanish writer and screenwriter Sergio Hernández, whose historical novel La añoranza won €200,000.

articles.title: ‘We’re not playing games’: Parents launch playground protests to fight school field sell-off
articles.summary:
School looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishments

On Saturdays throughout autumn, residents of Totnes have met at a field on the banks of the…

blocks.text: On Saturdays throughout autumn, residents of Totnes have met at a field on the banks of the River Dart to play ballgames, fly kites or simply sit on the grass and chat.
But it hasn’t just been about having fun – this has been a “play protest” aimed at trying to save a beloved piece of open land in the historic Devon market town.

The local comprehensive, King Edward VI Community College (KEVICC), has been given the go-ahead by the UK government to sell the 1.5-hectare plot – Lower Field – and it is likely houses will be built on it.

School leaders say they desperately need funds to revamp neglected buildings but campaigners claim the sell-off is an example of land that has been used by communities for decades being whisked away – a modern “enclosure” of public space.

“It’s devastating,” said Becca Robinson, who uses the field for women’s and girls’ fitness classes. “I’m trying to get women and girls to be more active and to get outdoors. The great thing about the field is it’s an open space, so it feels safe. It really worries me that, if we lost it, fewer women and girls will exercise.
“It’s also a spot people go just to do their own thing rather than take part in structured sport. You can just make an ad hoc decision to go and play a game or just to sit and read.”

Earlier this year, the anti-poverty charity Trussell published research revealing almost half of UK residents (45%) had lost access to at least one community space – such as a park, social club, library or post office – since 2023.

Danielle McIlven, who has been organising games of rounders on the field, attended the school and said Lower Field had been part of her life for years. “It’s about the unstructured play that can take place there. In the summer you see swarms of teenagers playing there or heading down to the river.”

Anna Ali, the organiser of a women’s football “kickabout” and a member of the campaign group Friends of Lower Field, said the town had a reputation for being middle class and affluent. “But there is quite a lot of hidden impoverishment. Public green spaces are vital. I was speaking to a woman who brings her grandchildren here. They can’t afford to join sports clubs, so kicking a ball around on the field is a lifeline.”

Lewis Winks, a leading member of the Right to Roam group, said Lower Field had been shared by the school and the wider Totnes community since it was gifted by the Elmhirst family, known for progressive farming, forestry and educational projects on the nearby Dartington Estate, about a century ago.

blocks.caption: Campaigner Lewis Winks said Lower Field had been shared by the school and community for about a century. Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian

blocks.text: A key issue the Friends group is digging into is the details of the Elmhirst gift – and whether it may have been legally given to the community or permanently protected for community use.
Winks said: “Lower Field is a vital place for young people and families to play, exercise and spend time together. Losing it would undermine the town’s vitality and wellbeing.”
after newsletter promotion

The Friends group wants Education South West, the trust the school is part of, to explore whether the field could be sold to the community. Winks said: “We are asking for a realistic window to raise the money. A community purchase could help fund improvements at KEVICC while safeguarding the field for its pupils and the wider community.”

But it is a race against time. The land is expected to be put on the market in January, giving little time to raise funds. Campaigners also highlight that measures under the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 aimed at giving communities greater influence over the places and assets that matter to them are unlikely to come into force in time. “We’re falling through the gap regarding a right to buy,” Winks said.
Matthew Shanks, chief executive of Education South West, said it understood how important the site was to the Totnes community and wanted to have an open and constructive conversation with people.

He said money raised would support significant refurbishment and modernisation across the school estate, including improvements to buildings and facilities. Shanks said the school would retain playing fields which would remain available for public use.

School principal Alan Salt said he understood the future of the field mattered hugely to the community. “We want to be open and transparent about what is proposed.” The trust and school have organised an open meeting to discuss the field.
Salt argued that selling it made sound financial sense. There had been little capital investment in the school for six years and it had “temporary” classrooms more than half a century old.

“So we’ve got a really acute set of challenges within a very difficult national context,” he said. “At the end of the day, we are a comprehensive school trying to get the best for the students in a really difficult national picture.”

articles.title: Pope to be discharged days after lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: The pontiff will give the traditional Angelus prayer and blessing in St Peter's Square on Sunday.

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV will be discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Saturday afternoon, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung.
The Vatican said the Pope will give the traditional Angelus prayer and blessing to a crowd in St Peter's Square on Sunday, as he did last week when he surprised the world by announcing the surgery.
On Friday, photographs were released of the Pope celebrating Mass and distributing communion in hospital for staff.
A statement from his doctors said blood tests and a chest X-ray showed "steady improvement" following his operation.

The surgery on Tuesday, which lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung. The results of further tests to check for any sign that the cancer has spread have not yet been announced.
The Pope also spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, in their first call since June 2025. The Vatican said the call was to urge "dialogue and peace".
It came as Russia's bombardment of cities across Ukraine intensifies, with a growing number of civilian casualties and no sign of Putin being ready to halt the invasion.

The Pope also called for a humanitarian ceasefire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshkiy, occupied by Russia and under constant shelling, to allow people to be evacuated and for the urgent delivery of food and medicine. The BBC recently reported on residents there being forced to eat garden weeds to survive.
The Pope's schedule has been cleared completely until 20 October, so his reappearance in public so soon is a surprise and will be some relief for Catholics around the world.
Those close to the Pope said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America, planned for early November and which includes a visit to Peru, where he was a missionary for many years.
It is not yet clear whether he might be fit to travel or require further treatment.

articles.title: Sara Duterte denies Jollibee franchise ownership
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte denied claims that she owns a Jollibee franchise, accusing online news platform Rappler of publishing misleading reports about her business interests.

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 8:19pm
Vice President Sara Duterte denied claims that she owns a Jollibee franchise, accusing online news platform Rappler of publishing misleading reports about her business interests.

“I do not own a Jollibee franchise or any other franchise. I previously invested in a company that is part of a legitimate business organization owned and operated by individuals with an established reputation for integrity and good standing,” Duterte said in a statement on Saturday.

“A basic level of research and due diligence should make this clear. Rappler should understand that investing in a company does not automatically equate to owning the company itself, much less owning, managing or operating its individual businesses or franchises,” she added.
She also raised concerns over the “apparent targeting of legitimate businesses, which inevitably causes unwarranted reputational and commercial damage.”
Jollibee was previously linked to Duterte in a forensic financial report presented by analyst Alexander Cabrera during her impeachment trial.
According to Cabrera, GenCorp, a company listed in Duterte’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN), reportedly owned five Jollibee restaurants.
GMA News has reached out to Rappler for comment and will update this story once a response is received. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Nursery owner in China jailed for life after hundreds of children poisoned
articles.summary: She and five staff members were found to have used the inedible paint in meals to make them look more appealing.

blocks.text: A nursery owner and five members of her staff have been jailed after they were found to have poisoned more than 200 children with lead-tainted food.

Li Huifang, who operated the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Tianshui, in the Gansu province, was sentenced to life in prison for producing and selling toxic and harmful food, according to Chinese state media.
In July 2025, 247 pupils and staff at the nursery were found to have abnormally high blood lead levels after children began falling ill.
A report into the incident found that chefs at Heshi Peixin had used inedible paint to "enhance the look" of its meals to attract more students - despite the paint being being clearly marked as such.
In addition to the sentence, the Lanzhou Intermediate People's Court also ordered the confiscation of 500,000 yuan (£56,200; $74,700) of Li's personal assets, state broadcaster CCTV reported.
Nursery executive principal Zhi Jinglin was sentenced to 15 years in prison and fined 300,00 yuan.
Four other members of staff who worked in the nursery's kitchen received sentences of between six to eight years, according to state media.
The court found the four had been instructed by Li and Zhi to add toxic and harmful ingredients to food served to children and staff.
Food samples were later found to contain lead 2,000 times in excess of China's national safety limit.
The investigation into the poisoning began after 235 children from Heshi Peixin nursery had to be treated for lead poisoning after eating steamed red date cakes and sausage corn buns.

Investigators found that the red date cake and the corn sausage rolls had lead levels of 1052mg/kg and 1340mg/kg respectively, both of which far exceed the national food safety standard limit of 0.5mg/kg.
Lead poisoning is "particularly harmful to young children" and can "severely damage the brain and central nervous system", according to the World Health Organization.
Officials later found that dozens of provincial officials and hospital staff attempted to cover up the incident by tampering with blood tests and accepting bribes from a nursery investor.

China has since published a set of national guidelines for the provision of meals on campuses. Among the measures is the requirement for every new batch of food to be tested, and for flour, rice and cooking oil to be purchased from centralised procurement points only.

articles.title: Who's a good mayor? Kitimat adds 2 dogs to the ballot to boost voter turnout
articles.summary: With just 21 per cent of eligible voters casting ballots in the last municipal election, Kitimat is hoping two canine candidates can get more residents — including children — interested in voting.

image.caption: Kitimat residents will be able to vote for Gus, left, or Koko in a separate dog mayor race on Oct. 17. (Cameron Orr/District of Kitimat)

blocks.text: British Columbia
With just 21 per cent of eligible voters casting ballots in the last municipal election, Kitimat is hoping two canine candidates can get more residents — including children — interested in voting.
Gus and Koko are vying to be Kitimat's dog mayor, with promises of more fire hydrants and pet-friendly sirens
In an effort to improve voter turnout and encourage youth to engage with politics, the District of Kitimat in northwest B.C. is running a separate mayoral campaign — for dogs.
On general election day Oct. 17, residents of all ages will be able to cast their ballots and vote for either Gus or Koko, in addition to the usual voting for mayor and council.
During the last municipal election, voter turnout was just 21 per cent, said Cameron Orr, the business and communications manager for the district of Kitimat.
In fact, voter turnout for the district has been gradually dropping over the last several elections, he explained.
So, it was time to get creative.
"We were just thinking about some ways that we can make it more exciting and encourage more people to come out and vote," said Orr.
"[We] thought, dogs can be a really great spokesperson for the community, and that kids would enjoy it and it would get a bit of attention."
Both canines have been campaigning diligently by visiting local classrooms, and even marching in the Canada Day parade on July 1.
The hope is that children will encourage their families to vote on the election day, said Orr, and so far the reaction has been positive.
"The kids go crazy for the dogs, they love seeing them," said Orr.
"There’s been some really interesting questions. The kids seem to be really paying attention to the campaign promises, and what the dogs have in mind for the community."
Some have even drawn campaign signs for their candidate of choice, he added, and parents have told him about their children debating with each other on the way to school.
More fire hydrants, pet-friendly sirens
Koko, a goldendoodle, promises pet-friendly emergency sirens and "dog days" at the local pool.
Her owner and spokesperson, Dawn Adams, said Koko loves children, frisbee and walks in the park.
As a responsible mayoral hopeful, Koko also gets her teeth brushed every night, and "will remind you if you forget."
Koko is campaigning on promises of pet-friendly emergency sirens and dog days at the local pool. (Cameron Orr/District of Kitimat)
"She's just super happy to come out and say hi to people and meet people and get kids interested," said Adams.
"I do hear from time to time when I'm out and about, people ask me, where's your dog? Where's Koko? We want to see Koko. And then it gets the questions going."
Meanwhile, Gus, an Australian Labradoodle, is campaigning on more fire hydrants "for obvious reasons" and improved poop bag access in local parks.
Gus and his owner were unavailable for an interview with CBC News.
However, a campaign statement says Gus would make Kitimat "better and more pet-friendly than ever."
"Together, we will achieve a better, and fuzzier future," it reads.
Gus is hoping to win voters over with a promise of a 'better and fuzzier future.' (Cameron Orr/District of Kitimat)
The district says the platforms do not represent actual campaign promises, and that the role is largely ceremonial.
The winning candidate will serve out a four-year term alongside the Kitimat mayor.
Voters can cast their ballot for either Koko or Gus at a dedicated ballot box at Kitimat polling stations.
Results from the race for dog mayor will be posted on District of Kitimat social media pages on Monday.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Catherine Garrett is a CBC News reporter based in Terrace, B.C., covering the province's northwest region. Born in Ontario and raised on Haida Gwaii, she has previously worked in Vancouver, Prince George, B.C., and Grande Prairie, Alta. She has received multiple awards for her work, including a Canadian Online Publishing Award. You can contact her at catherine.garrett@cbc.ca.

articles.title: UAE agrees with Saudi Arabia to re-enter Yemen conflict amid Houthi gains
articles.summary: United Arab Emirates will reportedly resume payments to Yemeni forces as gains by Iran-backed Houthi fighters alarm Gulf state rulers

blocks.text: The United Arab Emirates has agreed to re-enter the Yemen conflict by resuming payments to some government forces fighting Iran-aligned Houthis in the south, according to sources in Yemen. In return, Saudi Arabia has agreed to provide air cover for the anti-Houthi force.

The new cooperation agreement is the first tangible signs that the deep rift between the UAE and Saudi Arabia over Yemen’s future is starting to be healed – if only because the advance by Houthi forces across Yemen has alarmed all the rival Gulf state rulers.
Saudi Arabia is facing daily drone and missile attacks and is struggling to maintain an atmosphere of normality, as Houthi strikes immobilise its airports and some of its energy infrastructure.

Southern forces – mainly in the Giant Brigades – were previously trained and funded by the UAE, and are regarded as some of the most effective in the disjointed anti-Houthi military coalition. But the UAE quit operations inside Yemen in January, cutting off its funding supply line.

Neither Saudi Arabia nor the UAE have responded to a demand this week by southern Yemen separatists for a referendum on secession, a move that would restore the 1967-1990 borders, when Yemen was two separate states.

blocks.caption: Yemeni Southern Giants Brigades fighters celebrate and wave their weapons. Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The separatist Southern Transition Council has also not yet agreed for its troops to fight outside the borders of the old Southern Yemen, but an explicit agreement by Saudi Arabia to allow a referendum would be likely to lead to the lifting of that restriction.

Yemen’s UN-recognised government, based in Aden, declared last week a counteroffensive to drive Houthi forces from the capital Sana’a, but so far the military drive has met with limited success around Majzar near Marib and the Bab al-Mandab strait.

There is also no direct contact between the STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, and Saudi officials. Zubaidi fled to Abu Dhabi in January after a failed STC attempt to take charge across the south and announce a referendum on separation in two years’ time. In response, the Saudis bombed UAE arms shipments for STC forces.
The UAE then announced it was quitting all involvement in Yemen, and the Saudi-backed government said it would seek to try Zubaidi for treason.

UAE officials are deeply concerned by the state of the conflict. Despite massive losses, the Houthis are determined eventually to capture Taiz and Marib, the two remaining cities outside the boundaries of the old Southern Yemen.
On Friday two missiles fired by the Houthis struck the airport of Aden while a passenger plane was preparing to take off. No casualties were reported.
The missiles landed about 500 meters from the Yemenia Airways aircraft, and approximately 100 meters from the midpoint of the runway, said Yemen’s information minister, Moammar Al-Eryani.
The strike came a day after at least five people were killed and 16 injured in a Houthi attack on a presidential palace in Aden.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fattah el Sisi, said he was convening an emergency session of parliament to grant his country’s military the powers to take action in defence of Saudi Arabia. He stressed Egypt would not be taking any offensive action, and would only defend Saudi Arabia.

In the UK, discussions are continuing about a Saudi request for further military aid. The UK has sent an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft, but regional diplomats are pressing for the UK to do more. Some concern is being expressed over whether Riyadh should be engaging closer with other Gulf States, including Oman and Qatar, on the issue.

The legal implications of a blanket UK backing for the largely Saudi air campaign is also being considered, since the court of appeal in 2019 found the UK had acted unlawfully in issuing arms export licences during a previous Saudi bombing campaign of Yemen in 2015-16. The Campaign Against Arms Trade said the UK had made no proper assessment of potential Saudi breaches of international humanitarian law, forcing the UK to revise its procedures.

Saudi Arabia claims to have revised its methods substantially since then, and certainly argues that it is acting in self-defence in line with the UN charter. The UN security council on 15 October adopted a UN presidential statement on 15 October asserting Saudi Arabia’s right to act in self-defence in line with international law.

No accurate death toll in the war since August is available, but more than 200,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN, which is placing increasing pressure on Aden-based humanitarian groups.

articles.title: Ombudsman, Customs to formalize data-sharing deal in November
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman will sign a memorandum of agreement (MOA) with the Bureau of Customs (BOC) in November to facilitate data sharing, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said Saturday.

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 7:56pm
The Office of the Ombudsman will sign a memorandum of agreement (MOA) with the Bureau of Customs (BOC) in November to facilitate data sharing, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said Saturday.
“Itong November, we’ll be signing a MOA (memorandum of agreement) na with Customs, data sharing na. Customs, first time ‘yan mangyayari,” Remulla said in his radio program.
(This November, we’ll be signing a MOA with Customs on data sharing. It will be the first time this will happen with the BOC.)
In a statement, BOC Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno confirmed the planned agreement.

“Ombudsman Boying Remulla and myself have a common objective. To fight corruption in government. This is why the Ombudsman and BOC will formally sign an agreement to institutionalize the automatic sharing of data and other information so that cases will be strong and offenders will be held accountable. This is an effective deterrence against smuggling,” Nepomuceno said.
Remulla previously said the lack of data sharing with the BOC had hampered efforts to build strong anti-smuggling cases.
He also said the bureau had failed to provide complete documentation needed for the filing or investigation of cases.
The Department of Justice (DOJ), National Bureau of Investigation (NBI), and the BOC had previously signed a separate MOA aimed at combating economic sabotage. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Russia wants blackout in Ukraine as winter comes — Zelenskyy
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy says Russia is trying to cut electricity and heating to civilians ahead of winter. He also called the US president's waiver of new sanctions on Moscow a boost for…

image.caption: Zaporizhzia in eastern Ukraine came under renewed attack overnightImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Russia is stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in a bid to cut electricity and heating in the country as winter approaches, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday.
His remarks come as Moscow intensifies its attacks on civilian targets in the capital, Kyiv, and elsewhere, with key observers saying its objective is to render the country virtually unlivable.

blocks.caption: Overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia killed a 64-year-old man Image: Daria Nazarova/AFP

blocks.text: What did Zelenskyy say?

In a post on social media platform X, Zelenskyy said Russia had just carried out one of its biggest attacks on Ukraine's energy sector since it began its full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.
"More than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities were targeted across different regions of Ukraine," he wrote.
"Restoration work is ongoing, with all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies involved," he added.
Zelenskyy said that Russia was planning to leave Ukrainian citizens in the cold this winter.

"Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine — right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating," he wrote, calling on allies to put pressure on Moscow to stop this happening.
He said Russia had "expanded ‌its campaign ​against the energy system" and was trying "to stretch ⁠Ukraine's ​reserves ​and repair ​capacity as ‌thinly as possible." ​
Russia claims multiple infrastructure attacks
The Russian Defense Ministry, for its part, said on Saturday that its forces had attacked several infrastructure targets in Ukraine overnight.
Among those named was an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr.
However, it also said Ukraine's largest steelworks, in the city of Kryvyi Rih, had been hit, saying the facility supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex.
It said another steel plant in ​Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front ​line, had also been struck.
Ukrainian authorities have also said that one person — an ambulance driver — was killed ​and ‌19 others injured, including a child, in a Russian airstrike on Kherson in southern Ukraine.
Russian state news ​agency TASS has also reported the death of one woman as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes in Russia's Belgorod region that also injured a man.

blocks.caption: Russia's overnight attacks hit numerous civilian sitesImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Trump's sanctions waiver a boost for Putin: Zelenskyy
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy also reacted to US President Donald Trump's decision to waive a package of new sanctions on Moscow, saying the move would only encourage Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
"A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," Zelenskyy said.
On Friday, Trump signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia's energy revenues, two days before they were due to take effect.
The waiver has been hailed by a Russian presidential envoy as a "historic moment."
"The Trump administration's suspension of the [Lindsey] Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev said on social media.
Dmitriev said the act, named for the late US senator who sponsored the bill, "would have caused "serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets."
Trump's move came as he increasingly criticizes Zelenskyy, fueling speculation that the US leader is siding with Moscow in the conflict.

articles.title: It's over: Canada ends England's 41-match unbeaten streak in women's rugby
articles.summary: England's unprecedented 41-game unbeaten run was broken by Canada 24-21 and witnessed by the biggest crowd in North American women’s rugby on Friday in Toronto.

image.caption: Team Canada celebrates their win over England in women's rugby action in Toronto on Friday. It was the first loss suffered by the Red Roses in 41 matches. (Arlyn McAdorey/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Rugby
England's unprecedented 41-game unbeaten run was broken by Canada 24-21 and witnessed by the biggest crowd in North American women’s rugby on Friday in Toronto.
Top-ranked Red Roses fall to Canadians 24-21 in Toronto
Canada, unable to handle England's scrum, trailed 14-5 at halftime and 21-12 after more than an hour and didn't settle a compelling WXV contest until a 78th-minute try by Shoshanah Seumanutafa.
“We really had to grind it out and find a way,” Canada captain Sophie de Goede said. “That's kind of the DNA of our team.”
England suffered its first loss since the 2022 Women's Rugby World Cup final, its only previous defeat in 72 matches since 2019.

items: Canadian women's rugby aims to deal England its 1st loss in 41 matches during upcoming double-header

blocks.text: “Sometimes the flipped coin doesn't go on the side you want it to go,” England captain Meg Jones said. "It's just the nature of the beast."

England showed vulnerability last month at home where it drew with Canada 26-26, ending its 39-match winning streak. That effort gave Canada confidence for the return match at home, including the availability of world player of the year De Goede, rested from its last match, a loss in France, and wings Asia Hogan-Rochester and Alysha Corrigan after injuries.

The hope drew 18,621 spectators, 7,000 more than the previous biggest crowd for a standalone women’s match in North America. England should have scored first but Claudia Moloney-MacDonald dropped the ball over the tryline.
Then Canada used numbers after a Zoe Harrison yellow card for fullback Savannah Bauder to score in a three-on-one.

England stumbles continued with three turnovers in the Canada 22, two on the tryline. But after Canada lock Laetitia Royer was sin-binned, England powered ahead with tries by Maddie Feaunati and Harrison before halftime.

items: Canada halts England's record 39-match win streak in a gripping 26-26 rugby draw

blocks.text: Canada closed to 14-12 in the second half when Corrigan collected her own grubber kick and celebrated before scoring. But England moved further ahead 21-12 after 12 phases when prop Sarah Bern smashed over.

Canada was plagued by forward passes but stayed calm. A missed penalty touch-finder by England was countered and prop DaLeaka Menin, one of three Canada survivors from its last win over England 10 years ago, plowed over to cut the gap to two again. Another England clearance was returned by Canada from its half and De Goede and Gabrielle Senft lined up Seumanutafa to beat the cover to the left corner flag and cap a milestone night in Canadian rugby.
They go again in Ottawa next Friday.

articles.title: Plaque telling story of African-Caribbean prisoners in Britain stolen within days
articles.summary:
Descendants say theft from Portchester Castle reflects spirit of racism that has haunted ‘generation after generation’

The theft of a plaque in Hampshire that told the little-known story of…

blocks.text: The theft of a plaque in Hampshire that told the little-known story of African-Caribbean prisoners in 18th-century Britain reflects the enduring racism that has fuelled centuries of atrocities against Black and Indigenous Caribbean people, their descendants say.

Drummer Ronald Raymond McDonald was part of a delegation that travelled from Belize and elsewhere to Portchester Castle last week to honour their ancestors: 2,500 men, women and children transported to Britain as prisoners of war in 1796.

McDonald, whose Garifuna ancestors from St Vincent and the Grenadines were among the prisoners, said he was heartbroken to learn that the plaque had been stolen and a nearby bench vandalised with hateful graffiti.
“Why would somebody do something like that when people are simply honouring their ancestors … It’s very sad,” he said.

The plaque, installed at the castle, commemorated the more than 2,000 prisoners held there, marking an extraordinary chapter of Black British history: one of the largest known arrivals of African-Caribbean people in Britain before the Windrush era.

The unveiling was part of a ceremony organised by the St Vincent and the Grenadines 2nd Generation (SV2G), in partnership with the University of Warwick and English Heritage, and was attended by Caribbean communities, diplomats, researchers and heritage organisations.

blocks.caption: The unveiling was attended by Caribbean communities, diplomats, researchers and heritage organisations. Photograph: English Heritage

blocks.text: But days later, English Heritage staff discovered the plaque was missing. They said a padlock to one of the castle gates had been removed and the incident had been reported to police.

Garifuna advocate Princess Eulogia said the theft reflected “a spirit of racism that haunts generation after generation and hides in plain sight”. It was time, she said, to recognise that “we are all connected” and to end the hate.
Queen Mother Chief Freda Paulino-Sideroff, who is Garifuna and had travelled to the UK for the ceremony, was returning home to the US when she learned of the theft.

“Hate will never define who we are as a people. We are resilient survivors of our ancestors who have endured,” she said. In the 1700s, her Garifuna ancestors were expelled from St Vincent by British forces and left to perish on the barren island of Baliceaux as Britain sought to crush decades of resistance to colonisation.

Emilio ‘Sásamu’ Thomas, a Garifuna cultural ambassador who also travelled from Belize for the ceremony, echoed Paulino-Sideroff’s defiance, saying Garifuna people would not allow themselves to be victimised. His message to the perpetrators, he said, was: “Whatever pain that they are experiencing, we’re here to help them to relieve that pain.”

The missing plaque was meant to honour the prisoners, whose story, researchers say, had been largely lost to history. They came from a coalition that included formerly enslaved Africans, Caribbean-born people, Indigenous people and French soldiers who fought against British control of St Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines and Grenada. Their defeat and removal helped strengthen British rule in the region.
It was unveiled on 9 October, exactly 230 years after one of the ships carrying the prisoners was wrecked at Rapparee Cove in Devon, with many of those on board losing their lives.

Iona Keen of English Heritage called the removal an act of vandalism, while University of Warwick professor Katherine Astbury said the plaque was intended to provide a visible memorial of the prisoners, and a reminder of “an important, forgotten part of Caribbean history”.

The incident comes during Black History Month and amid renewed debate over slavery reparations. Campaigner and author Sir Patrick Vernon said vandalism of memorials representing Black British history had occurred repeatedly over decades, citing damage to other memorials.
He described the theft as symbolic of an “ongoing battle and the legacy of enslavement”.

Jacqueline Roberts, SV2G chief executive, said the theft could not erase history, and stressed the importance of continuing research to uncover more hidden stories. “Our history is intertwined with British history,” she said. “It’s important to understand that part of our journey, because it is part of the complexity of our identity, and affects our sense of belonging.”

Anthony Severin, St Lucia’s high commissioner and chair of the Caribbean community diplomatic caucus in the UK, described the theft as a “desecration of the memory and spirit of our commemorated ancestors”. He pledged that the plaque “whether returned or replaced, will remain affixed to the walls of Portchester Castle”.

articles.title: Rare pink diamond goes on display in France 100 years after amateur heist
articles.summary: The French royal jewel will be on public display for the first time since it was found hidden in an apple after a 1926 theft.

blocks.text: A rare pink diamond is going on display in France for the first time since it was stolen almost 100 years ago to the day - the last time it was shown to the public.
The nine-carat, pear-shaped gemstone known as the "Grand Condé" was pilfered in an overnight raid on the Château de Chantilly in October 1926 and concealed in a hollowed-out apple.
The diamond - one of few royal jewels to survive the French Revolution - was recovered a few weeks later when a hungry maid at the hotel in which the thieves were staying took a bite of the apple.
It will once again be on display in the Condé Museum at the Château de Chantilly until 3 January.
The museum's director Mathieu Deldicque said that while the apple story may sounds far-fetched, it was widely covered by newspapers at the time.

Deldicque has faced questions about whether the exhibition may be tempting fate, especially given the string of heists on European cultural institutions in the past 12 months, including the daring daylight robbery of jewellery from the Louvre museum in Paris.
While he declined to reveal to CNN how much the diamond was insured for, he noted that extensive academic study into the properties of the diamond had taken place to make it uniquely identifiable.
The results of this analysis, as well as previously unseen archive material about the gem's history and theft, form part of the exhibition, according to the museum.

Naturally occurring pink diamonds are exceptionally rare and often sell for tens of millions of dollars. The highest price ever fetched for one at auction was $71.2m (£53.6m) in 2017, according to Sotheby's.
The exact origins of the Grand Condé remain a mystery.
It was first mentioned in 1740 in an inventory of Louis Henri de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, drawn up following his death, the Château de Chantilly said.
It then became part of the collection of Queen Marie-Amélie of Bourbon-Sicily, the wife of French King Louis Philippe I, and then her son, Prince Henri of Orléans, the Duke of Aumale.

He bequeathed it to the Institut de France, which now owns the Château de Chantilly, 50km (31 miles) north of Paris, along with thousands of artworks and manuscripts which became the Musée Condé collection.

articles.title: Germany news: Berlin's leftist parties move step closer to forming government

image.caption: Leaders of the Left, the Greens and the SPD in Berlin reached an initial agreement to start coalition negotiations — now it's up to their parties to decide if the talks go aheadImage: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: October 17, 2026
Berlin coalition hopefuls to focus on housing
Berlin's Left Party, the Greens and the Social Democrats (SPD) revealed details of what they hope will be their governing policy, should the coalition be approved by their parties' members.
Among the policies, the possible left-wing Berlin state government could bring around 160,000 apartments under public ownership.
The Left's Elif Eralp, who is seeking to become leader of Berlin, said the compromise would affect five companies, including Germany's largest property company, Vonovia.

It all comes as voters made unaffordable housing a central issue, one that The Left campaigned on, as rent costs in Berlin have spiraled in recent years and public apartments have been in short supply.

Eralp said the three parties also agreed on a "very ambitious new building program" for public housing, where they hope to get 100,000 planning permissions by 2031, which will then lead to 100,000 new affordable flats.
The coalition hopefuls would also work to implement a rent cap for publicly owned apartments.

articles.title: From ‘killing the golden goose’ to better than ever: Has Alberta's relationship with Ottawa changed?
articles.summary: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith once said Ottawa "couldn't help" but be fixated on "punishing" the energy sector. Now, she says Canada is working better than it ever has. So what changed? And will it…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney has a beer with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith as he visits supporters of a Vote to Stay event in Red Deer, Alta., on Oct. 16 ahead of a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty. (Todd Korol/Reuters)

blocks.text: The relationship between Alberta and the federal government has faced its share of political and economic conflict over the years. Some Albertans would argue more than its fair share.

From the drawing of the province’s boundaries to natural resource control to the creation of the National Energy Program to pipeline cancellations and political representation, generations of Albertans have expressed feelings of alienation.

Last year, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith added to the litany of rebukes of Ottawa from Alberta leaders over the years. (Her predecessor, Jason Kenney, once said the federal government was "killing the golden goose".)

After launching a panel tour to hear citizens' frustrations, Smith said, “You know what Ottawa can't help but be fixated on? ... Punishing our energy sector and layering on policies to keep it in the ground."
She made those remarks nearly two months after the Liberals won a fourth-consecutive election under new leader Mark Carney.
Members of the Alberta Next panel gathered for a public town hall meeting in Red Deer at the Westerner Park grounds on July 25, 2025. (Jason Markusoff/CBC)
Fast forward to this fall, with Albertans poised to go to the polls in a referendum that could ultimately lead to a separation vote, and Smith is expressing a very different view.
“I do think Canada is working better than it ever has,” Smith told CBC News, noting she will be voting for the province to stay put.

The remarks follow months of Smith saying that, in her view, working out the differences between Alberta and Ottawa would be the key to quelling separatist sentiment, a blueprint she said is shared by Carney.
Premier says Alberta and Canada 'walking together' for first time in a long time
So what changed in the relationship between the province and Ottawa? Is Alberta really in a better place than a year ago? And if so, for how long?

For her part, Smith said that Alberta has “finally” found a government willing to move swiftly on major projects, such as the Pacific Link pipeline, while not “standing in the way” of Alberta developing its resources.
Carney, the premier said, is a “different type of leader.”
“I think he understands the Constitution. I think he respects the constitutional division of powers,” she said. “There’s areas that are federal jurisdiction, and areas of provincial jurisdiction.”
That’s why, the premier argued, Albertans should vote to remain in Canada, with a newfound belief that federation can function fairly.

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: But those who say the province needs to go its own way to realize its true potential see Carney’s promises as mere window dressing after years of policy that stymied economic growth and personal freedoms.
Constitutional lawyer Keith Wilson argued in favour of Alberta independence at a debate in Calgary held in late May. (New West Video)
“They’re just saying, 'Hey, we’re getting along.' Well, what if they stop getting along?” said Keith Wilson, one of the most prominent leaders in the Alberta separatist movement.
“I am not satisfied to have the future of my children’s success and prosperity hinge upon whether the prime minister and a premier have a good personal relationship.”
No to the nine ('bad laws')

In addition to the proposed Pacific Link pipeline and other federal investments, Smith has praised federal movement around what she calls the “nine bad laws” that she demanded be addressed in order to avoid an “unprecedented national unity crisis.”
As detailed by Smith in March 2025, they were, in brief:

items: the oil and gas emissions cap;
returning oversight of the industrial carbon tax to the provinces;
the net-zero power regulations;
the EV mandate;
repealing Bill C-69, otherwise known as the Impact Assessment Act;
guaranteeing Alberta “full access” to oil and gas corridors;
lifting the B.C. tanker ban;
ending the prohibition on single-use plastics; and
“halting the federal censorship” of energy companies.

blocks.text: A spokesperson in the premiers’ office said it considers seven of the nine “scrapped or reformed.”
“Investment is soaring and major projects are moving forward again. This is proof of progress and a more collaborative relationship,” Ryan Fournier wrote in an email.
Ottawa and Alberta engaged in 'tough collaboration,' says Carney
The federal government revised those policies amid criticism from some that the moves would claw back environmental protections and concern from others surrounding Indigenous consultation.

Wilson isn’t satisfied with progress to date, citing, among other developments, a recent Alberta Court of Appeal ruling that stated the federal government’s Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional.
“I’m sorry, but this is just … political platitudes, absent substantive action. If the prime minister was serious about these things, he would offer to change equalization,” he said.
“He would announce that he’s going to follow the court decision, and repeal Bill C-69 [the Impact Assessment Act]. Surely, people aren’t this gullible. But maybe they are?”
The Alberta Court of Appeal in Calgary is seen in this file photo. Earlier this month, it ruled the federal government's Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional. (Google Maps)

Heather Exner-Pirot, director of energy, natural resources and environment at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute in Ottawa, said that Canada had a “terrible reputation” for investment due to policies implemented under former prime minister Justin Trudeau.
“The corrections to the ‘nine bad laws’ … those are all meaningful, in that they have attracted investment,” she said.

“You can always say that things aren’t perfect, or there’s things we can still do to improve competitiveness, but I don’t think anyone would have anticipated two years ago that we could be where we are here today.”

Earlier this month, the federal and Alberta governments announced that the proposed Pacific Link pipeline, which would carry one million barrels of oil a day from Alberta to the B.C. coast, had become the first project designated in the national interest. That classification means that federal approvals and regulatory reviews will be fast-tracked.
Prominent separatists, meanwhile, have argued that the Pacific Link pipeline is not a point in Carney’s favour.
How much money could the new Pacific Link Pipeline cost Canadian taxpayers?

“This is a nationalized pipeline. Is that really the only way to get something done in Canada, is to have the government do it?” said Cory Morgan, who heads the third-party advertiser Pathway to Independence, in a recent video. “That’s not a good sign, guys.”
Exner-Pirot said government de-risking is necessary for West Coast pipelines given challenges tied to past projects.

After Kinder Morgan halted construction on the Trans Mountain pipeline, the federal government under Trudeau took over, buying the troubled project for $4.5 billion in 2018. The project cost eventually spiralled to $34 billion.

items: Trans Mountain pipeline will soon be at full capacity amid global energy crisis

blocks.text: “The particular circumstances of a west coastal pipeline are terrible,” Exner-Pirot said. “I think, [it is] justified for government to de-risk it, and to show that it can be done.”

Heather Exner-Pirot, director of energy, natural resources and environment at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, says changes to laws and regulations under Prime Minister Mark Carney have made Canada more competitive and attractive for investment. (Paula Duhatschek/CBC)
However, Exner-Pirot said many other energy projects, including other pipelines, are moving forward successfully without government subsidies — like LNG Canada's Phase 2 expansion in Kitimat, B.C.

items: Enbridge breaks ground on $4B natural gas pipeline expansion

blocks.text: “So, the idea that we’re not building anything else except for this one project with government funding or backing is simply not true.”
Fault lines
In the eyes of the Alberta government, the “nine bad laws” may be well on their way to a resolution under Canada’s new prime minister.
But Carney’s comments tied to the “No to the Nine” campaign drew prompt opposition from the provincial government on Thursday.

"No to the Nine" is a prominent federalist advertising campaign that urges Albertans to reject the nine referendum ballot questions not concerned with separation. Five of those questions deal with immigration, while four are aimed at constitutional reforms, like abolishing the Senate.

At a Thursday event, Carney suggested Albertans should vote “No to the Nine." The premier then posted on X that despite the two finding common ground on many issues, it appeared Carney “had yet to fully understand just how damaging the open-border policies” of his predecessor were.
Ian Brodie, a political scientist at the University of Calgary who was chief of staff to former prime minister Stephen Harper, called Carney’s comments a “miss.”

“The winning federalist campaign here is to acknowledge that Alberta has had a short shrift from Confederation over the last few years, and that changes are needed if the province is going to get a fair deal,” Brodie said on CBC Radio's Calgary Eyeopener.
Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke alongside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Friday at a brewery in Red Deer, Alta. (CBC)
For his part, Carney said Thursday that he didn’t “need a referendum” to co-operate more with the provinces on immigration.
“The province is closer to the needs of the industries here, where the shortages are,” Carney told Global News, adding the federal government had already taken “control” on changes to immigration.

items: Alberta referendum pitches more control over immigration. Here's what you need to know

blocks.text: Despite the potential awkwardness, Carney made a campaign stop with Smith at a brewery in Red Deer on Friday, where he made a point of characterizing the relationship between the two as involving “tough collaboration.”
“In our time working together, the premier has consistently put the most difficult issues on the table, with the intention of finding a common way forward,” Carney said.
The conversations to come
“Ottawa may be 2,000 miles away, but destructive federal policy travels on winged feet and strikes like the wrath of God.”

That’s how Monte Solberg, an Alberta MP from 1993 to 2008 for the Reform Party, Canadian Alliance and Conservative Party of Alberta, characterized the relationship between the West and Ottawa in a 2018 column on alienation written for CBC News.

Today, he’s pushing for the federalist side in the referendum, as part of the Vote to Stay campaign. In his view, now is not the time to separate, as Canada is locked in negotiations with the United States.
“That doesn’t mean that, over time, there shouldn’t be a discussion about how we address some of the unfairness in Confederation,” he said.
As to whether the prime minister is the person who will have that conversation?
“Well, I think it’ll be a priority for the premier [of Alberta], and for some other premiers. They’ll have their chance to make their case that this needs to be addressed,” Solberg said.
“I think there is a potential to do so with this prime minister that there wasn’t with, certainly, Justin Trudeau.”
Voters at a downtown Edmonton polling station are pictured on Oct. 13. (Jack Farrell/The Canadian Press)
For Wilson, who believes in an independent Alberta, none of what’s been offered up can be seen as a win.
In his view, there’s been no offer whatsoever to address what he sees as the “structural unfairness” of how Alberta is treated within Confederation.
“None of what [Smith] is doing is addressing those core issues. I don’t know what’s happened to her. I just don’t,” he said.

Some separatists have argued that Albertans should consider Option 2 — to commence the process to hold a future binding referendum on whether Alberta should leave Canada — so as to preserve leverage in negotiations with Ottawa.

items: Alberta independence campaigners go for soft sell, even if they want a hard exit

blocks.text: Others say they’re opposed to both options on the ballot.

“What Canada needs — is a middle-ground path into the future — a set of constitutional reforms that restore the legal primacy of provincial governments for policies in health, education and social services,” wrote Ted Morton, an Ed Stelmach-era cabinet minister and one of the authors of the well-known "Alberta firewall" letter, which advocated for Alberta to exit the Canada Pension Plan, among other ideas.
Competing referendum signs line a boulevard in Calgary on Oct. 15. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)
Polling has suggested that Carney is the most popular politician in Alberta, ahead of Smith and federal Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre.

Duane Bratt, a political science professor at Calgary's Mount Royal University who has argued for the federalist side at events during the referendum campaign, said it is inevitable, as political gravity kicks in, that the prime minister won’t be able to hang onto that level of support forever.
“There’s always frictions between the federal and provincial governments,” Bratt said.
“The question is: are we going to see that same friction that we saw in the Trudeau era?”

articles.title: Rappler’s Gelo Gonzales named 2026 East-West Center Jefferson Fellow
articles.summary: The three-week fellowship will bring journalists to Honolulu, Tokyo, and Seoul to examine artificial intelligence’s impact on societies and economic security in the Asia-Pacific region

blocks.text: FELLOW. Rappler's Gelo Gonzales, senior multimedia reporter for tech, is one of the 12 fellows for the 2026 Jeffersons.
Rappler
The three-week fellowship will bring journalists to Honolulu, Tokyo, and Seoul to examine artificial intelligence’s impact on societies and economic security in the Asia-Pacific region

MANILA, Philippines – Rappler senior multimedia reporter Gelo Gonzales, who covers technology and its impact on society, is among 12 journalists selected for the East-West Center’s 2026 Jefferson Fellowships.

This year’s fellowship, themed “New Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence: Navigating AI’s Impacts on Societies and Economic Security in the Asia-Pacific Region,” will explore the opportunities and challenges posed by artificial intelligence (AI) across the region.
The program, organized by the Honolulu-based East-West Center, will run from October 25 to November 12, 2026, taking fellows to Honolulu, Tokyo, and Seoul for a three-week reporting and study tour.
The Jefferson Fellowships is the East-West Center’s flagship journalism program, aimed at enhancing public understanding of cultures, issues, and trends in the Indo-Pacific region through news media.

This year’s program will examine how AI is transforming economies and societies, from its potential to improve public administration, healthcare, manufacturing, and agriculture to its implications for employment, economic inequality, data privacy, and the environment. It will also explore concerns that developing economies could be left behind in the AI revolution due to limited connectivity, unreliable power grids, and shortages of technological skills.

During the fellowship, journalists will meet with government officials, researchers, business leaders, and civil society representatives. They will also visit healthcare facilities, laboratories, schools, AI-driven manufacturing facilities, chip makers, and farms to see firsthand how the technology is being deployed.

Gonzales served as Rappler’s technology editor from 2016 to 2025, then specialized on covering technology as a senior multimedia reporter in 2026. He also worked as a lifestyle writer and editor for FHM Philippines from 2009 to 2016.
His reporting focuses on technology and its intersections with society, including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, digital infrastructure, and technology policy.
Gonzales is one of two Filipino journalists among this year’s 12 fellows, along with Purple Romero, digital verification editor, at Agence France-Presse’s Hong Kong bureau.
Here is the full list of fellows for 2026:

items: Anusha BRADLEY, investigative reporter, Radio New Zealand, New Zealand
Ju Min (Amy) CHIEN, freelance reporter and researcher, The New York Times, Taiwan

articles.title: N.S. growers eye new apple export markets amid U.S. trade tensions
articles.summary: Nova Scotia's apple growers are finding international markets beyond the U.S., in a move to secure a better position amid trade tensions.

image.caption: Nova Scotia is seeing a bumper season for apples, according to the province's fruit growers association. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
Nova Scotia's apple growers are finding international markets beyond the U.S., in a move to secure a better position amid trade tensions.
Apple producers hope to enter Taiwan market this year while targeting Thailand next year, says association
Nova Scotia's apples are poised to reach more overseas tables this year.
The province's fruit growers association said it's taking steps toward the goal of shipping some of this season's apple harvest to Taiwan.
It marks a new move by Nova Scotian growers to diversify their global markets amid Canada-U.S. trade tensions.

The United States currently accounts for 90 per cent of Nova Scotia's apple exports, according to the Nova Scotia Fruit Growers' Association. While the sector remains untouched by direct tariffs, local growers are seizing the moment as an opportunity.
"We've built a great relationship with the consumers in certain American states and cities," said Emily Lutz, the association's executive director.
"But it is important now more than ever to have alternatives available, and just for other markets to be aware of the quality of fruit that we grow in Nova Scotia."
The move will help growers find a stronger position in case there is a future trade disruption.
Data shared by the association show the province's apple exports to the U.S. exceeded $28 million last year. It was followed by Vietnam, which imported nearly $750,000 worth of Nova Scotia apples.
Lutz said Vietnam has become Nova Scotia's second-largest apple market after a foothold was established about seven years ago.
Growers are now targeting the Taiwan market this year, while also looking to enter Thailand. Lutz said many Southeast Asian countries do not grow apples, which creates opportunities for imports.
Although those countries are closer to Australian and New Zealand producers, Nova Scotia will benefit from having the opposite harvest season.
Emily Lutz said some Southeast Asian countries do not grow apples, which creates opportunities for fruit producers like Nova Scotia. (Paul Légère/Radio-Canada)

In February, the federal government launched the Agrimarketing program, providing $75 million over five years to agriculture businesses nationwide to find new markets. Out of that, the Nova Scotia Fruit Growers' Association secured $300,000.
Lutz said the funding can support their various market development activities, such as attending international exhibitions and hiring local marketing experts.

Michael Van Meekeren, vice-president of Van Meekeren Farms Ltd. in Lakeville, N.S, said while this year's apple crop is not the largest on record, it is still a bumper season, and having access to new markets is an exciting opportunity for growers.
Van Meekeren said Nova Scotia will prioritize exporting varieties with a strong global competitive edge, such as honeycrisp and ambrosia.
He believes exports will not strain local supply, as the Atlantic region has a small population and abundant apple resources.

"We just export the ones that really shine from Nova Scotia," Van Meekeren said. "I think it is the right thing to do for Nova Scotia when we have something that is as good or better than any others in the world."
