articles.title: Mimicking populists will not ease cost of living or boost productivity, Mathias Cormann warns
articles.summary:
Former minister and OECD head urges Australia not to adopt migration caps, with research showing migrants boost employment among Australian-born workers

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australia’s mainstream political parties are being warned not to adopt populist policies such as migration caps to address voters’ grievances over the cost of living.
Instead, Australia’s longest-serving finance minister Mathias Cormann is urging politicians to deliver housing, real wage growth and lower energy costs by boosting productivity.

Now the secretary general for the influential Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Cormann will deliver an address to the Centre for Independent Studies on Saturday night spruiking productivity as the only way to reliably lower the cost of living over the long term.

Though not directly named in his address, One Nation – which largely runs on an anti-immigration platform – has surged in popularity since the 2025 federal election, with its primary vote reaching 25%, according to the latest Guardian Essential Poll, rising above the Coalition’s 22%.

While populist parties may have gained popularity by speaking to real grievances over rising energy bills, homeownership and real incomes going backwards, Cormann is expected to warn Labor and the Coalition not to follow suit.

“Mainstream parties that respond to a populist surge by adopting its economics do not recover their voters. They lose twice: once to the original, which the electorate will always prefer to the copy, and once to the centre, which has nowhere else to go,” he will say in his address.
“The lesson is consistent: deliver homes, lower energy costs, real wage growth and a credible budget, and the populist tide recedes.
“Mimic the populists, and you simply confirm that they were right all along. The way to defeat populism is to solve the problems it feeds on.”
Cormann will point to “arbitrary migration caps” imposed regardless of their effect on business, hospitals, aged care, or universities.
He will acknowledge more Australians now than any time in 20 years say the migration intake is too high and may support such policies, with many attributing their concerns to housing.
But the answer is to address housing supply, infrastructure, services and the composition of the migration intake, he will say.

According to OECD research across Australia’s regions, in places where more migrants arrived, employment among Australian-born workers grew faster, not slower, with no measurable effect on their wages.
Without migration, Australia’s working-age population would decrease as the number of older people grows.
after newsletter promotion

“An ageing country that chooses to shrink its working-age population while promising to spend more on health, care and defence has not developed a plan – it has put forward a contradiction,” Cormann will say.

Tariffs, which have been imposed by US president Donald Trump and proposed by One Nation, would also fail to address the cost of living and could instead raise costs for farmers, miners and builders, Cormann says.
He believes Australia can only grow its way out of the issue through productivity.
“There is no shortcut to a lower cost of living. There is no populist shortcut, through tariffs and caps and state banks,” he says.
“There is only the long way round: an economy that produces more, competes harder and grows faster than its costs… anyone offering you a quicker route is offering you a poorer country.”

articles.title: The uncertain future of Canada's 30 rescued belugas
articles.summary: An international rescue operation for the last 30 captive whales in Canada made headlines. Then five of them died.

blocks.text: Tofino approached each of his handlers in turn as they knelt in shallow water and stroked his sides.

Shortly after, a crane hoisted the more than 1,500kg beluga whale into a lorry to be shipped out of Canada to his new home, SeaWorld San Antonio - the last of 30 belugas and four dolphins to leave Marineland, a shuttered sea park near Niagara Falls.

Marineland needed to find a new home for its whales. But when the Canadian government rejected its plan to sell them to China over concerns about animal welfare, the park's operations said they would have to be euthanised.

That spurred an international rescue operation by several aquariums, leading to the largest ever transfer of captive whales this summer. But hopes that the animals were headed to a better life have been dampened by a number of deaths in the group.
Photographer Carlos Osorio documented the move, which involved whales being flown to Chicago, Atlanta, San Diego, San Antonio, and even Valencia, Spain.
Osorio recalls watching footage from a drone overhead as Tofino appeared to say his own goodbyes.
Tofino was the last captive whale in Canada. The country banned cetacean captivity and breeding seven years ago, and Osorio felt the weight of the moment.
"This is the last one to happen, and it's never going to happen again," he says.
Despite the rescue operation, tragically, five of the belugas have since died, as well as one dolphin.

Chicago's Shedd Aquarium has seen the most deaths. Peekachu, 23, Rain, 20, Orisis, 26, and Caspian, 27, were all transferred from Marineland, while longtime Shedd resident Beethoven, 34, also died after eight Marineland belugas were brought there over the summer.
Necropsies found chronic inflammatory disease in the gastrointestinal systems in Peekachu and Rain.
Foreign objects were also discovered in their stomachs, including feathers, large rocks and flecks that appear to be paint – objects Shedd believes were ingested before they were moved to Chicago.
Osiris's preliminary examination identified chronic liver disease.

Europe's largest aquarium, Oceanogràfic València in Spain, recorded the death of one beluga, Jelly Bean, and one dolphin, Echo. The dolphin arrived with "serious vision problems" and other health issues, it said, and "began having difficulties swallowing and respiratory problems" in the hours before she died.

Experts say it is too early to judge the outcome of the transfers, especially considering the whales were facing euthanasia and had been living in an ageing facility. According to a tally by the Canadian Press, about 20 whales died at Marineland between 2019 and September 2025.
Once the country's most popular amusement park, Marineland closed in 2024 after years of animal welfare concerns and financial woes, and following the death of its longtime owner.

Public attitudes towards keeping whales in captivity have also changed drastically since Marineland opened in 1961. Like Canada, more countries are moving to ban or restrict the practice, including France and Mexico.

Melissa Matlow, a spokeswoman for World Animal Protection Canada, says that worldwide there are about 3,600 captive cetaceans – a group of marine mammals which includes whales, dolphins and porpoises.
But there are few alternatives for whales raised in captivity without the skills to survive in the wild.
Matlow says that leaves a "growing animal welfare crisis on our hands".
Still, her organisation had concerns about the relocation of the Marineland whales.
"If an animal was not healthy enough to withstand the stress of transport, it should not have been transported," she said in a statement.
In early October, Shedd said it knew some of the Marineland belugas "could have substantial, longstanding medical needs".

Assessments before the move "informed our planning but could not reveal every underlying condition or predict how each whale would respond to the transition. The rescue offered a path to continued, specialised care".
They said the remaining rescued belugas show positive signs, including eating well.

World Animal Protection Canada had suggested two alternatives: repurpose Marineland into a hospice-style facility for the remaining captive whales and dolphins, or fast-track development of a proposed seaside sanctuary in Nova Scotia, the Whale Sanctuary Project.

As they can't be released, "the next best thing we could do is provide sanctuary for them, where they can at least live in the ocean, and they can have back their autonomy", says Lori Marino, a neuroscientist behind the Whale Sanctuary Project, which she hopes could eventually house about 12 to 15 whales.
"I look at it as an exit ramp," she adds.
The project was initiated a decade ago, she said, but construction only began in the last two months. Fundraising is continuing and needs an additional C$6m ($4.2m; £3.1m).
But offshore sanctuaries have yet to be proven a successful solution for retiring performing whales.
One offshore facility for belugas is being created in Iceland, but in July organisers determined that more work was needed, and delayed the introduction of two whales until next summer.

"They are kind of more theoretical and aspirational at this point," says Michael Weiss, research director at the Center for Whale Research in Washington state, who adds that they would definitely "improve the welfare of the animals" compared to concrete tanks.
"It's a very old idea," he says, noting that net pens have been used to rehabilitate injured wild whales, or temporarily used while re-introducing captured orcas back into the wild.

Many critics note that Canada's law banning captivity also banned the breeding of whales - but the places where they were sent do not have the same laws, and some are likely to breed them, perpetuating whale captivity.
Jason Jones, senior curator of animal well-being at Georgia Aquarium, says "breeding is a natural part of an animal's life".
"Breeding is part of good animal welfare, and so we want to make sure that they get the opportunity to do so."
Georgia Aquarium recently took in two male Marineland belugas, named Balor, 10, and Zephyr, 7. They joined the four females already in their care.
They arrived "bright, alert and responsive" and quickly began "vocalising to the females on the other side of the gate", he says.
"There was a little bit of a meeting and greeting period, but afterwards they were all kind of swimming together in a big group."

"They were exploring their new habitat, coming over and participating in sessions, eating and interacting with enrichment. So those were all really positive signs from the get-go, and we've just seen progress since then."
Phil Demers, a former Marineland handler, like many people who the BBC spoke to, said the end of Marineland is "bittersweet".

He's grateful to see the facility shut down, and hopes that Canada's ban will inspire changes in other countries. But for now, the ban won't mean the end of captivity for the Marineland whales, only a change of habitat.
He says for people curious about whales, they should join a whale-watching tour, or watch a nature documentary on TV.
"I'd rather see a whale fart in the wild than do a triple backflip in a tank," he says.

articles.title: Baligod, 4 ex-bodyguards of Zaldy Co post bail
articles.summary: Lawyer Levito Baligod and four former bodyguards of ex-lawmaker Zaldy Co posted bail and were freed on Friday after their arrest in San Juan City.

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 8:55am
Lawyer Levito Baligod and four former bodyguards of ex-Ako Bicol party-list Representative Zaldy Co posted bail and were freed on Friday after their arrest in San Juan City.
They were freed after 5 p.m., according to a report by GMA News reporter Jun Veneracion.
Ten other former bodyguards of Co meanwhile were not able to post bail in time on Friday before office hours ended.
San Juan City Police chief Police Colonel Anthony Gantang earlier said Baligod and the others were arrested at the San Juan Hall of Justice at around 9:30 a.m. Friday.
Baligod was at the Hall of Justice to attend a court hearing.
The arrest warrant was reportedly issued by the Iba, Zambales Regional Trial Court Branch 69, which set the bail at P10,000 each.
“Doon po sa warrant of arrest niya, ang nakalagay po ay, ang kaso ay unjust vexation, in relation to RA 10175. ‘Yun pong Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012,” Gantang said.
(The warrant of arrest states that the case is unjust vexation in relation to RA 10175, the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012.)

To recall, the bodyguards previously claimed that they delivered suitcases of cash to President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., Leyte Representative and former Speaker Martin Romualdez, and other individuals. Marcos, Romualdez, and others have denied the allegations.
However, in August, four of the 18 signed affidavits recanted their allegations. They said they just wanted to live quietly, adding that there are threats to their lives. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: A thousand slogans echoed here - but it could be the end for iconic Delhi protest site
articles.summary: Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century site almost synonymous with demonstrations in Delhi, has been denotified as a protest site.

blocks.text: A thousand slogans echoed here - but it could be the end for iconic Delhi protest site

blocks.caption: Image caption, The "cockroach" demonstrations over the summer of 2026 could well become the last time Jantar Mantar was home to a sustained protest movement

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The "cockroach" demonstrations over the summer of 2026 could well become the last time Jantar Mantar was home to a sustained protest movement
BySharanya Hrishikesh
BBC News, Delhi
What is the point of a protest?
To raise your voice against injustice? To draw attention to a cause? Or to make those in power uncomfortable enough to listen?
For more than three decades, Indians have tried to do all three in a narrow, tree-lined road near Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century astronomical obervatory in Delhi.
But that may now be coming to an end.
This week, Delhi Police said Jantar Mantar, located close to parliament, would no longer be a designated protest site.

The decision comes months after the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - not a political party but a collective which began as a joke - led a massive protest there demanding the resignation of federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Tens of thousands turned up and Pradhan subsequently resigned.

Police barricaded Jantar Mantar soon afterwards, preventing further demonstrations. Last week, an attempt by CJP supporters to march there, this time demanding the resignation of India's election chief, ended in a police crackdown.

Protesters have now been directed to three other sites. Two are far from parliament, while the third, the sprawling Ramlila Ground, is often booked months in advance. Unlike Jantar Mantar, which is free, all three charge tens of thousands of rupees a day.

Delhi Police says, external it acted after the Supreme Court suggested identifying alternative sites with adequate infrastructure. But critics say the move could push protests beyond the reach of ordinary Indians, further from the seat of power and into venues many cannot afford.

Over the years, Jantar Mantar has witnessed everything from mass movements that shook governments to small, lonely demonstrations by people desperate to be heard. Farmers, students, grieving parents and ex-soldiers have gathered under its trees, holding placards and shouting slogans. Not every protest made headlines, but for many, it was a place to turn to when other doors had closed.
This week, when the BBC visited, those scenes seemed a distant memory.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jantar Mantar is an 18th Century astronomical observatory in Delhi - the protests were held not in it, but in the road next to it

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Jantar Mantar is an 18th Century astronomical observatory in Delhi - the protests were held not in it, but in the road next to it
Yellow barricades blocked both ends of the road, with hundreds of paramilitary personnel standing guard, batons in hand.

In a nearby lane, uniformed men sat in shops drinking tea or scrolling through their phones. At one of the few shops without policemen, the shopkeeper folded his hands and said he did not want to answer any questions.
Built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in the 1720s, Jantar Mantar was once better known as a tourist attraction than a place where a thousand revolutions were imagined.
Its story as a protest site began in 1993, when the then-Congress government stopped allowing demonstrations at the Boat Club lawns opposite the old parliament.
Historian Harleen Kaur has traced how, from the 1960s onwards, successive governments brought in new rules that shifted the site of protest in Delhi further away from parliament.

"Jantar Mantar, situated 3km (1.86 miles) from the Parliament House, [allowed the government] to contain protesting crowds at some distance from the Parliament House and PM's residence," she wrote in a 2023 paper, external.
Yet, the road saw countless spirited protests over the years.

Rachna Dhingra, an activist with the Bhopal Group for Information and Action, an advocacy group for survivors of a 1984 gas leak disaster, camped at Jantar Mantar with hundreds of others for around five months in 2008, trying to get the government to agree to demands including setting up a commission to allocate resources for rehabilitation schemes.

Through a scorching summer, they held press conferences, met politicians and even chained themselves to railings opposite then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's residence to draw attention to their cause.

It was also where she formed solidarities with others - Tibetans protesting against China, activists opposing the displacement of people over large dam projects and even just lone protesters who caught a train from their home towns with nothing but a placard and a grievance.
"It can be lonely to protest but that place became a home for so many of us. We shared each other's stories, struggles and victories," says Dhingra.

blocks.caption: Image caption, In 2008, Rachna Dhingra and other activists camped for months at Jantar Mantar demanding justice for survivors of the deadly 1984 gas leak in Bhopal - when it rained, they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets

blocks.text: Image source, Courtesy Rachna Dhingra

In 2008, Rachna Dhingra and other activists camped for months at Jantar Mantar demanding justice for survivors of the deadly 1984 gas leak in Bhopal - when it rained, they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets

Dipa Sinha, an academic associated with the Right to Food campaign, has seen ground-breaking laws - a landmark rural jobs guarantee scheme, the National Food Safety Act and Forest Rights Act - take shape at Jantar Mantar.
"It was a place where you could discuss issues with people who came to Delhi from across the country," she says.

Protesters would demonstrate outside government offices, including the erstwhile Planning Commission and the agriculture ministry, where they were often detained by police, before returning to Jantar Mantar to "gather, discuss and strategise".
But sustaining a protest for months was not easy.
Dhingra says they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets when it rained, used public toilets near the site and went to nearby gurdwaras to freshen up.
In 2017, the National Green Tribunal cited the lack of infrastructure, along with complaints from locals, to have Jantar Mantar shut down for protests.
A year later, the Supreme Court overturned this, citing the rights to free speech and peaceful assembly guaranteed under the constitution.
When asked whether the proximity to parliament made a difference to their cause, Dhingra quoted the reactions of her co-protesters who had come to Delhi for the first time.
"That's the president's house? Does the prime minister live there? How can they not listen to us when we are at their gates?" she remembered them saying.
Sinha points out that Jantar Mantar was also near institutions like the Press Club and Constitution Club, making it easier to get media coverage, and for politicians to drop by and meet protesters.
It was a simpler time - sometimes they would ask for permission from police only on the morning of the protest.
Those rules have become much stricter, external now.
In recent years, when Dhingra tried to protest at Jantar Mantar, she was told no-one could stay the night.
"Where do you go with hundreds of people who have travelled all the way to the capital to protest?" she asks.

blocks.caption: Image caption, In 2006, Narmada Bachao Andolan (Save the Narmada river movement) leader Medha Patkar (grey sari), sat on a 20-day hunger strike at Jantar Mantar

blocks.text: In 2006, Narmada Bachao Andolan (Save the Narmada river movement) leader Medha Patkar (grey sari), sat on a 20-day hunger strike at Jantar Mantar

blocks.caption: Image caption, In 2015, retired soldiers held protests at Jantar Mantar against the delay in the implementation of a pension scheme

blocks.text: In 2015, retired soldiers held protests at Jantar Mantar against the delay in the implementation of a pension scheme
While Jantar Mantar has its supporters, others share memories of an even more vibrant protest culture.

Mary E John, a gender studies scholar who lived in Delhi both as a student and as an academic, says that before 1993, she attended protests at the Boat Club on issues ranging from workers' rights and women's issues to topics of international significance.
"We lived in a climate where protest was part of life. In fact, we took it for granted," she says.
When the spacious Boat Club lawns made way for Jantar Mantar, it actually felt "claustrophobic", she said.
She pointed out that they, and others before and after them, protested at multiple sites - universities, colleges, streets - instead of just at Jantar Mantar.
She sees signs of that in protests by farmers who camped at Delhi's borders for months, and people who sat at the Shaheen Bagh neighbourhood demanding the repeal of a controversial citizenship law.
Even the 2012 anti-rape protests, she points out, were not restricted to Jantar Mantar but almost reached the Indian president's heavily guarded complex and beyond into other parts of Delhi.
It's not clear what Jantar Mantar's future is - the Supreme Court is hearing pleas challenging its removal as a protest site.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and CJP leaders have said that Jantar Mantar belongs to the people and will be "reclaimed".
As the debate rages on, Jantar Mantar is the quietest it has been in decades - will it hear slogans again?

articles.title: Judge throws out child sex abuse charges against actor Timothy Busfield
articles.summary: The judge in the case said on Friday that the prosecutor "failed to act in a fair and impartial manner".

blocks.text: State District Judge Joseph Montano granted the defence's motion to dismiss the indictment on Friday, citing mistakes that undermined the grand jury process.

"Our office has received the order and is evaluating our options to determine how we will proceed," a spokesperson for the Office of the Second Judicial District Attorney in Bernalillo County told the BBC on Friday.
The BBC has contacted a legal representative for Busfield.
The actor surrendered to state authorities in January when a warrant was issued for his arrest. A judge later ordered his release pending trial.
Busfield had originally been taken into custody in Albuquerque on two counts of criminal sexual contact with a minor and one count of child abuse.

The indictment against him, reviewed by the BBC, said that on or between 19 October 2022 and 10 September 2023, Busfield "touched or applied force to the intimate parts" of one of the unnamed boys when he was under the age of 13.

The Thirtysomething actor's defence team submitted more than 70 letters from people vouching for his character and said that he underwent and passed a polygraph test pertaining to the allegations against him.
In a warrant for Busfield's arrest, prosecutors had said the parents of the boys alleged that he groomed and sexually abused the youngsters while working on The Cleaning Lady.

Authorities claimed the boys referred to Busfield as "Uncle Tim" and alleged that he "would tickle them on the stomach and legs". Both boys told authorities they were touched inappropriately for years, his arrest affidavit stated.
Busfield's lawyers had said the actor was being accused as an act of revenge after the children were fired from the series, which angered their mother.
The BBC's Nardine Saad contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC
articles.summary: Defence Minister Guido Crosetto tells the BBC the US risks prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to end it.

blocks.text: Italy's defence minister has said it is a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks.

In a BBC interview, Guido Crosetto warned that any such move by US President Donald Trump's administration "makes absolutely no sense" and risked prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to bring peace.

US officials have said Trump has not asked for the slowdown of internet speeds the US provides to Ukraine and which are vital for its war effort. Trump has also denied that the US has stopped sharing early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks with Ukraine.
Crosetto's comments continue Italy's sharpening criticism of the US.
Earlier this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia a "very risky choice", and said it would "grant Russia legitimacy" as it bombed cities in Ukraine.
Trump agreed the deal with Vladimir Putin, blaming Kyiv's own attacks on Russian refineries for rising fuel prices.
Meloni, once considered so close to the US president she was dubbed a "Trump whisperer", said the move ran counter to efforts to bring Putin to the negotiating table.
"Peace will come when Putin is convinced there is a stalemate, that he cannot advance any further," her defence minister told the BBC at his ministry building in Rome.
Crosetto was a co-founder of Meloni's hard-right Fratelli d'Italia party, which has led a right-wing government coalition since 2022, shortly after the start of Russia's full-scale war.
"If [Putin] sees weakness on the Ukrainian side – and if the US deprives Ukraine of resources, that creates weakness – then he will believe he can win. So he will continue the war," Crosetto warned.
"I think that is completely wrong."
Despite widespread public scepticism, Meloni's Italian government has been a strong ally of Ukraine from the start, sending both military and humanitarian aid.
The specifics of those deliveries have always been classified.

In our interview, the defence minister vowed that Italian military support would continue "for as long as this government is in place", though he warned that getting parliament to approve further deliveries would be "more difficult" as elections approached.
The vote has to take place by the end of 2027 and opinion polls currently put a new far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, ahead of all Meloni's coalition partners.

That party's leader, former general Roberto Vannacci, is openly sympathetic to Russia and opposes aiding Ukraine, arguing that Europe is wasting its money as Russia's military "continues to advance" on the ground.
At a recent event in Tuscany, he described himself as "neither pro-Putin nor pro-Russian" but "pro-Italian".
Crosetto brushed off questions about Vannacci, including on whether his views reflected those of many Italians, saying he had more "serious matters to deal with".
But, perhaps to underline the difference, he was unequivocal on Russia.

"When one state crosses another state's border with tanks, when it bombs hospitals and schools, kills civilians and bombs power plants, and has been doing so for four years, I can only describe that as evil," he said.
But Italians, like many Europeans, are seeing prices go up, driven by the high cost of energy.
During street protests in Rome on Friday, where firecrackers were thrown, secondary school students complained that resources were being diverted to arms, instead of education.
Some chanted: "We want more classroom, not more bombs."
In southern Italy, truckers have begun blocking roads complaining at the hike in fuel prices.

Polls here regularly show that a majority of Italians want an end to military aid for Ukraine. One, conducted for the Ixè institute in September, put support for continuing to supply arms at just 18%.

There are many factors behind that, from a long-standing pacifist tradition to a history of strong business ties to Moscow. Unlike Poland or the Baltic states, Italy feels physically distant from the danger, too.
But the defence minister also blamed an active campaign of disinformation by Moscow – targeting, he said, "certain political figures... and narratives to weaken the political climate against Russia".
"In some way they shift public opinion," the minister argued.

"It's very hard to explain to a citizen who's having trouble at the petrol pump that we can't give any concessions to Russia right now. But that's the only way to defend the future of that very citizen who's complaining."
Italy has not been targeted for major acts of sabotage, unlike other allies of Ukraine in Europe.
The minister said a fire at an arms depot outside Rome in August was not arson, but "human stupidity".
A report last month that Russia was planning to launch drone attacks at Italy, France and Spain from the container ships in the Mediterranean was not proven, Crosetto also told us.
But cyber-attacks, which he linked to Russia, were now routine - "there are hundreds every day" - and he believed Europe had been too weak in its response.
"You can't win a war... if you don't fight back," the minister said.
With additional reporting from Rome by Davide Ghiglione.

articles.title: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
articles.summary: The 16-year-old suspect previously attended the primary school and had targeted a special educational needs classroom, police say.

blocks.text: Police say the suspect was armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.

"To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence, and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said on Friday.

Police offered more information on the attack at at a news conference on Friday, where they identified two of the four victims. They include five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.
The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.
Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.
Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school saved lives.
He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman was not hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
He identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, who previously attended the school and was a special educational needs student there.
A search warrant has been executed at the suspect's home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said.
Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but police are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun. A motive is also not clear.
Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect.
But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action.

The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school then shoot through a window and go inside.

Police said he had a legally concealed .40 caliber in his vehicle and his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him.
In a statement to the BBC's partner CBS News, Giamanco's family said he is a "lifelong resident of Bend" and that he "is not seeking recognition".

The family said Giamanco wants to express his "gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support". He and his family "respectfully ask for privacy".
US President Donald Trump praised the bystander's actions on Friday, calling him a "great hero".
Addressing reporters at the White House before departing for Georgia, Trump said the situation could have been "much worse" with no intervention.
"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said.

Without naming the bystander, Governor Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions stopping further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well".
Kayla Epstein contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trial of German steakhouse heiress that sparked a huge spy scandal
articles.summary: For 15 months, a high-security courtroom in Hamburg has been hearing the case of Christina Block, accused of ordering the abduction of her children.

blocks.text: It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history.

Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband.
There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel.
In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage.

Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children.
There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year.

Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire.

Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark.
They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others.
The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car.
On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands.

The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-Württemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg.
Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention.
Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting.
All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation.
The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children.
Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him.
In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed.

A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back.
In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending.
He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her.
She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative.
She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that.

The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation.
Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them."
The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022.

Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case.

However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers.
Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation.
Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded".
Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months.
The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court.

articles.title: Gone to the dogs: racing fans mourn closure of ‘Wenty’, Sydney’s historic greyhound track
articles.summary:
Thousands pack Wentworth Park for the final time before the stadium is demolished and returned to parkland

  • Get our

blocks.text: The end of an era has fallen upon an Australian sporting landmark as the greyhound races at an inner-city track kicked off for the very last time.
Thousands packed into Wentworth Park in central Sydney on Friday night, where greyhound races have been held since 1932, for the last race meeting before the track’s planned demolition.
The final race of the night was the richest in the world – the Million Dollar Chase – and was won by Magical Ang.

blocks.caption: Magical Ang, winner of the Million Dollar Chase at Wentworth Park, with her handler.   Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/AAP

blocks.text: For Geoff Rose, the closure was a sign of the times – the land in the inner-west suburb of Glebe is worth a fortune in a city where growth will not slow down.
But the NSW Greyhound Breeders, Owners and Trainers Association chair remained sad to see the park go.
“It is quite heartbreaking to a lot of people,” he said.
Another spectator mourning the closure was Jeff Collerson, a veteran greyhound writer who first set foot on the track at Wentworth Park in December 1962 as a 17-year-old cadet journalist.
Now 81, he was trackside as the dogs raced around the circuit, nestled against the Sydney city skyline, for the final time and reminisced about his career.

blocks.caption: Jeff Collerson not longer wants his ashes scattered at Wentworth Park. He is pictured at the track on Friday night. Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/AAP

blocks.text: He said the closure of what locals refer to affectionately as “Wenty” was tragic.
“I remember saying to my wife years ago, I want you to cast my ashes in front of the winning post at Wentworth Park, but I told her not to do that now,” Collerson said.
“Wentworth Park’s got a special aura about it that the other tracks won’t have … it’s got a special buzz to it.
“That will be lost forever because having a city track is just fantastic.”
All buildings are slated for demolition after October 2027, and the site is planned to be returned to parkland under the auspices of Sydney’s council.
Wentworth Park was created between 1876 and 1880 using silt dredged from Sydney’s harbour. Greyhound racing began in the park in 1932, and by the 1970s, the sport was attracting large crowds.

blocks.caption: Spectators at Wentworth Park on Friday. Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/AAP

blocks.text: Greyhound Racing NSW, the state’s regulator for the sport, announced this week it had chosen the existing Richmond race club, about an hour north-west of central Sydney, as the replacement site for the industry.
Rose said his association was also exploring another option, which could see it establishing race meetings at a site near Appin, south-west of Sydney.

Either way, the state’s racing minister, David Harris, has previously promised $10m in government funding to help the industry find a new home – a move criticised by those calling for the industry to be shut down altogether.

blocks.caption: Anti-greyhound racing protesters outside the stadium. Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/AAP

blocks.text: Some have welcomed the track’s closure as a move towards the whole industry’s end.
A crowd of protesters stood outside the park as punters filed in, chanting that the sport kills dogs, and calling for an end to taxpayer dollars propping up the industry.
Aleisha Kernan and Kirsten Lambros work for Greyhounds as Pets, which helps facilitate the adoption of retired racing dogs.
Kernan said the sport’s potential new facilities would “open new avenues”.
“I think people should look at the future as well,” she said.
But for one young punter, Harry Dunlop, nothing would replace what he described as a “prominent piece of Australia”.
“It’s very unlikely that we’ll be going out to Richmond,” he said.

articles.title: Brazil: Amazon deforestation lowest in nearly 40 years
articles.summary: The latest figures show that 3,335 square kilometers of the Amazon rainforest were cleared in the year ending in July, the lowest level since 1988. The drop has been described as an "historic…

image.caption: Brazil's president said his goal is zero illegal deforestation by 2030Image: Rafael Guadeluppe/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Brazil has recorded the lowest level of deforestation in the Amazon rainforest in nearly 40 years.

According to data released by the Brazilian space research agency Inpe on Friday, between August 2025 and July 2026, 3,335 square kilometers (1,288 square miles) of forest were cleared, the lowest level witnessed since records began in 1988.
The numbers showed a nearly 42% decrease from last year's figure of 5,731 square kilometers.
The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest and one of its most biodiverse ecosystems, most of which lies in Brazil.
It also extends into parts of Peru, Colombia and other South American countries. Deforestation and the illegal exploitation of resources have been pushing it closer to a climate tipping point.

blocks.caption: The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforestImage: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

blocks.text: Drop hailed as 'historic achievement'
"It's an absolutely stratospheric drop...it's like a dream," said Environment Minister Joao Paulo Capobianco at a press conference in the capital, Brasilia.
"Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030," said President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a post on X.
"The figures released today are a historic achievement," said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima.

"They put Brazil at the forefront of the forest protection agenda and show the world that, with political will, it is possible to stop the chainsaws and curb greenhouse gas emissions," Astrini said on his organization's website.

Observatorio do Clima said the figures were the result of a "sustained commitment" to protecting the environment by the government, which introduced greater monitoring and stiffer penalties for illegal logging.
The news comes ahead of the October 25 runoff election between Lula and conservative senator Flavio Bolsonaro with the two running neck and neck according to polls.
Brazil's $125 billion plan to save the world's rainforests

articles.title: Katie Zacharia leaving her White House role less than five days on the job
articles.summary: Her public debut as White House press secretary on Tuesday ended with a flurry of media criticism about her credentials and preparedness.

blocks.text: Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, the BBC has confirmed, as the fallout from her shaky public debut appears to have reached its climax.

Speaking to reporters moments before news of her exit dropped on Friday, President Donald Trump said he had told her "you don't have to do this if you don't want to" and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider".
Zacharia faced heavy criticism for her first press briefing in the role on Tuesday, which lasted less than 15 minutes and included only three questions from reporters.
She spent the days after playing defence, answering tough questions from news outlets about her credentials and preparedness for the job.
Trump hinted at her impending exit early on Friday afternoon, during a press gaggle outside Marine One.
"I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this," Trump said.
"You don't have to be treated this badly," he continued, adding that he believed she had been treated "pretty nastily" by the media.
The BBC confirmed she was leaving the job a few hours later.

As the country draws closer to the November midterm elections, which will decide who controls the US Congress, Democrats are seizing on Zacharia's abrupt departure as a sign of failure in the Republican White House.
"The White House Press Secretary is gone. MAGA extremists continue to fall apart," the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, posted on X.

Zacharia's tumultuous week began on Tuesday, after she appeared visibly nervous during her inaugural White House press briefing that lasted 14 minutes, where she read talking points from a notebook, answered only a few questions, and referred to her husband as the president.

During the briefing, a reporter asked Zacharia - who had been called an attorney by Trump and others and who graduated from Pepperdine University's law school - about where she passed the bar exam. To practice law in the US, an attorney must be admitted to a state's bar association by passing a rigorous exam.
She replied: "When I was in China."
After intense scrutiny and digging by the press, Zacharia admitted on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam.
She did say in a statement that she had practised international transaction law in China with the "appropriate credentials".

Questions about her legal credentials became a major talking point throughout the week, with Sean Hannity from conservative-leaning Fox News lobbing particularly pointed questions at her during an interview on Thursday.
When she said she had not passed the bar, he replied: "Why didn't you just say, 'I never practiced law?'"

Zacharia also described for Hannity how quickly she had taken on the press secretary role - having been hired less than a week before her debut - prompting him to ask: "Am I hearing that you think the staff should have better prepped you?"
When she appeared on Fox & Friends, which Trump often watches, on Friday, Zacharia faced a similar line of questioning.
She told the show's hosts she did not disclose to Trump that she was not an attorney, because "those questions weren't asked", saying she was hired for a communications role, not a legal one.
Host Lawrence Jones, asked her: "Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?"
She avoided offering a direct answer but ended by saying: "I hope to be able to build the confidence and trust of everyone around me."
Zacharia's early exit is the quickest among Trump's White House press team.
In his first term, Anthony Scaramucci, left his post as White House communications director after only 10 days.
"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci wrote on X on Friday. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

articles.title: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy speaks at EU summit amid spat with Donald Trump
articles.summary: EU leaders reaffirmed support for Ukraine at the Brussels summit. But souring relations with the US over Russia and Starlink and a big hole in the budget will make for a difficult winter for Ukraine.

image.caption: Zelenskyy, seen her with EU leaders Antonio Costa (left) and Ursula von der Leyen (right), made an impassioned plea for his country at the EU summit on FridayImage: Geert Vanden Wijngaert/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was applauded by EU leaders when he appeared at this week's summit in Brussels. But getting what he needs from Europe will be tough, and a public dispute with US President Donald Trump has put him in a very difficult position.
Speaking to press at the summit, he said that "Putin wants to destroy us" and that Ukraine must prepare for a hard winter.
Experts view the upcoming cold season as a rough one for Ukraine as well.

"Ukraine is arguably entering the most difficult winter since [Russia's] full scale invasion," Olena Prokopenko, a senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, a nonpartisan think-tank, told DW.
Three painful topics were on the table at the summit for discussion between Zelenskyy and EU leaders: US relations with Russia, Starlink ― and money.
Is the US siding with Russia?

Zelenskyy's visit to Brussels comes at a time when he needs European support more than ever. That's because his relationship with the US is worsening. Worries are growing in the EU and Ukraine that the US is growing more sympathetic to Russia.
President Trump told US news channel Newsmax: "I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin."
Trump struck a deal to buy Russian diesel on October 12, which signifies a step back from sanctions placed on Russia and a blow for Ukraine.
When Zelenskyy ordered Ukrainian forces to conduct fresh strikes on Russia's oil refineries, Trump labelled the Ukrainian leader's decision as "a disgrace."
How Russia turned sanctions into a diesel deal
At the press conference at the summit on Friday, Zelenskyy told reporters that he knows that US-built missiles "are being sent to the Middle East, so it is no secret that we are not a priority."
He is asking Europe instead to supply the military power Ukraine needs to get through the winter.

Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the US has been the biggest military donor to Ukraine. But the relationship between the two countries has become more difficult since the start of Donald Trump's second term in the White House.
The Starlink slowdown

Ukraine uses Starlink, a satellite Internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The country also uses Starshield, the military-grade version, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones, though not for long-range strikes in Russia.

At the summit, Zelenskyy spoke of his "deep and unpleasant" surprise upon finding out that Ukraine was experiencing disruptions to the systems. He said this has hobbled Ukraine's ability to defend itself.
Both Elon Musk and the White House say they are not responsible for the slowdown.

The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told the press at the summit before the talks began: "Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in [the] short term Europe can't replace this capability."

Prokopenko said that this was the reason "why Ukraine's most credible medium-term solution here is to continue relying on the US. And the EU is critical in this context in terms of backing Ukraine's requests for the US administration to keep those technologies on offer" for Kyiv.

Speaking to journalists at the summit, Zelenskyy said the speed of Starlink had still not been fully restored but had improved. He said Ukraine is cooperating with various countries, including France, to search for a partial solution.
Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown?
Ukraine's budget problem
Zelenskyy urged EU leaders Friday to keep backing Kyiv financially as well, asking for nearly $80 billion (€70 billion) more next year.
"This is a realistic amount and I ask you to find this support," Zelenskyy said. "It will help us hold Russia back."
The EU gave Kyiv an approximately $100 billion (€90 billion) loan last year, making the EU Ukraine's biggest international backer. But the Ukrainian government is saying it needs more.

"The war is becoming objectively more expensive, and the Ukrainian economy is increasingly affected by the Russian strikes, leading to a drastic decline in tax and customs revenues," Prokopenko said. "So the needs will continue growing."

So will Ukraine get what it needs? Closing the summit, President of the European Council Antonio Costa said that Ukraine "remains a priority" and asked the European Commission to come up with a proposal to pull together more funds for the country in 2027.
Essentially, it looks as though the EU will try to find a way to meet Ukraine's cash demands ― though it is not yet clear how.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised the EU will "continue to lead" but urged international partners to step up as well.
Ukraine to 'keep living and fighting with dignity'
Zelenskyy will leave Brussels without concrete promises or numbers, but with renewed commitments for support from Europe.
The Ukrainian president concluded his press conference with an emotional statement: "We will keep living and fighting with dignity."

articles.title: Body of P.E.I. man recovered months after fatal accident at Alberta oilsands site
articles.summary: Kenneth Joseph MacAulay, 66, of Souris, P.E.I., was working at Suncor Energy’s Fort Hills operation on Jan. 13, 2026, when the heavy equipment he was operating sank into the muskeg. The cause of the…

image.caption: Kenny MacAulay with his wife, Pamela Grant, in a photo provided by his family. (Supplied by Sasha Bruce)

blocks.text: Edmonton

Kenneth Joseph MacAulay, 66, of Souris, P.E.I., was working at Suncor Energy’s Fort Hills operation on Jan. 13, 2026, when the heavy equipment he was operating sank into the muskeg. The cause of the accident is still being investigated by the province.
Kenneth Joseph MacAulay was recovered earlier this week by emergency workers
Emergency workers have located and recovered the body of a Prince Edward Island man who died in a January workplace accident at an oilsands mine north of Fort McMurray, Alta.

The man was working at Suncor Energy’s Fort Hills operation on Jan. 13, 2026, when the heavy equipment he was operating sank into the muskeg. The worker’s family has confirmed to CBC News that the victim was Kenneth Joseph MacAulay, 66, of Souris, P.E.I.
MacAulay's family learned on Tuesday that the body was recovered, according to a statement from the family provided to CBC. A Suncor spokesperson did not confirm when MacAulay’s body was recovered.

“Recovery has remained our top priority with continuous efforts underway since the event. These activities were technically and operationally complex, and we needed to ensure the safety of response personnel at every stage,” said Suncor spokesperson Tara Weber in an email.
“Our thoughts continue to be with the individual’s family, friends and colleagues.”

A statement to CBC News from MacAulay’s wife and two stepdaughters described MacAulay as a selfless and dedicated family man and “loyal friend,” as well as a “dearly loved and respected” volunteer with the Alcoholics Anonymous community.
The family thanked the emergency workers for their efforts, and said the recovery will help bring closure to MacAulay’s friends, family and community.
Kenny MacAulay, centre, with his stepdaughters Sasha Bruce and Deanna Chaisson. (Supplied by Sasha Bruce)

“Our hearts remain incredibly heavy as we continue to navigate the grief of losing him. But through that heartbreak, we hold onto the hope of finding some peace and closure, knowing that Kenny is finally coming home to us, to the place he loved most,” read the statement.

“While these past nine months have been nothing short of heartbreaking for our family, we recognize that this has not been easy for anyone involved, and we are deeply thankful for their dedication, compassion and perseverance.”
The cause of the accident is still being investigated by Alberta Occupational Health and Safety. No charges have been issued.

Previous workplace fatalities at Fort Hills include the 2019 death of Jonathan Murphy, who was run over by a vehicle, and the 2020 deaths of two workers in a pickup truck that came into collision with a bulldozer.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Vincent McDermott covers Fort McMurray and the Wood Buffalo region for CBC News. He was previously the editor of Fort McMurray Today, where he was part of a team that won a National Newspaper Award for coverage of the 2016 Horse River Wildfire. He is also a former contributor to the official magazine of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada. He can be reached at vincent.mcdermott@cbc.ca
With files from Jamie Malbeuf

articles.title: West Bank: US journalist injured by Israeli settlers
articles.summary: Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine said she was beaten by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank. Reporters Without Borders slammed the attack as "brazen violence."

image.caption: Veteran photojournalist Heidi Levine said she was attacked and pushed to the ground Image: Debbie Hill/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine was injured on Friday after being attacked by a group of Israeli settlers while on assignment in the occupied West Bank, according to the publication.

The Post said that the incident took place near the village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, and involved "dozens of masked Israeli settlers" who attacked Palestinian villagers gathering the autumn olive harvest.
Washington Post says Levine clearly identifiable
Matt Murray, the paper's executive editor, called for an investigation into the incident.
"This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank,” Murray said. Levine is a US citizen.

"She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist. While we are relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe, we are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities."

Speaking from a hospital bed later, veteran photojournalist Levine, who is in stable condition, said: "I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me."
Blogger Andrey Khrzhanovskiy filmed the incident and told The Post that the settlers beat Levine with sticks while journalists and villagers were forced back.
Palestinian American watches as West Bank house under siege
Netanyahu's office says facts 'remain unclear'
The office of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu issued a statement saying it was not yet clear exactly what had happened.
"The facts surrounding the confrontation near Abu Falah, during which Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was allegedly assaulted, remain unclear and are under investigation.

Netanyahu's office went on to say there were reports that "some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths." It said that there was footage of masked individuals from both sides "hurling objects."

"Other footage appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual. The investigation must establish the facts, including who initiated the violence," Netanyahu's office said.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that both the IDF and the Israel Border Police attended the scene.

"Foreign media personnel were present at the scene and a female journalist was injured during the confrontation. All details of the incident will be examined. Upon arriving to the scene, the forces acted to disperse the confrontation using riot dispersal means," the IDF said in a statement on X.
"The IDF strongly condemns this incident. Attempts to incite friction between populations undermine security in the area," the IDF said.
US condemns 'criminal violence'
The US said it condemned "criminal violence by any party" in the occupied West Bank.

"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible," the AFP news agency quoted a State Department official as saying, on condition of anonymity, without directly criticizing the settlers.
"The Department has reached out to the Washington Post to offer consular assistance," the official told AFP.

US Democratic Senator Chris Coons of Connecticut, in a post on X, called the attack "appalling" and said "there must be swift justice and accountability for perpetrators of violent extremism in the West Bank, which stands in the way of regional peace and is escalating an already unpredictable and dangerous situation."
EU to impose new sanctions against Israeli settlers
Attack condemned by press association and advocacy group
The Foreign Press Association represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories and said Levine's passport, phone, wallet and equipment were stolen by the attackers.
"This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank," it said.
"Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities," it added.

International press watchdog Reporters Without Borders strongly condemned the attack and called on Israeli authorities to "put an end to this impunity and prosecute the perpetrators of this heinous assault."

"This brazen violence... is evidence of the impunity with which extremist Jewish settlers operate, often under the protection of Israeli armed forces," added the advocacy group, known by its French initials RSF.

articles.title: What we learned from heated US midterm Senate debates
articles.summary: As the 3 November election approaches and both parties fight for control of Congress, some clear themes have emerged.

blocks.text: Republicans running for office are facing the same question they have been asked in elections since 2016: how aligned are they with President Donald Trump?
Conservatives who have bucked the president in the past have generally not fared well with voters.
The president has seen low approval ratings in recent months, with polls suggesting voters are largely concerned with the cost of living and high fuel prices.

While some Republican candidates have remained in lockstep with Trump, a Reuters analysis indicated, external that two-thirds of candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with the president in some way this election cycle.
Susan Collins, a Maine Republican running for her sixth term in the Senate who has repeatedly broken with Trump, is again putting clear distance between herself and the president.
"I voted with President Biden 91% of the time," Collins said during a debate last week.
"The fact is, this year alone, this Congress alone, I voted against President Trump 137 times," she said.

Collins is fighting a tighter Senate race than she expected against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate. A New York Times/Siena University poll from mid-September suggests Collins could be ahead in that race by 3%, while others indicate Jackson is in the lead.
There are 35 Senate seats up for grabs this November, but in 21 there are no debates scheduled among the main candidates, an ABC News analysis found.
One race's lack of debates has surprised many observers: the Texas contest between James Talarico, a Democratic state representative, and Ken Paxton, a Republican and former state attorney general.

Polls in the typically Republican state suggest that Talarico could be in reach of a surprise win. Should he succeed, he could help give Democrats control of the US Senate by flipping one of the four seats they need to create a majority.
Talarico has accepted four debate invitations from different news networks. Paxton, meanwhile, has not accepted any of those invitations.

In July, Paxton's campaign spokesperson told media outlets that he would debate Talarico. But since then, the campaign, and Paxton, have said little on the matter. Trump, who backed Paxton in the Republican primaries, has even urged the candidates to debate.

"One thing about not showing up is you lose the opportunity to make the case for yourself, and instead, what you do is you give your opponent the ability and the opportunity to make your case as negative as possible," Peter Trumbore, a political science professor at Oakland University, told the BBC's US partner CBS News last month.

articles.title: Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote looms
articles.summary:
Forest clearance lowest since records began in 1988 in success for Lula ahead of presidential run-off

Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen its lowest level since records began,…

blocks.text: Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen its lowest level since records began, new government data shows.

But whether this globally important success is maintained or reversed is on a knife edge ahead of a presidential election run-off on 25 October between two candidates with sharply different visions for the future of the rainforest and how that affects relations with the US under Donald Trump.

The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, fell behind in the first round of voting despite an impressive record in slowing the destruction of the Amazon while also reducing poverty and food insecurity. He is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro.

The Prodes satellite data series, which is considered the most accurate measure of deforestation, showed forest clearance in the Amazon fell by 41.8% over the past year to 3,335 square kilometres, the lowest value since the start of such measurements in 1988.
This beats the previous record low by 1,236 sq km, equivalent to an area the size of Rio de Janeiro.

Since the start of the Lula administration in 2022, the deforestation rate has slowed by 71.2%, according to the data collated by Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research. This was largely as a result of stronger enforcement measures and state investments in environmental agencies.

The Brazilian states with the worst records in 2026 were Pará, which registered 33.9% of all Amazon deforestation in the year, Mato Grosso (25.5%) and Amazonas (15.7%). However, even in those places the figures were down by more than 45% on the previous year. The state where the problem grew worse (up 0.4%) was Roraima, which is a Bolsonaro stronghold.

Outside the Amazon, the neighbouring biome of the Cerrado – an area of savanna – registered its lowest annual deforestation since 2001, at 5,516 sq km. This is significant as the Cerrado has long been treated as an area of environmental sacrifice, where soy and beef producers could clear more forest than they were allowed to do in the Amazon. Over the past four years, Cerrado deforestation has fallen by 48.4%.

blocks.caption: Deforestation near a forest on the border between the Amazon and the Cerrado in Mato Grosso state. Photograph: Amanda Perobelli/Reuters

blocks.text: These spectacular results, which brought some conservationists to tears, stand in sharp contrast to the 2019-23 term of Jair Bolsonaro, who oversaw a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying more than a million trees a day, through cuts to forest protection agencies, reduced implementation of penalties for environmental crimes, and verbal encouragement for illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers.
Bolsonaro was then convicted for attempting a coup but his son has vowed to release his father and let him take any position in government that he chooses.

The younger Bolsonaro has followed his father’s example in courting support from predatory landowners in the Amazon and other extractivist interests while ignoring the climate crisis in his manifesto.

The former environment minister Marina Silva, who has arguably done more than anyone to defend the rainforest, has warned that Flávio Bolsonaro will try to finish his father’s “perverse project” to destroy the Amazon.
after newsletter promotion

The stark contrast between the two candidates is evident in the electoral results map in the Amazon, where Bolsonaro secured the most votes near areas of degraded forest, mines, ranches and soy monocultures, while Lula’s support was higher in big cities or areas of forest where the vegetation was relatively intact.

It is also evident in their very different relations to the US. Lula has warned that Trump is trying to colonise the country and capture its resources. He defends the Amazon as a sovereign asset for Brazil, an important home for Indigenous peoples and an essential element in global efforts to stabilise the climate.

The Bolsonaro family, by contrast, has close ties to the US. Flavio’s brother Eduardo has lived in Texas since last year and called upon the Trump administration to impose punitive tariffs on his own country. Jair has saluted the US flag and led chants of “USA, USA”. If the family secure power, they are expected to shift Brazil’s trade priorities, particularly when it comes to critical minerals, from China and Europe to the US.

The biggest difference, however, is likely to be the far right’s willingness to exploit natural resources in the Amazon and elsewhere in Brazil and then sell them to the highest bidder, regardless of environmental and social concerns.
Conservation groups said the new deforestation data showed how much was at stake in the presidential run-off.

Marcio Astrini, the executive secretary of the Climate Observatory, said: “The figure makes it clear that putting an end to forest destruction in Brazil is entirely possible. However, everything depends on the election result. The country will decide whether we move toward the end of deforestation or toward the end of the forest.”

articles.title: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
articles.summary: Australia has proposed a switch to force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content.

blocks.text: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
Watch: Many social platforms already have following-only feeds - here's how they work
ByTiffanie Turnbull
Sydney
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder
Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.
Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.
"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.
"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."
Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Varsha Yajman says social media aggravated her eating disorder

blocks.text: Image source, Tiffanie Turnbull / BBC
Varsha Yajman says social media aggravated her eating disorder
It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.

The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.
It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.

Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier.

But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.
The choice
Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.
Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.
It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.
He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order.
"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC.

"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."
The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Flynn Martin says he's still finding a healthy balance with social media

blocks.text: Image source, Daniel Fermer / ABC News
Flynn Martin says he's still finding a healthy balance with social media
Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."
Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.

Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.
Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.
But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.

Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.
Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line.

"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Consent education campaigner Chanel Contos lobbied the government for change after founding the Teach Us Consent website in 2021

blocks.text: Image source, Cordelia Hsu / Reuters
Consent education campaigner Chanel Contos lobbied the government for change after founding the Teach Us Consent website in 2021
While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change.
"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.

Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.
More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.

The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off.
"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said.
"If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Communications Minister Anika Wells (left podium) and Australian PM Anthony Albanese (right podium) held a press conference with parents in September around the upcoming Digital Duty of Care bill

blocks.text: Image source, Hilary Wardhaugh / Getty Images
Communications Minister Anika Wells (left podium) and Australian PM Anthony Albanese (right podium) held a press conference with parents in September around the upcoming Digital Duty of Care bill

The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".
